articles.title: Prosecutors end evidence presentation vs. Marcoleta on first day of trial, says Remulla
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said that prosecutors have finished presenting their evidence against Senator Rodante Marcoleta in the plunder case lodged against him --on the first day of trial.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 11:27pm
Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said that prosecutors have finished presenting their evidence against Senator Rodante Marcoleta in the plunder case lodged against him —on the first day of trial.

In a "24 Oras" report from Raffy Tima on Friday, the prosecution was quickly able to present before the Sandiganbayan all of its evidence on the first day of Marcoleta’s trial for plunder and the violation of Presidential Decree 46.

This came only three months and three days after the case against Marcoleta was lodged on July 3. Marcoleta’s co-accused in the case are former House lawmaker Mike Defensor and businessmen Joseph Espiritu and Aristotle Viray.
Remulla said that this was the fastest that a case has been resolved in the history of the Office of the Ombudsman.

“We rested our case; we presented our evidence. Ang ibig sabihin niyan, is that, if it took us three months, two or months or three months to present our case, he would have to do the same,” Remulla said.
(We rested our case; we presented our evidence. This means that, if it took us three months, two to three months, to present our case, he would have to do the same.)

The case stemmed from Marcoleta’s own admission that he accepted P75 million from his co-accused as a campaign donation while he was still sitting as a House lawmaker. However, this was not declared in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures.

“Ang lumalabas kasi sa case ni Senator Marcoleta is actually purely a legal question. Yung nangyari, everything is admitted, so there is only one question, whether or not he committed plunder. And that’s what we presented before the court,” Remulla said.

(What is apparent from the case of Senator Marcoleta is actually purely a legal question. What happened was, everything is admitted, so there is only one question: whether or not he committed plunder. And that’s what we presented before the court.)
Remulla explained that it was Marcoleta’s own request for bail that quickened the process, as the prosecution had to lay out all the evidence already, with most of the facts being uncontested.
The Ombudsman said that Marcoleta “brought it upon himself to make us do it also if you think about it.”
The Office of the Ombudsman is hoping that the defense will also be able to present its case fast. The prosecution did not present witnesses for Marcoleta’s co-accused.

“We might be breaking records here, especially if the Sandiganbayan will really do its job, in less than one year pwedeng matapos ang isang kaso (the case could be done),” Remulla said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Judi Dench joins calls by The Archers cast to keep show in Birmingham
articles.summary:
The actor, who made a cameo in the Radio 4 drama in 1989, has signed a letter urging BBC not to move studio elsewhere

The cast and crew behind The Archers, including the one-time guest star…

blocks.text: The cast and crew behind The Archers, including the one-time guest star Judi Dench, have written to the BBC director general urging him to keep the recording of the Radio 4 drama in Birmingham.

It emerged this week that the corporation was planning to stop recording the rural community soap opera in the city for the first time in the show’s 75-year history, after it scrapped plans for a radio drama studio.

Staff were informed last week that the BBC, as part of its £500m cost-cutting drive, had ditched plans to build a bespoke studio at the Tea Factory in Digbeth, the corporation’s new Birmingham headquarters.

Production staff will still move to the Tea Factory, but the broadcaster is looking for an existing studio where the show could be recorded. The West Midlands is included in the search, but there is no guarantee The Archers will be recorded in the region.

blocks.caption: Actors rehearse an episode of The Archers in the BBC studios in Birmingham.  Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images

blocks.text: A letter to Matt Brittin, the BBC’s director general, signed by more than 100 current and previous cast members, says: “The Archers leaving the Midlands is akin to Corrie leaving the north-west, or EastEnders the south-east. It is born of the very fabric of the place, and deserves to stay at home.”

It adds: “Removing the recording of The Archers from the Midlands and divorcing the production team from the cast will have a tangible impact on the quality of the programme and represents an existential threat to its future.”

The letter, which is also signed by current and former editors, scriptwriters, sound effects workers, programme advisers and the trade unions Equity and WGGB, highlights the history and heritage of the show, which is set in the fictional village of Ambridge in the West Midlands.

blocks.caption: The Archers’ recording studio. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: “A flagship show deserves flagship facilities, from which both the BBC and the city of Birmingham would benefit for decades,” the letter says.
It ends by saying: “[We] stand in solidarity with our colleagues and the region, and to safeguard this beloved programme for generations of listeners and artists to come.”
Dench played the character Pru Forrest in a cameo for the 10,000th episode of The Archers in May 1989, meeting guest star Terry Wogan, who played himself, during the show.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: The studio’s semi-anechoic room, known as the dead room, because of the extensive soundproofing.  Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian

blocks.text: In an email to staff last week, a BBC executive said: “After careful consideration and as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, the decision has been made … to not build a new radio drama studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory in Digbeth.

“Consequently, options are being explored to identify suitable studio facilities where The Archers will be recorded. That currently includes looking into potential opportunities in the West Midlands, as well as across other parts of the UK.

“To be clear, no decision has yet been reached. The priority is to find the most cost-effective solution which will maintain The Archers’ high production standards in addition to delivering significant savings.
“The Archers is a jewel in the BBC’s crown. It’s been going for an incomparable 75 years – as has its connection with the West Midlands. It remains a hugely vital part of our future.”

A BBC spokesperson said: “We recognise and value The Archers’ longstanding relationship with the West Midlands, which remains an important part of the programme’s future and The Archers production team will remain in their current home in the Mailbox and move, as planned, to the Tea Factory in Digbeth in early 2028.

“However, after careful consideration, as part of the BBC’s wider drive to reduce costs, we are no longer building a new recording studio for The Archers in the Tea Factory. We’re currently assessing the BBC’s existing studio facilities around the UK as well as other external studio options in the West Midlands to find a more cost-effective solution, which will deliver significant savings while also maintaining The Archers’ high production standards.”

articles.title: Russell Brand was ‘wild-eyed maniac’ when trying to drag woman into toilets, court told
articles.summary:
Woman says she ‘wrenched’ herself free of assault that allegedly took place when she was working at MTV in 2001

Russell Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag a…

blocks.text: Russell Brand transformed into a “wild-eyed maniac” when he tried to drag a woman into the men’s toilets for a sexual encounter before she “wrenched” herself free, a court has heard.
The 51-year-old comedian is accused of indecently assaulting the woman who told Southwark crown court: “I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me.”
The woman, who was working for MTV at the time, said she did not report the incident at the time because she was “scared” as Brand was famous “and a big asset” to the TV channel.
Brand is facing three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999 to 2009. He denies all the charges.
Wearing a dark pinstripe suit, the TV personality sat bolt upright in the dock on Friday as the woman gave evidence from behind a screen.

She said she was working at MTV in 2001 when she met Brand and they had “banter” about an I Am Spartacus T-shirt he was wearing. She later offered to show him the way to the toilets where he allegedly assaulted her.

The woman said she felt “bewildered and confused”, telling the court: “This person went from someone jovial and friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet.”

Detailing the alleged assault, she added: “His demeanour changed. He grabbed my forearm and he was leaning into the door. It was quite forceful, the grip. It took me unawares, I wasn’t expecting that.”

In response to questions from the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, the woman said Brand allegedly began pleading with her to come into the toilets as she tried to get away. “I said to him, ‘What are you doing? Are you mad? Let me go’. Then he started to plead, almost ‘Go on, go on, come in’,” she told the court.
He allegedly had a “wild” look in his eyes and the woman had to use her strength to escape his “hard” grip in an interaction that lasted about 20 seconds.

The woman said she told two colleagues what had happened but did not make a police complaint until she saw a 2023 documentary which accused Brand of sexual misconduct. “It brought everything back,” she said. “I thought I’d managed to get away. It could’ve been very different … I thought it was the right thing to come forward.”

In cross-examination, the defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, suggested the woman had reassessed her memory of the incident after the documentary, but she said it had not changed her mind. “I don’t think it’s quite as straightforward as that,” she said. “It would have been my word against his, I had a job to consider, I emerged relatively unscathed. He didn’t manage to rape me. I managed to get myself out of the situation.”

She also rejected the barrister’s suggestion that Brand had “invited” her into the toilet for a consensual sexual encounter. “You don’t drag someone by the arm, not in my world anyway. You don’t grip someone to drag them in, that’s not consensual,” she replied.
She said he was “grabbing and pulling” her, telling the court: “That’s not inviting someone in. That’s forcing someone to do something against their will.”
Winter suggested it was “a short-lived very, very minor incident” and after the woman declined, Brand “left it there”. The woman responded: “The intent was there. It could have been very different.”

Earlier, the court heard evidence from witnesses relating to the first complainant, who gave evidence on Thursday. She alleges Brand raped her after a fringe cabaret show at the 1999 Labour party conference in Bournemouth.

Andrew Dobson, a former flatmate of Brand who composed the music for the show, described his impressions of the comedian, saying he was “a very vibrant character, very egotistical … lively, sort of quite demanding and persuading”.
Dobson told the court: “I think sex was a huge preoccupation for him. I do recall clearly nights where the pursuit of ultimately getting somebody into bed would have been a preoccupation.”

He said there was a “hurried and rushed” tone at their shared guesthouse in Bournemouth on the morning after their final show. “I recall Russell coming in and there suddenly being an urgency to leave,” he said.
John Rogers, who wrote the show, described Brand’s reaction to an “encounter” the actor had had with a woman during the week of the conference, saying it was “a bit odd” and he appeared “flustered”.
The court also heard statements from two women whom the first complainant had told about the alleged rape after the 2023 documentary.
The trial continues.

articles.title: Police search for clues to deadly shooting at Oregon elementary school
articles.summary:
Schools closed after one teacher and three children killed, and child and teacher hospitalized with critical injuries

Police are investigating a deadly shooting at an elementary school in…

blocks.text: Police are investigating a deadly shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old opened fire on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher, before being shot dead by an armed bystander.

Authorities in Oregon said that the three children killed at Silver Rail elementary school were aged five, eight and 11, and that a seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were also hospitalized with critical injuries.
Officials said on Thursday that the gunman was a 16-year-old resident of Bend and that he forced his way into the school at around 1pm by shooting at locked doors.
As of Friday morning, authorities have not named the victims, the shooter or the bystander who shot and killed him. Bend Police said that the families of the victims had all been notified.

The Bend police chief, Mike Krantz, said on Thursday that the police received an emergency call at 12.59pm on Thursday from a person “in a vehicle who reported being shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun”.
Within minutes, he said authorities received “dozens of 911 calls” reporting that a “shooter had entered the building at Silver Rail elementary school”.
He said that the school went into lockdown at 1.01pm and that at 1.02pm, the first officers arrived on scene.

“Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him.” Krantz said, adding: “our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead.

“They cleared the school to ensure there were no additional threats and then rendered emergency aid to the victims,” he said. Officers at the scene then subsequently located “five people who had succumbed to their injuries, including the suspect”.
“This is going to be a long investigation,” he said, adding that the police would maintain a large presence at the school for the next few days.
“There are not really any words I can say to any of you that will make this better,” Krantz said. “But please know that we are working hard to ensure that we conduct a thorough investigation.”
The FBI director, Kash Patel, said on Thursday that the FBI’s local office is on the scene and assisting local law enforcement with the investigation.

The Associated Press reported on Friday, citing a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting who spoke on the condition of anonymity, that the shooter used a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother.
At the news conference on Thursday, the mayor of Bend, Melanie Kebler, said: “Like so many in our community, I’m struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable.”
Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, also attended the conference.

“My heart is absolutely broken today, and our hearts will stay broken in the days and weeks ahead, and my daily prayers will be with this community, with the children, with the parents, and with the educators,” she said.
“All Oregonians mourn this loss today,” Kotek added. “This is a horrible day.”
She also praised the person who “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life”.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.

The city of Bend, home to arbout 100,000 residents, held a candlelit vigil on Thursday night. Hundreds of people gathered in gathered in Bend’s Drake Park as the sun set. Both Kotek and Kebler attended the vigil.

“There is power and love in this park tonight,” Kotek said. “On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day.”
All schools in Bend and La Pine, a neighboring city, are closed on Friday.
In a statement, Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine schools, said: “We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy.
“We extend our deepest sympathy to the families and to everyone affected by this violence,” Cook said. “No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing.”

The US education secretary, Linda McMahon, also expressed her condolences in a social media post on Thursday, saying that she was “heartbroken by the horrific shooting” and that her “prayers are with the students, faculty, their families, and the entire community”.

articles.title: Pope Leo recovering from surgery, will deliver Sunday prayer
articles.summary: The Vatican has said that Pope Leo XIV is recovering from lung surgery. Photos released on Friday showed the pontiff celebrating Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital unaided.

image.caption: Pope Leo XIV thanked staff at Gemelli Hospital in Rome for the care they provide for the frail and those suffering diseaseImage: Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: The Vatican on Friday announced that Pope Leo XIV is swiftly recovering from lung surgery and will make his first public appearance on Sunday, when he will deliver the traditional noontime Angelus Prayer.
Vatican representatives did not specify whether he would deliver the prayer at St. Peter's Square or from the hospital.
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin said Friday that a recitation from the hospital was a possibility but would depend on Leo's post-operation recovery.

Leo, who is 71, shocked the world and its 1.4 billion Catholics last Sunday by announcing that he would be undergoing surgery within days. Two day's later, on October 13, doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung after the pontiff was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Doctors are awaiting the results of Leo's biopsy, which will tell them about the make-up of the tumor and give insight into whether his cancer has spread, allowing them to determine whether he may need to undergo further treatment, such as radiation or chemotherapy.

On Friday, the Vatican said Leo was going about normal activities on his own and released photos of the pontiff saying Mass at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. He was seen wearing vestments and standing next to his personal secretary, Edgard Rimaycuna, a Peruvian priest.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo XIV celebrated Mass alongside his personal secretary, Peruvian priest Edgard RimaycunaImage: Vatican Media/AFP

blocks.text: "His post-operative recovery allows him to carry out his normal daily activities completely on his own," said a medical update signed by Dr. Luigi Carbone, Leo's personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, head of thoracic surgery at Gemelli Hospital.
The doctors said blood tests and chest x-rays had confirmed Leo's steady improvement.

"At the moment, we have not received any communication from the doctors ⁠regarding ​his discharge, other than what we ​were told from the beginning about a one-week timeframe," a Vatican spokesman ​said.

"The question now is when he will return, under what circumstances he will return, and what the doctors say. And based on all these factors, the pope will then adjust his pontificate, if it needs to be adjusted," said Cardinal Parolin, who added, "We can't make any predictions."
One of the first questions raised by Leo's hospitalization and surgery was whether he would be able to go through with a planned papal trip to South America in just a few weeks' time.

Though this remains an open question, the Vatican on Friday said planning was "going forward" regardless, releasing the names of those journalists accredited to travel with Leo to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17.

articles.title: UK police force pays out after claims it protected officers accused of abusing women
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Devon and Cornwall police formally apologise to nine women and settle claim without admitting liability

A police force alleged to have promoted and protected male officers despite…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: A police force alleged to have promoted and protected male officers despite knowing they were accused of attacking women has formally apologised and paid compensation to nine female victims, the Guardian has learned.
The women allege they were subjected to a range of abuse including rape, assault, threats, harassment and coercive control while in relationships with male officers from Devon and Cornwall police.

Some of the officers served in positions protecting women from male violence, with one appointed after allegations were made, and another kept in the sensitive position after the force received accusations.
The women allege that the force in south-west England “covered up” the serious crimes, which it denies. The force has vowed to improve how it protects women from police-perpetrated domestic abuse.
Some women suffered for about 15 years, with their tormentors allegedly weaponising the force’s “reputation” for protecting male police abusers to break their victim’s will to seek justice.

The nine women, some of whom served in Devon and Cornwall police, say their claims were mocked or disbelieved and investigations were bungled. Three of the women were arrested after accusations from their alleged abusers. One, a teacher, was cautioned, which was eventually erased from her criminal record.
One senior source who served in the leadership of the force told the Guardian: “At best it was bad investigations, at worst it was collusion with the attackers.”
The women say at least four of the officers who abused them are still serving. The force refused to answer that question. Four of the women served in the force but have now left.

One of the male officers is accused of abusing and threatening his partner, who was then a serving police officer. The woman said: “I had my baby … in my arms. My other child was screaming as he rained punches on any area of my body he could get at. He cornered me in a room and repeatedly kicked me as he stood over me. I was terrified and was begging him to stop.”

It is alleged the male officer was promoted twice after the force received the allegations, and was appointed to a leadership position in the force’s effort to tackle violence against women and girls.
Starting in 2004, the woman complained to police for more than 14 years, and she says nothing was done.
Devon and Cornwall police has agreed to pay compensation to all nine women who sued, and the chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said.
Police settled the women’s claim without admitting liability after a two-year legal battle.

blocks.caption: The Devon and Cornwall chief constable, James Vaughan, has personally apologised for the failings, the force said. Photograph: Zoe Head-Thomas/PA

blocks.text: Another of the accused male officers was known by colleagues as “Teflon” because nothing stuck to him despite repeated allegations, and known also as “rapey”, and was allegedly promoted.

His former partner Sarah* told the Guardian the officer pursued a prolonged, deliberate and sustained campaign of abusive, controlling and coercive behaviour over 15 years. It included physical abuse, financial abuse, intimidation, manipulation of childcare arrangements and repeated harassment, intended to undermine, distress and exert control.

Another woman, June*, a teacher, said of the officer with whom she had children: “Threats he’d made against me had been routinely dismissed, belittled and ignored. [He said] ‘you’ll lose your house, your job and the kids. Don’t make me angry, I’m about to load a gun.’

“I will never under any circumstances cooperate with the police again. I have lost all faith in their willingness … to protect women from police-perpetrated domestic violence. He knows he has the full protection of the police.”
Another, Freya*, said: “Absolutely it was a cover-up. The police harboured him until his retirement. I got called a liar by officers online.”

While a minority of male officers allegedly abused their female partners, other male and female officers tried to help the women but still the force failed to act, according to the combined testimony from the women.

The scandal comes after repeated promises by policing nationally to prosecute male officers who abuse women. Some of the women who received compensation and an apology say the reality was, and still is, different.

Paula Kressinger, who served in the force for 30 years and has waived her anonymity, criticised the force’s refusal to admit liability. She said: “The police are always trying to cover up their mistakes … trying to protect their reputation. However, I believe we would have more respect and trust in them if they were to … take responsibility for their failings. I know they continue to fail victims of crime.”
Sasha* said: “The police did cover up. Devon and Cornwall promoted my ex-partner … while the abuse continued. This gave a ticket to my abuser to continue his abuse post-separation.”

The inaction by the force spurred on abusers, Sasha said. “During the course of the investigation my ex-partner said everyone in the police laughed at me, and the behaviour by the investigating officers made this seem to be a true statement. The continued disrespect and disregard by Devon and Cornwall police collectively became death by a thousand cuts.
“I cannot express enough how much myself and my children have suffered over a period of 15 years, and to then be totally let down by the police …”
The Devon and Cornwall force was placed into special measures a fortnight ago because of overall poor performance. The force declined to answer a series of questions from the Guardian.

Asked what exactly the apology was for, the force replied that the chief constable met with the women in March 2026 and “apologised for the conduct of Devon and Cornwall police in its investigations of their reports of police-perpetrated domestic abuse”.

Asked whether the nine women were regarded by the force as victims of a crime, it said: “In general terms, any allegations of criminal conduct or misconduct are considered through the appropriate investigative and legal processes. These are recorded and assessed and, where appropriate, subject to criminal and/or misconduct investigation.”
The force also said: “No evidence has been identified to suggest that this was, in whole or in part, the result of a cover-up or misogyny.”
It said none of the accused male officers were any longer in positions to do with protecting women from male violence.
The legal case was brought by the Centre for Women’s Justice, a small charity.

Debaleena Dasgupta, a solicitor for the women, praised their determination and courage and said: “Litigation should never have been necessary. Each of these nine women repeatedly tried to have their reports properly investigated but instead faced errors, indifference and incompetence at every turn. Some even faced contempt.

“The similarities in the failures … indicate a broken system. And none of the safeguards one might expect to pick this up did. There have been endless reviews, inquiries and recommendations, and yet litigation remained my clients’ only option.”

The force said: “Our processes have changed. All police-perpetrated domestic abuse will now be investigated by the force’s professional standards department. We are currently in the process of creating a bespoke advocate role for victims of police-perpetrated domestic abuse and similar offences to ensure their voices are heard and that they are provided with a gold-standard service.”
* Names have been changed.

articles.title: UK risks losing key role in European space industry over satellite contract, says Airbus boss
articles.summary:
Guillaume Faury writes to Andy Burnham warning him against choosing US firm Lockheed Martin to build Skynet satellites

The boss of Airbus has told Andy Burnham that choosing US rival…

blocks.text: The boss of Airbus has told Andy Burnham that choosing US rival Lockheed Martin to manufacture military satellites could cost the UK a key role in the European space industry, intensifying a last-minute lobbying effort for the £2.4bn contract.

It is understood that Guillaume Faury, chief executive of France-headquartered Airbus, has written to the prime minister suggesting that the choice of provider of the Skynet system could have effects for decades to come on the UK’s strength in military satellites in Europe, in an effort to tip the contract away from its US rival.
Yet politicians in north-east England have lobbied in favour of the Lockheed Martin bid, which would include a new factory in Durham.
The military satellites under the Skynet 6 contract will carry the British armed forces’ most sensitive communications up to 2042, replacing the Skynet 5 system operated by Airbus.

The delayed decision on which company will manufacture the UK’s sovereign satellites comes at a sensitive moment, after Ukraine complained that its access to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network was restricted, apparently at the behest of the US government.

Several sources said they believed no final decision on the contract had been made. However, some said they believed that Lockheed Martin’s bid was preferred by the Ministry of Defence. The final decision will rest with Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey.

It is thought that Faury’s letter warned of longer-term consequences for the UK’s role in the European space sector if Airbus were to lose out. Senior industry figures have previously claimed that Airbus’s UK satellite operations would not be viable without the next Skynet contract, meaning the company might close its sites at Stevenage and Portsmouth, which employ 600 people.

The manufacturers Airbus, Thales and Leonardo are working on a long-awaited merger, known as Project Bromo, between their space subsidiaries in an effort to build a single European champion with the scale to rival the leading US companies. Faury is understood to have warned that if its British operation were no longer viable it could mean the UK missing out on the chance to be the European hub for military satellite communications once the merger was complete.

Lockheed Martin is one of the US’s largest defence “prime” contractors, but it says that its UK subsidiary will have full control over the satellites eventually built in the UK. People close to Lockheed Martin have strongly denied that the US government would have control over the satellites.

A Lockheed Martin spokesperson said the company was “unable to comment on the ongoing procurement process”, but added: “Lockheed Martin UK, a British company, will establish facilities to develop an ecosystem alongside our regional partners in the north-east of England to provide the UK with a sovereign space capability.
“It will create jobs, supply chain opportunities and the potential for exports. It will have a UK design authority and a UK chief engineer.”

Luke Akehurst, the Labour MP for North Durham, said Lockheed’s bid would mean a “state-of-the-art new manufacturing facility” in the region. “This represents a massive investment in the reindustrialisation of the north-east of England, building on our region’s proud heritage of advanced manufacturing.”
The personal intervention from Faury, one of the most powerful executives in Europe, is a sign of the importance of the contract to Airbus, which is headquartered in Toulouse.
A decision had previously been expected in the summer, but it has been delayed in part by the arrival of Burnham in office.

Unite, one of the Labour party’s biggest union backers, had warned against “handing the British space industry over to the Americans” at a time when there are increased questions over whether the UK can rely on the US government.
Burnham will also have to consider the two bids on their financial terms and the capabilities the two companies can offer.

A government document for a related system said satellites have to deal with the “proliferation of counterspace capabilities to disrupt, deny, degrade or destroy space-based enablers”. It highlighted radio jamming, hacking and direct physical attacks on the satellites as possible concerns.
The first Skynet satellite was launched in 1969 (well before the use of the name for a hostile artificial intelligence in the 1984 film The Terminator).

Kim McGuinness, the mayor for north-east England, said: “Bringing satellite manufacturing to the north east is a huge opportunity to build on what we have already achieved, including the close ties we have forged between our world-class universities and industry. If secured this investment would be a gamechanger for the space and security sector bringing £100m of investment and creating 500 high-skilled jobs as well as a much greater impact through the supply chain.”
Airbus declined to comment.

articles.title: German colonialism: Why hasn't there been a reckoning?
articles.summary: Germany's opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the genocide against the Ovaherero and Nama. But will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

image.caption: Gaob David Timotheus Frederick (left) and Mutjinde Katjiua visited Germany this week to demand recognition and restitutionImage: Christian Ditsch/epd

blocks.text: Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.
In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.

Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority: Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said, "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."

Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this, or why the German government is yet to issue an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement.

The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara, and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.

According to historian Jürgen Zimmerer of Hamburg University, the Bundestag and German government lack the will to confront this episode in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, it could happen very quickly, Zimmerer told DW.

blocks.caption: Descendants of the Ovaherero and Nama visited the Bundestag this weekImage: Tina Gerhäusser/DW

blocks.text: German government prefers reconstruction to reparation

The socialist Left Party instigated the debate in the parliament by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "Restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.

Since 2021, Windhoek and Berlin have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, the German head of state is also set to issue a formal apology.

But the Foreign Ministry also warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."
Political scientist Andreas Mehler, director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute, sees it differently. He says the government's plan sounds like "checkbook diplomacy."

According to Zimmerer, there is also a financial calculation to the implication of paying reparations: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."
German MPs rebuke far-right AfD during Namibia genocide debate
Promise in the government's coalition agreement

In the coalition agreement of the current German government, between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), there are four lines in the 144 pages that summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.

"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."

But political scientist Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg of Bayreuth University says that, compared to the efforts to address colonialism by the previous center-left German government, "the issue has lost visibility."
Zimmerer is harsher: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."

blocks.caption: Many historians argue that Germany has not done nearly enough to recognize its colonialist pastImage: KHARBINE-TAPABOR/IMAGO

blocks.text: Restitution of culture goods and human remains

Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: Tens of thousands of human remains are believed to still be in Germany. Direct descendants of the victims — such as Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick — have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.

In March, the government established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set, or how restitutions should be handled."

Foreign Ministry official Serap Güler, chair of this coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she claimed, "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security, and prosperity."
A dignified place of remembrance?

Zimmerer argues that Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes," which, he says, represents "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.

Colonialism does not appear to be included in the government's memorial policy. Even in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen, Zimmerer detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes." He notes that victim groups have not been included and that the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.

Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."

Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
articles.summary: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery
Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.
The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital.
Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said.
On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure.
His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung".
The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.
"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers

blocks.text: The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers

Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.
The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure.

articles.title: Montreal police suspend 2 officers following report officer urinated on unhoused person
articles.summary: Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours.…

image.caption: The SPVM confirmed that it has launched an internal investigation into two officers from Station 21, which covers downtown Montreal. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·Updated

Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours. One advocate said it's "hard to imagine a more degrading or violent act."
Allegations 'undermine the dignity every person deserves,' says Montreal mayor
Montreal police have confirmed the suspension of two officers assigned to a downtown station following a report that an officer urinated on a person experiencing homelessness during working hours.

In a statement to CBC News, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) confirmed that it has launched an internal investigation into two officers from Station 21, which covers downtown Montreal.
The police response comes after a report published Friday by La Presse detailing the alleged incident, which reportedly disgusted colleagues who then reported the behaviour to superiors.
The SPVM declined to provide further details on the investigation, citing privacy obligations under provincial law.

"Be assured that the SPVM takes any allegation against one of its members seriously," police said in its statement. "Regardless of the nature of an internal investigation, we are determined to get to the bottom of things and take the required actions."

items: Montreal opening 9 warming centres for unhoused people ahead of winter
Woman dies following fire at homeless encampment in Montréal-Nord

blocks.text: Another officer from the same station was also suspended in recent weeks in connection with a separate case. According to La Presse, the officer allegegedly appeared to be posing and mocking a suspect placed in a humiliating position during an arrest.
The officers have not yet formally presented a defence.
SPVM should not treat incident as isolated: advocate

Annie Savage, executive director of the advocacy group RAPSIM (Réseau d'aide aux personnes seules et itinérantes de Montréal), said she was "extremely shocked" but not surprised by the allegations, citing what she regularly hears from people living on the streets.
"It's hard to imagine a more degrading or violent act," Savage told Radio-Canada's Tout un matin.

Savage added that relations between police and unhoused residents have deteriorated as the city's homelessness crisis has deepened. She warned that police should not treat the incident as an isolated case.

Last June, RAPSIM released a joint report with legal aid organization Clinique Droits Devant that outlined tension between unhoused Montrealers and law enforcement, including Montreal police officers and special constables patrolling the city's transit network.

The study found that 40 per cent of unhoused individuals surveyed felt heavily ticketed or targeted, while 66 per cent reported rarely or never being treated like other members of the public. None of the respondents expressed high confidence in police during an emergency, with many saying they avoid calling 911 out of fear of being treated as suspects.
The report documented cases of physical and verbal abuse, unjustified searches, an increased reliance on private security guards in public spaces, and heightened surveillance across the Metro system.
The allegations come as Montreal prepares for La Nuit des sans-abri, an annual event held across Quebec to raise awareness about homelessness.
In a statement to CBC, Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the allegations are "extremely serious and undermine the dignity every person deserves."
She added: "I applaud the police officers who spoke up to report this situation. The investigation must now run its course so the full truth can come to light."
The Montreal police brotherhood, the union representing SPVM officers, said in a statement it "firmly condemns" any behaviour that violates human dignity or breaches professional standards.

items: Internal police documents describe 'radicalized' subculture at Montréal-Nord station
Montreal police allegedly cut locs from people's hair. Here's the anti-Black history behind that

blocks.text: While declining to comment on the specific allegations, the brotherhood called the reported conduct contrary to the values of Montreal police officers.
The SPVM is in the midst of another scandal involving its officers. A patrol unit at Station 39 in Montréal-Nord was disbanded last June after officers allegedly racially profiled residents.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Shingler is an investigative reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press, CTV and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. He can be reached at benjamin.shingler@cbc.ca or on Signal at @bshingler.67

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians, American journalist during West Bank olive harvest
articles.summary: Dozens of masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and injured an American journalist during olive harvesting in the occupied West Bank, according to witnesses and video footage. The Israeli…

image.caption: Videos and photos from the West Bank village of Abu Falah on Friday showed Israeli settlers using slingshots to launch stones toward Palestinians as olive trees burned. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Dozens of masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians and injured an American journalist during olive harvesting in the occupied West Bank, according to witnesses and video footage. The Israeli army says the incident "will be examined."
Israeli army says incident in Abu Falah 'will be examined'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 16, 2026 10:34 AM EDT | Last Updated: 25 minutes ago

Dozens of masked Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians and injured an American journalist during olive harvesting in the occupied West Bank, according to witnesses and video footage from the incident.
About 80 settlers descended from a hill toward Palestinians who were collecting olives on Friday in Abu Falah, a Palestinian village about 25 kilometres northeast of Ramallah, Reuters reported.
Videos from the scene showed some of the settlers using slingshots to launch stones toward the Palestinians. Photos also showed olive trees burning next to a large group of settlers.
Reuters said at least two Israeli military jeeps sped through the area partway through the attack, which continued after the army's arrival.
Israeli soldiers also fired tear gas ⁠in the direction of Palestinians who had dodged the jeeps, the news agency added. Some Palestinians threw stones to defend themselves during the attack.
An Israeli settler casts a projectile toward Palestinians in Abu Falah. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

Caught up in the attack was Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine, who was reporting in the village, the U.S. newspaper said. The Post reported she was knocked to the ground, repeatedly kicked and stripped of her cameras and phone.
Video footage showed Levine — who was wearing a helmet and vest marked "press" — lying on her side on a dirt path, with her hands over her face as at least three settlers surrounded her.
"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist," Matt Murray, the Post's executive director, said in a written statement Friday morning.

"While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."
Speaking to reporters from a Ramallah hospital bed, a visibly shaken Levine said she was "brutally attacked."
"I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and my helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be ‌here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me," she said.
Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine says Israeli settlers 'kept kicking and kicking' her during the attack in Abu Falah. (Ali Sawafta/Reuters)
'Incident will be examined,' Israeli army says
The Israeli military said in a written statement on social media that troops and Israel Border Police were dispatched to an area near Abu Falah "following a report of a violent confrontation."
"All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the army said.

It also said that at another location where confrontations were taking place, soldiers fired "toward a suspect who ran toward them, carrying a sharp object and posed a threat to them." The statement didn't provide additional information about that suspect.
"Violence against innocent civilians is a grave and intolerable phenomenon that requires a co-ordinated, multi-agency response," it said, adding that it would work "to eradicate this phenomenon."
Palestinians and an Israeli military vehicle are seen near a fire in the West Bank village of Abu Falah on Friday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Wave of settler violence
Friday's incident comes amid escalating Israeli settler violence against Palestinians across the West Bank.

Earlier this week, the United Nations humanitarian office (OCHA) said nearly 200 settler attacks linked to this year's olive harvest — an annual event that holds historical and cultural significance for Palestinians — have led to casualties or property damage so far.
"That is more than the 185 incidents recorded during the entire 2025 season," it said.

Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories are illegal under international law, which states that an occupying power cannot transfer its civilian population into the territory that it occupies.
Palestinians walk in Abu Falah after the olive harvest was disrupted by an Israeli settler attack on Friday. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)
Israel rejects that, calling the areas "disputed," and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has overseen a rapid expansion of the settlements.

In late September, Netanyahu condemned "violent riots" by settlers after a wave of attacks on Palestinians in the village of Qusra. "The handful of rioters are not representative of the law-abiding settler public," he said in a written statement.
Human rights groups have accused the Israeli government of facilitating settler violence as part of an effort to displace Palestinians.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Tesla unveils Roadster that can flip in the air and land using thrusters
articles.summary: Tesla has unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first ‌showed a next-generation version of its…

image.caption: Tesla unveils its long-delayed Roadster nearly a decade after first revealling a next-generation version of its original electric sports ​car, at a launch event near Waco, Texas, on Thursday. (Tesla/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Tesla has unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first ‌showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.
Vehicle reaches highway speeds in about 1 second, gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed deadlines

Tesla unveiled a redesigned Roadster powered with rocket-style thrusters on Thursday and said it would start production in 2028, more than a decade after it first ‌showed a next-generation version of its electric sports car.

The white two-seater vehicle, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, drove upside down on a ramp using a suction system, turned in the air and landed using built-in thrusters. Later in the event, it used the thrusters to jump over a truck and other vehicles, twisting in the air during the manoeuvre.
Some watchers saw the collaboration as Musk drumming up interest in a merger of the two big companies he controls, an idea he ​has explored by discussing their overlap.
Tesla shares were up five per cent in pre-market trading on Friday.

The reveal ​gives Tesla a showpiece car after years of missed Roadster deadlines, but it comes as the company shifts its focus to self-driving technology and robotics, and days before third-quarter results that analysts say matter more to investors.
'An engineering flex'

"It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers," Gene Munster, ​managing partner at Tesla investor Deepwater Asset Management, said on social media platform X.
"The Roadster event is the latest example of why Elon can't wait to bring [Tesla] ⁠and [SpaceX] together," Munster said.
Musk has played down ⁠the car's importance to Tesla's finances, describing it in 2023 as a "small potato situation" that would not "move ‌the needle in a major way financially."

items: Director Alex Gibney on terrifying Musk documentary: 'It's not a funeral; it's a warning'
Trolling or part of a larger plan? Why Elon Musk waded into the separatism debate

blocks.text: But the car still carries symbolic weight.

"Tesla does not currently have a halo car, or high-performance luxury vehicle designed to showcase an automaker's best engineering and technology. The Roadster will be Tesla's new halo car," Morningstar analyst Seth Goldstein said in a note last month.
Viewers and witnesses gushed over the spectacle of the launch.
"That was the most insane product demo I've ever seen," Tesla fan and investor Sawyer Merritt posted on X. "I just saw this in person, and ⁠I'm still asking how this wasn't AI."
$50K US deposit needed
Musk and other executives did not specify any target prices at Thursday's event, although Tesla nearly a decade ago quoted a base price of $200,000 US for the vehicle.

Tesla's reservation page for the Roadster after Thursday's event showed a "Performance" version of the vehicle requiring a $50,000 US deposit and a "Thrust" version with "acceleration thrusters" requiring a $250,000 US deposit. A "Rocket" variant, which Tesla says is "invite only," is described as a ‌single-seat model with a "full flight system."
The event at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, had all the elements of a classic Musk product reveal: dramatic music, smoke, mechanical hissing sounds and a launch countdown.

"This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX engineers working closely together to make something that you haven't seen in any movie," Musk, wearing a silver Western-style belt buckle emblazoned with the Tesla logo, told a cheering crowd of enthusiasts and investors.
Zero to 97 km/h in under a second
The Roadster can ​accelerate from zero to 97 km/h in less than one second and can hit a top speed of over 370 km/h, Tesla vehicle engineering chief Lars Moravy said.
"Definitely much faster than that," an excited Musk said. "I think you've got to crack ⁠halfway to the speed of sound."

The Roadster can also travel over 480 kilometres on a single charge. That is less than half of what Musk promised in 2017, when Tesla ⁠first revealled a prototype of the second-generation Roadster and said that deliveries would begin in 2020.
The Roadster, developed in collaboration with CEO Elon Musk's rocket company SpaceX, comes in for a landing at the unveilling on Thursday. (Tesla/Reuters)

The original Roadster, released in 2008 and on sale until 2012, was Tesla's first-ever electric vehicle ⁠and used a ⁠Lotus Elise chassis. It helped change the world's view of what an ​EV could be. The company has since been known for its Model Y and Model X SUVs and Model S and Model 3 sedans.
The reveal of the second-generation Roadster comes amid a sharp ​shift in Tesla's focus to artificial intelligence-led self-driving tech and ⁠robotics from manufacturing cars for human drivers.

This year, Tesla stopped selling Model S and X vehicles to make space for production of its Optimus humanoid robots. It also launched Cybercab — a two-seater robotaxi that comes without manual controls such as a steering wheel, pedals and mirrors.
Tesla is set to report third-quarter results on Oct. 21.
Sales of Tesla's aging lineup of EVs have declined over the past two years, although high gas prices helped boost deliveries in the third quarter of 2026.
"The margin and cash flow numbers will carry far more weight with investors than anything they saw at the reveal," said Josh Gilbert, lead analyst for Asia-Pacific at ⁠trading platform eToro.

articles.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
articles.summary: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.

blocks.text: Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
ByLucy Williamson
Middle East correspondentReporting fromAbu Falah
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.
The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.
"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.
Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.
"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack

blocks.text: Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attack
Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.
The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.
Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack

blocks.text: Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack
All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."
But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.
There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others
American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."
In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.
"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.
As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.
Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.
The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.
Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.
What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.

articles.title: Iran: When 'honor' becomes a death sentence for women
articles.summary: The brutal murder of a young mother has once again sparked debate in Iran over so-called honor killings, the social acceptance of violence against women, and the lack of protection for those at risk.

image.caption: According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, so-called honor killings accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provincesImage: DW

blocks.text: In the early hours of Monday, October 5, 2026, the life of Maryam Yarmohammadi came to a violent end. The 28-year-old mother of two was attacked with knives by her brother and husband on Qeshm Island in southern Iran. Her genitalia were mutilated. She died shortly afterward in hospital. Both her husband and brother were arrested.

According to media reports, around 50 relatives gathered outside the hospital to protest the arrests. They reportedly believed that death had been the "least severe punishment" Maryam Yarmohammadi deserved.

What exactly the young woman had done, and why her relatives considered her guilty, remains unknown. Yet both the circumstances of the case and the extreme violence involved follow a familiar pattern seen in so-called honor killings.

In such cases, the underlying belief is often that a man must erase a perceived "dishonor" brought upon the family by a sister, daughter, or wife. Failure to do so may expose him to rejection, humiliation or social exclusion within his community.
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival
No opportunity to defend themselves

What constitutes "honor" or "proper conduct" is often defined by family expectations or local social and cultural norms. In some traditionally conservative regions, even laughing loudly or engaging in a friendly conversation with an unrelated man may be viewed as a violation of these norms.
Women accused of such transgressions are frequently denied any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves against the allegations.

For years, women's rights activists in Iran have sought to establish nationwide support networks offering counseling and protection to women at risk. One such initiative is the Campaign to End Honor Killings.
Rezvan Moghaddam, a spokesperson for the campaign, told DW that there appeared to be no activist or local group in the region capable of supporting Maryam Yarmohammadi.
Through civil society networks, the campaign has in some cases succeeded in relocating threatened women to safe locations and securing shelter for them.

Moghaddam stressed that Maryam Yarmohammadi's death should not be interpreted as criticism of women's rights activists in those regions: "I myself come from Khuzestan in southern Iran and am fully aware of the restrictions that exist there."
Failure of the justice system

Iran's laws, based on the interpretations of Shariah, or Islamic law, do not treat women as equal citizens in many areas of life. Their ability to make decisions about education, employment or travel may depend on the consent of their fathers or, later, their husbands.
Even after a woman's death, male relatives can, under certain legal provisions, influence the course of criminal proceedings.

Iranian criminal law applies the principle of retribution in certain offenses, including murder. In homicide cases, the victim's relatives may choose either to demand retribution, which can result in the death penalty, or to pardon the perpetrator.

These provisions raise particular concerns in cases of honor killings. When an alleged perpetrator is also among the relatives empowered to influence decisions on punishment or forgiveness, a serious conflict of interest emerges.
Such situations expose the protection gaps critics say exist within Iran's justice system regarding violence against women.
Iranian Revolution: From Shah to Mullahs

According to a 2020 study by Iran's Police Academy, honor killings — defined as the murder of a woman by male relatives such as her father, brother or uncle for allegedly violating social norms of modesty and family honor — accounted for up to 45% of all murders in some traditionally conservative provinces in western and southern Iran.
In March 2025, the UN Special Rapporteur on human rights in Iran reported that at least 179 women were murdered by men within their family circles in 2024. These cases were recorded as femicides.
When violence is socially legitimized

In Maryam Yarmohammadi's case, it was above all the extraordinary brutality of the crime that shocked the public. The murder triggered a wave of grief and outrage on social media. Many women reacted strongly to what they saw as a femicide driven by hatred in the name of "honor" and "shame."

At the same time, numerous comments focused on victim-blaming, holding the victim responsible for her own death. Others described the killing as the "punishment of an unfaithful woman" or attempted to justify it by "understanding the men's anger."

Psychoanalyst Saba Alaleh argues that, for years, men have been socialized to believe they are responsible for controlling women and monitoring their behavior and decisions. Male identity, she said, is simultaneously tied to a woman's "obedience."
Violence becomes normalized when beliefs, social approval and silence reinforce one another within this structure, Alaleh explained.

"When cultural, social, political, economic, legal and educational factors are closely intertwined, they acquire enormous power. Under such conditions, women are also highly economically dependent and lack sufficient social support. Preventive mechanisms are absent as well. All of this increases the risk of violence."
Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement?
Women's struggle for self-determination

Atefeh Rangriz, a sociologist and women's rights activist, told DW: "Femicides have always existed, and their political manifestations can be traced throughout history, from forced unveiling [under Reza Shah Pahlavi in the 1930s] to the slogan 'Either the headscarf or blows to the head' in the Islamic Republic."
Rangriz believes that women understand the path toward liberation and, despite tremendous obstacles, have achieved significant progress over the past decades.

Women in Iran have been driving since 1940. They have been allowed to vote and run for political office since 1963. Women account for half of all university graduates in the country. The number of women filing for divorce or mutually ending unhappy marriages has also continued to rise.

The "Woman, Life, Freedom" movement, which emerged from the nationwide protests following the death of Jina Mahsa Amini in police custody in 2022, has further transformed public perceptions of women in Iran.

"Women have learned to focus on the present rather than postponing justice to the future. They demand it now," said Rangriz. "They want to exercise autonomy over their own bodies, live as they choose, and free themselves from the structures of domination, oppression and exploitation. It is a kind of radical revolution."
Many Iranian women no longer wear the mandatory hijab in public, openly defying the Islamic Republic's dress regulations.
Yet hardly anyone asks what the young mother Maryam Yarmohammadi wanted, or how she wished to live. She was brutally killed.
This article was originally written in German.
