articles.title: Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama
articles.summary: Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

image.caption: Student protests in the Albanian capital, Tirana, turned violent on TuesdayImage: Hameraldi Agolli/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.
She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."
University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.
Escalation after months of protests

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution," which began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.

blocks.caption: Protesters destroyed an ATM during clashes with police during an anti-government protest by students on ThursdayImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down and say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.
"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.
Rama breaks his silence
During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.

blocks.caption: A total of 152 people have been arrested over the past three days, with injuries reported among both protesters and police officersImage: Florion Goga/REUTERS

blocks.text: "These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.
Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.
The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.
The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the European Union. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.
Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"
Students against the political establishment
For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," he told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.
But the anger is not directed at Rama alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.

blocks.caption: The students are demanding that the government step down and say they are not willing to negotiate with the prime minister, Edi RamaImage: Brunilda Kazani/DW

blocks.text: "We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.
What could come after the protests?
For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.
"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.
But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.
"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."
Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.
"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

articles.title: Video shows moment Utah police dog seriously injured in leap from overpass
articles.summary:
Bomb-sniffing dog Bruno is recovering after surgery having broken several bones while responding to suspect package

Video of the moment a police dog named Bruno leapt from a freeway overpass…

blocks.text: Video of the moment a police dog named Bruno leapt from a freeway overpass and received serious injuries has been released by authorities in Utah, as the animal continues to recover at home.

Bruno, a bomb-sniffing dog, suffered two broken legs and a fractured jaw in the September incident as he helped Utah state troopers investigate a suspicious package found abandoned on the roadside in Summit county.
The Park City police department this week released dash-cam footage of the moments before, during and after Bruno’s sudden leap on to a roadway beneath a ramp connecting I-80 and US 40.
The video ends with the two-year-old chocolate labrador being airlifted by helicopter to a veterinarian in Salt Lake City for an emergency operation.
One distressing scene shows Bruno being comforted on the ground by his handling officer, Wayne Henderson, after the dog tried to get back on his feet.

“As this video shows, this was an unfortunate incident that occurred during a serious law enforcement response,” Wade Carpenter, the Park City police chief, said in a statement, reported by the Park Record.

“Bruno is more than a police K-9. He’s a partner, a companion, and part of our police family. From the moment he was injured, Officer Henderson and fellow first responders did everything they could to comfort Bruno and get him the care he needed.
“We’re grateful for the outpouring of support for Bruno and his handler as he continues to recover.”

The video includes the 911 call, and other footage related to the emergency response to Bruno’s fall. The dog is seen racing after a ball thrown by Henderson towards the object, an action described in the video as a cue for Bruno to work, then veering across the carriageway and leaping over the concrete wall.
The package, called in as suspicious by a motorist, was found to be harmless road debris, specifically a battery believed to have fallen from a vehicle.

Carpenter said Bruno was continuing to recuperate from his injuries. It is not known if he will return to work. In a statement after his surgery, the police department said: “Bruno still has a long road ahead, but we are very happy to see him home and on his way to recovery.”

articles.title: Israeli settlers attack olive farmers and Washington Post journalist in West Bank
articles.summary:
Settlers hurl rocks at Palestinians and beat photographer Heidi Levine as part of yearly attacks to disrupt harvest

Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank…

blocks.text: Israeli settlers have attacked Palestinians across the occupied West Bank in a coordinated movement to disrupt the annual olive harvest, burning cars and trees and injuring Palestinians and a Washington Post photographer.

Masked settlers wielding clubs and other weapons attacked people attempting to harvest their olives in towns across the West Bank on Friday. At least six people were injured in the town of Abu Falah near Ramallah, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

At least 80 settlers, some of whom were carrying firearms or clubs, gathered to stop Palestinians from harvesting their olives in Abu Falah, using slingshots to hurl rocks at the farmers in view of Israeli military vehicles. When some of the Palestinians then picked up rocks to defend themselves, the Israeli military fired teargas in their direction.

blocks.caption: Teargas fired by Israeli forces. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli Foreign Press Association said in a statement: “This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank. Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities.”

Among those injured was the Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, who was beaten by settlers in an attack that lasted more than 10 minutes, according to witnesses. Settlers stole her passport, phone, wallet and equipment.

“I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily, I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn’t even be here, because they just kept kicking and kicking me,” Levine said from a hospital bed in Ramallah. She said the attack ended when her Palestinian colleagues intervened to save her.
In a statement, the Washington Post said Levine had been wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist.

blocks.caption: Levine speaking to journalists in hospital after the attack. Photograph: Ali Sawafta/Reuters

blocks.text: There has been a surge of settler violence against Palestinians over the past month. Settlers have carried out at least 170 attacks since 27 September, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli rights group.
Every year, settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest their olives, but this year’s harvest has seen an uptick in violence as Israel’s elections approach at the end of October.
At least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 others have been injured over the past month, Palestinian authorities said. Thousands of trees have been damaged.

Israel imposed new rules on the olive harvest this year, barring Palestinians from harvesting their trees located in Area C – an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.

blocks.caption: Palestinians and activists collecting olives after the attack on Friday. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The new orders prohibit Palestinians from entering about 8,800 hectares (21,800 acres) of agricultural land – a 30% increase from the year prior – without approval of the Israeli military. By contrast, the military gave Israeli citizens access to more land this year.

The rights group Peace Now says the military decreased the amount of land Israeli citizens were prohibited from entering from about 1,070 hectares in 2025 to 680 hectares in 2026, for the purpose of preventing settler violence.

The olive harvest is an economic lifeline for Palestinians and has grown in importance since Israel revoked work permits for many Palestinians in the West Bank after the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023.
Photos and videos showed large swathes of agricultural land with uprooted olive trees in Kufur Malek, outside Ramallah, where Israeli bulldozers had razed trees.

Settlers rarely face accountability for their violence, even when well documented. Rights groups say settlers enjoy the protection of the Israeli military, which intervenes only if Palestinians try to defend themselves.

blocks.caption: Israeli soldiers move towards a Palestinian man lying wounded on the road after they shot him during the settler attack. Photograph: Léo Corrêa/AP

blocks.text: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has on occasion condemned the violence, which he says is due to just about 100 settlers, but he has taken few steps to stop settler violence.

Settlements have rapidly expanded across the West Bank under his rightwing government, leading to international condemnation. The UN and most countries judge settlements to be in violation of international law.
Friday’s attack in Abu Falah followed a similar attack hours earlier near the West Bank village of Turmus Ayya, where settlers burned three cars after attacking Palestinians harvesting olives.
Videos shared by the Israeli rights group B’tselem showed hundreds of bags of olives “violently” stolen by Israeli settlers from Palestinians and taken to Israeli olive presses.
Sarit Michaeli, an independent activist, said settlers were stealing Palestinians’ olive crop on a scale “never seen before in my 22-year history of working on this issue”.
A spokesperson for the US embassy in Jerusalem said it was aware of reports of the attack and declined to comment further due to privacy laws.

articles.title: Houthi attacks on strategic Saudi assets threaten Riyadh's regional leadership and economic ambitions
articles.summary: As Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis continue to target Saudi Arabia, Riyadh's vulnerability threatens its claim on regional and religious leadership — as well as its standing as an economic powerhouse.

image.caption: Ongoing Houthi attacks threaten Saudi Arabia's claim to be a regional powerhouse. Is Riyadh's economic overhaul Vision 2030 in danger? Image: Rafiq Maqbool/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen continues to escalate, Saudi Arabia's most important national priorities are increasingly at risk. On Tuesday, the Houthis hit the headquarters of Aramco, the Saudi state-owned oil company in Dhahran. On Wednesday, the Houthis vowed to continue attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, and on Thursday a cruise missile was intercepted over the Medina region. While it remains unclear who launched it, the mere attempt raises questions about Saudi Arabia's role as guardian of Islam's holiest places, the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina.

Following last weekend's Houthi attacks that killed more than a dozen people and injured more than 300 at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, tourists and potential investors are keenly aware of the growing uncertainty over travel and security in the kingdom.

Several airlines suspended flights to Riyadh and the airport was expected to remain closed through at least October 17, according to media reports published earlier this week. Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative, an economic summit that usually draws foreign leaders and key players in business to the country, plans to offer remote participation instead of hosting attendees on site.

"The hostilities between the Houthis and the Saudi government challenge Riyadh's image of stability and security amid the wider US-Iran war," said Timothy E. Kaldas, deputy director of the Washington-based think tank Tahrir Institute for Middle East Policy.

"The attacks on Saudi Arabia also threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify the economy," Kaldas told DW, noting that these ambitions depend on potential tourists viewing the kingdom as a safe destination.

Since the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran in February, Tehran, and later the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, have been targeting Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States. Saudi Arabia also supports the Yemeni government in its fight against the Houthis with airstrikes in Houthi-held areas of Yemen.

blocks.caption: The Houthis targeted the headquarters of the Saudi Arabian oil company Aramco in Dhahran, after also successfully attacking the international airport in Riyadh this weekImage: AFP

blocks.text: Houthi attacks are a blow to Saudi Arabia's ambitions
A decade ago, Saudi Arabia launched Vision 2030, a sweeping economic and social reform plan, to reduce the kingdom's reliance on oil and transform its economy and society.

"Saudi Arabia is pursuing a highly nationalist 'Saudi-First' policy, aimed at propelling the nation to the global forefront as an aviation power, a hub for artificial intelligence and a major tourism destination," Simon Wolfgang Fuchs, a professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told DW.
Fuchs views the Houthi attacks as a significant blow to these ambitions and the financial resources available to pursue them.

Pauline Raabe, a senior analyst at the Berlin-based Middle East Minds think tank, points out that Saudi Arabia urgently needs to find a solution that shields its population from the conflict while limiting the economic damage and reputational costs.

"It is a race against time," she told DW, even though the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis is no new occurence. Saudi Arabia supported the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis between 2015 and 2022.
"The conflict has been flaring up again with renewed intensity due to the general situation in the Gulf and is as such actually a tightening of the status quo," Raabe said.
However, she views Saudi Arabia's loss of authority as a threat on the horizon. "In the short term, Saudi Arabia is a belligerent [player] in a region ravaged by conflict," she said.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia failed to secure US assistance in the fight against the Houthis, but regional states voiced firm supportImage: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Symbolic support from partners like Turkey, Pakistan, Egypt
Fuchs agrees.

"Riyadh remains a key player through its investments, its position as the world's largest oil exporter and its role as custodian of Islam's holy sites in Mecca and Medina," he said, adding that "by virtue of this role, Saudi Arabia can count on allies and call for the formation of alliances."

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement. While the latter two have since offered intelligence and defense support for Saudi Arabia, they also made clear that they will not put boots on the ground in Yemen. France and the United Kingdom also offered limited defense support for Riyadh. Egypt, the most populous Arab country with a Sunni majority like Saudi Arabia, voiced verbal support.
"Riyadh is prioritizing the symbolic value of these countries, projecting an image of strong ties with regional powers," Kaldas said.

However, much attention has focused on Saudi Arabia's failure to secure defense support from the United States, he added. While Saudi Arabia's closest ally — the US signaled willingness to support Riyadh with intelligence sharing and targeting assistance against the Houthis — Washington has so far stopped short of committing US forces to direct strikes. For Saudi Arabia, the understanding is therefore that the US prioritzes avoiding opening another front in the regional conflict against Iran.

articles.title: Nova Scotia to host massive data centre to power artificial intelligence
articles.summary: A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under construction just outside a town on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia.

image.caption: Nova Scotia announced on Friday morning that a data centre to power artificial intelligence is under construction in Cape Breton. (Taryn Grant/CBC)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New
A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under construction just outside a town on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia.
EverWind Fuels will own it, an unnamed AI company will lease it
A massive data centre to provide computing power for artificial intelligence is under construction just outside Port Hawkesbury in Cape Breton.
EverWind Fuels said it will build the facility in two stages, with the first phase to come online by the end of 2027 and the second in 2028.
The company, headed by Australian-American private equity veteran Trent Vichie, had previously confirmed it has data centre ambitions, but said little else.
On Friday, EverWind released more information about its plans.
The company is building the facility and has signed an agreement with an as-yet unnamed AI company to lease the first phase for a term of at least 20 years.
The first phase would have a capacity of 95 megawatts and the second, 325 megawatts, for a total of 420 megawatts. Nova Scotia’s current electrical generating capacity is close to 3,000 megawatts.
EverWind raising $8 billion for project
EverWind said it will pay for any required upgrades to Nova Scotia’s electricity system.

“Nova Scotians should expect us to demonstrate that we can protect ratepayers, safeguard local resources and deliver lasting community benefits, and we intend to be accountable for those commitments,” Vichie said in a news release.
EverWind said it is raising $8 billion in private capital to fund the project and an additional $2 billion for four of the onshore wind farms it is planning to build.

It said those wind farms would eventually support the data centre’s electricity needs, but existing generation on the provincial grid would be the primary supply to begin. Company officials said the provincial grid operator has done a system-impact study that indicates the grid can support the first phase.
EverWind's data centre will be in Point Tupper, just outside Port Hawkesbury. (Tom Ayers/CBC)
EverWind has been trying to develop renewable energy projects in Nova Scotia for several years. It says those plans remain unchanged.
The data centre is to be built at the same site as one of EverWind’s other proposed projects — a green hydrogen and ammonia facility — in the industrial park at Point Tupper, Cape Breton.
Data centre controversies

Data centres have become a flashpoint across Canada, especially those that power AI, because they can have huge footprints and require vast amounts of energy and water for cooling. Concerns about AI’s potential impacts on jobs and dire warnings about risks to human existence also have some people pushing back.

There are some proposed data centres that would dwarf this one in size, including the Wonder Valley data centre in Alberta — the first phase of which is meant to be more than a gigawatt — but this project is still on the larger end of facilities that have been recently announced in Canada.
EverWind said it has signed on to Ottawa’s responsible data centre development principles — a set of non-binding guidelines the federal government released last month.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston recently laid out similar guidelines. Both levels of government say they expect any data centre to have local benefits, minimal environmental impact and minimal water use, and for there to be no resulting power rate spikes.

“We applaud the federal and provincial governments for setting high standards for responsible development,” Vichie said in the release. “And we will continue to work with communities to ensure that our work meets their expectations.”
Community benefit program

EverWind said it will use a closed-loop water-glycol system. The company’s preliminary estimate for water usage is an average of 100,000 litres per day for the first phase and 500,000 litres of water per day including both phases.

Water would be drawn from nearby Landrie Lake. The provincial regulator has approved the Landrie Lake Water Utility to withdraw 34 million litres from the lake each day, which would make EverWind’s daily requirements about one per cent of the total safe withdrawal volume.

The company promised the data centre would come with a community benefit program worth tens of millions of dollars. A specific dollar figure was not provided. Local communities and the data centre’s unnamed customer would consult on how to spend the money.
A consortium of Mi’kmaw communities, fronted by Membertou First Nation, is negotiating a nine per cent equity stake in the project.

articles.title: House leader pushes investigation into Cale88 linked to VP Sara's spouse
articles.summary: House Deputy Speaker Jefferson Khonghun is pushing for a motu proprio investigation by the House of Representatives into the alleged remittance of hundreds of millions of pesos into Cale88, a company…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 9:41pm

House Deputy Speaker Jefferson Khonghun is pushing for a motu proprio investigation by the House of Representatives into the alleged remittance of hundreds of millions of pesos into Cale88, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

"Definitely kailangan ’yang imbestigahan, kailangan ’yang tingnan dahil importante na makita iyong involvement ng China, lalong-lalo na doon sa mga kumpanya na pag-aari ng ating bise presidente. Dahil katulad nga ng sinabi ng Department of (National) Defense, it is a national security risk na kailangan tignan," Khonghun said in an online interview today.
"Gusto nga naming i-motu proprio investigation na lang yan. Para kahit na walang resolusyon na ifa-file, makakapag-investigate ang House," he added.
When asked when the investigation will be conducted, Khonghun replied, "Sana magsimula na during recess para at least nalalaman na natin kung ano yung totoo."
Congress is currently on recess until November 8.
Among the House committees that may be involved in the investigation are the Committee on National Defense and the Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability.

When asked if Vice President Duterte will be invited to the hearings, Khonghun replied, "Well, it's up to the committee handling the investigation if they will invite the Vice President. Ang problema kasi, kahit imbitahan mo naman ang bise presidente, hindi naman nagpupunta. Hindi nagpunta sa impeachment, hindi nagpunta sa committee hearing. Napakagaling umiwas ng ating bise presidente. So if ever na magkaroon ng hearing, hindi natin ine-expect na pupunta siya."
Khonghun also said it is up to the committees if Carpio and former senator Antonio Trillanes IV will also be invited.
House Impeachment Prosecutor and Manila 3rd District Rep. Joel Chua, who chairs the House Committee on Good Government and Public Accountability, supports the investigation.

"Yes, dahil siyempre, gusto rin natin malaman kung bakit pumasok yung ganoong kalaki galing sa mga offshore accounts. Hindi lang naman ito tungkol sa isang bansa. Dahil kung nakikita po natin yung account, maraming bansa ang pinanggalingan ng mga account," Chua said in a separate online interview today.
In case the investigation is covered by the sub judice rule of the Senate impeachment court, Chua said he will assign one of his vice chairs to conduct the hearings. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: California brush fires force evacuations and tens of thousands of power shutoffs
articles.summary:
Hot, windy weather stokes fires in southern California as utilities shut off power to 150,000 customers as precaution

Several brush fires stoked by hot, windy weather forced evacuations in…

blocks.text: Several brush fires stoked by hot, windy weather forced evacuations in southern California, and tens of thousands of people woke up in the dark after their electricity was turned off.

A rapidly spreading blaze in Malibu, west of Los Angeles, prompted evacuation orders and warnings for a large swathe of the Santa Monica Mountains. Firefighters also worked to contain fires in the city of Azusa, north of LA, and Camp Pendleton, the large military base north of San Diego.

In the Santa Monica mountains, more than 285 firefighters battled the Bryson fire overnight, which grew to about 200 acres (81 hectares) and threatened a Los Angeles county juvenile detention and rehabilitative facility. Fire officials planned to give an update Friday morning.

A large cloud of black smoke over the hilltops could be seen on nearby cameras and miles away. Wind gusts of up to 30mph (48km/h) were reported early Friday and were forecast to increase, the National Weather Service said.
With humidity levels dropping, “this will favor a critical fire weather threat,” the service said.

The wind-driven fire in Azusa burned more than 40 acres (16 hectares) on Thursday and briefly prompted evacuation orders for a neighborhood in the foothills of the San Gabriel mountains. Forward progress on that blaze has been stopped.
At Camp Pendleton, evacuation orders were issued in the Las Flores area of the military base on Thursday afternoon, but lifted by evening, military officials said in a statement.
California is facing several days of extreme fire-risk weather, with dry conditions, high temperatures and gusty winds intensifying the risk that a fire quickly gets under control.

Dry, warm and gusty north-east winds known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior of southern California toward the coast and offshore, were forecast in the south of the state, with the strongest winds expected through Friday afternoon.
“It’s a pretty widespread event of elevated fire weather, so the whole SoCal region should really be on alert,” said Rose Schoenfeld, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service.
Because some of the state’s worst wildfires in recent years have been sparked by power equipment, utilities proactively shut off power to more than 150,000 customers across the state.

In Los Angeles, the city’s mayor, Karen Bass, who faced criticism for her city’s response to deadly fires in 2025, directed the fire department to deploy personnel and equipment ahead of the winds. The fire department also requested assistance from the state’s office of emergency services.
In January 2025, fires in the Palisades and Altadena neighborhoods, which were fanned by Santa Ana winds, killed more than 30 people and destroyed thousands of homes.
Schoenfeld said the Santa Ana winds are not going to be as strong as during those fires, when they were gusting 60mph to 100mph (96km/h to 160km/h).

articles.title: At summit, EU leaders pledge support for Ukraine's Zelenskyy
articles.summary: President Zelenskyy has received words of encouragement from EU leaders, who pledged support for Ukraine's self-defense against Russia. This comes as winter approaches and the US seems to be…

image.caption: Zelenskyy thanked European leaders for their support in Brussels, saying Ukraine wants to end the war on its country but needs to survive the winterImage: Geert Vanden Wijngaert/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy attended the final day of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, where leaders from across the bloc pledged continued support for the Ukrainian leader and his country in a turbulent week.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa both took the fore in calling on allies to continue their support of Kyiv as it faces increased Russian attacks and detrimental US foreign policy decisions.
Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again?
What did EU leaders say about the bloc's support for Ukraine?

"This is no time to withdraw support to Ukraine," said Costa as he stood next to the Ukrainian president. "This is no time to relieve Russia's sanctions. Now it is time to increase our support, to increase our pressure."
"One ​thing is absolutely clear," pledged von der Leyen, "we will ​not lift any sanctions unless Russia ⁠stops ​this ​war."

The EU leaders' remarks come just one week after Ukraine and its European allies were blindsided by US President Donald Trump's unilateral decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports and purchase diesel from the Kremlin after a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

On Wednesday, a US official said Washington was also considering easing sanctions on Russia's shadow fleet — unflagged tankers that turn off transponders to transport and transfer illicit oil while circumventing international export sanctions.

After undermining years of Western sanctions against Russia over its illegal invasion of Ukraine, Trump is now seeking to increase pressure on Ukraine — calling for Zelenskyy to be replaced as its leader and blasting Kyiv's targeting of Russian energy infrastructure as a "disgrace."
Diesel deal between Trump, Putin angers Ukraine
Trump seeks to deflect blame for high energy prices onto Ukraine

Upon arrival at Friday's Brussels summit, Zelenskyy said, "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that ​they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter."
"The winter package is not only energy, ​it's also air defense and funding," he added.
During his speech at the summit, Zelenskyy asked European Union leaders to provide an additional €70 billion ($79 billion) in funding to Kyiv next year to help it continue fighting Russia.

"The war will cost €155 billion next year. And we need at least €70 billion euros more from you — for defense, for weapons, and for our resilience. This is a realistic amount. And I ask you to find this support," the Ukrainian president said.

When asked after his meeting with EU leaders if Trump was scapegoating him for troubles in the US, Zelensky gave a knowing smile and stayed mum. "This is my answer," the Ukrainian president said, as journalists broke into laughter at a press conference in Brussels.

Trump last week justified his calls for Zelenskyy to be removed from office by claiming the Ukrainian leader did not want to stop the war — which Russia launched on February 24, 2022 — as well as attempting to divert anger over high global fuel prices away from his own war in Iran, which triggered the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and sent global oil and gas prices through the roof.

"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher," Trump told far-right US media outlet Newsmax on Thursday. Asked about Ukraine resuming attacks on Russian energy infrastructure, Trump said, "Well, I think that's a disgrace."

Earlier this week, Kyiv reported restrictions on its use of Elon Musk's Starshield system, Starlink's military-grade satellite service which Ukraine relies on for its battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territories and interceptor drones.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Zelenskyy hails 'very good' meeting with Hungary PM
The Ukrainian president also praised his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar on the sidelines of the summit.

"We had a very good meeting," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels. He added that he and Magyar had discussed "many things, including relations, the economy, and logistics — all of which are important to our two countries."
Zelenskyy also said that he "won't mind" visiting Budapest.
After meeting, Magyar announced that Budapest and Kyiv had agreed to put their relations on a new footing.

"I ​assured the Ukrainian president of my full solidarity over the inhuman Russian aggression against his ​country," Magyar wrote in a Facebook post. He also said that Hungary was ready to assist Ukraine by all possible diplomatic means to reach a ceasefire and lasting peace.
The meeting occurred just days after Kyiv passed legislation addressing Budapest's long-standing concerns regarding the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine.

articles.title: The EU wants an AI revolution. But on whose terms?
articles.summary: As the US and China race ahead, the European Union seeks to boost its economy with AI. Can it compete while protecting workers, safety and the climate?

image.caption: Microsoft's vice chair and president, Brad Smith, addresses delegatesImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: Step-dancers spun across the circular stage in the middle of a dark hall, entrancing an audience of policymakers and tech bosses. Not simply another bureaucratic conference, the International AI Summit, hosted in Dublin this week, aspired to something more spectacular — a grand announcement that Europe is ready for its artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

Among the more than 1,500 expected guests were Google DeepMind co-founder and chair Demis Hassabis and Microsoft president Brad Smith, in addition to high-ranking European Union and Irish officials. The event was a key part of Ireland's term as president of the EU Council, but a lack of critical voices to counterbalance the AI enthusiasm on display has drawn accusations of tech boosterism.
The summit was "almost like a party political broadcast on behalf of AI," Barry O'Sullivan, an AI professor at University College Cork, told DW.

blocks.caption: Prime Minister of Ireland Micheal Martin and Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence Niamh Smyth were also present at the summitImage: Cillian Sherlock/PA/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: AI to help Europe's competitiveness
The overarching theme was how to use AI to get Europe's sluggish economy moving, boost innovation and catch up with the US and China.

On panels packed with senior executives, the potential benefits were made clear: detecting early signs of cancer, improving warnings of extreme weather, and optimising power distribution to save energy. Turning those promises into reliable services, however, still requires testing and validation.

Ireland's interest in these issues doesn't come purely from goodwill towards its fellow EU member states. The country hosts the European operations of several of the world's largest technology companies, and relies heavily on the taxation of multinational firms. Foreign-owned multinationals paid €28.8 billion in corporation tax in 2025, accounting for 87% of the total, excluding exceptional Apple tax proceeds. That includes pharmaceuticals and other sectors, not just technology.

This means Dublin has a clear interest in shaping European rules while keeping investors on board. But Europe's financial firepower remains far behind America's: Private AI investment reached $286 billion (about €253 billion) in the US in 2025, compared with $21 billion (€18.6 billion) in Europe, according to Stanford University's AI Index.

But does Europe even need to compete on the same terms? O'Sullivan thinks it should focus on its own strengths, including industrial robotics and specialised applications: "We have a unique kind of AI opportunity in Europe, and that's what we should back."

Using foreign models could help European businesses move faster. But it also leaves them dependent on suppliers elsewhere, which can change prices, restrict access and decide which capabilities to release.

blocks.caption: Michael McGrath speaks to reporters at the AI Summit in Dublin, where he underlines the EU's approach between control and innovationImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: EU rules under pressure
EU representatives at the summit were quick to underline that rules were now in place to reap AI's benefits while mitigating its risks.

Michael McGrath, the Irish commissioner responsible for democracy, justice, the rule of law and consumer protection, spoke of a balance between AI's potential and the "appropriate guardrails" required to ensure trust.

The AI Act bans certain practices and imposes stronger requirements on sensitive uses. Its Omnibus amendments, in force since July 2026, aim to simplify compliance, though have als delyed some safeguards. Rules covering areas including employment and education now apply from December 2027; those for AI embedded in regulated products from August 2028.
The Commission has said that companies need time to adjust to new standards and guidance. Critics, however, believe protections being delayed under pressure to compete.
For O'Sullivan, regulation and innovation are not contradictory. "The idea that you can't have regulation and innovation is just a nonsense," he said, pointing to pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

blocks.caption: Paul Murphy from 'People over Profits' sees major drawbacks to AI developmentImage: Tessa Walther/DW

blocks.text: Demonstrations outside the venue

For protesters outside, assurances made by politicians and tech firms ring hollow. Paul Murphy, an Irish lawmaker from the socialist People Before Profit party, argued that even though Europe's regulations are strong than those in the US, the bar remains low. With the latest amendments, he sees a move towards deregulation.
"Big tech is setting the pace and everybody's expected to just get on board," he told DW.
Instead, he wants civil society, trade unions and politicians to discuss how the technology should develop and how limited resources like water and electricity should be used.

Inside, union representative Fionnuala Ní Bhrógáin, one of the few critical voices on stage, questioned who would benefit from higher productivity. Optimization, she said, can put higher pressure on workers.

Murphy, too, fears an increased pressure to work faster, with less autonomy and more supervision. Whether an hour saved on emails becomes time to think, or leads to more assignments, depends on employers' decisions and workers' bargaining power.
O'Sullivan, on the other hand, said that AI removing mundane tasks gives employees "more time to think, and to be more creative in their jobs."

blocks.caption: Google was one of the main tech representatives at the AI SummitImage: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: A heavy environmental toll

In Ireland, the question of resources is particularly pressing. Data centres used 23% of the country's metered electricity in 2025. That includes cloud storage and other services, not just AI. Murphy argued that their expansion raises household bills and undermines climate goals.
Renewable energy could help meet demand. But additional clean electricity must also replace fossil fuels, while housing and other industries need grid capacity too.
"The sustainability of AI is a huge problem," O'Sullivan agreed, calling for the sector to reduce its overall energy footprint.

blocks.caption: Participants were able to try out AI's newest features, like cyber-cycling through major world cities on a bike.Image: Paul Faith/AFP

blocks.text: The future of AI

Back inside the hall, even industry leaders acknowledged the need for boundaries. Hassabis, the chief scientist of Alphabet, called recent AI hacking incidents "early warning shots" and advocated international oversight. Microsoft president Smith said: "We need law. We need regulation."

Their warnings follow concrete failures. During cybersecurity evaluations in July, OpenAI models bypassed isolation controls, hacked the infrastructure surrounding the test, broke containment, and attacked a real company, Hugging Face, which hosts AI models and datasets. Had similar behavior occurred inside a hospital, power grid, or other critical system, the results could have been much worse. Anthropic separately disclosed unintended actions by its AI on real websites, including a ​false homicide tip to the Philadelphia police, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.

Speakers on and off the stage agreed: The incidents show just how difficult it can be to keep increasingly autonomous systems under control. Developers' assurances alone cannot guarantee safety. Nor can regulation eliminate every risk. But for O'Sullivan and Murphy, it remains essential.

Europe wants to shape AI without compromising on the benefits its promises.This balancing act is a difficult one, involving choices about investment, resources and the distribution of gains. Even a spectacular opening performance cannot dance around those questions.

blocks.text: A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country.
The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday.
Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other".
Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented.
Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country.
Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province.
This is where some of those found at this facility come from, the department said in a statement on Friday.

articles.title: Ombudsman Remulla sees charges filed vs. Legarda, Leviste soon
articles.summary: Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said the filing of criminal cases against Senator Loren Legarda and Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste over an undelivered power supply by Leviste"s solar firm are…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 8:59pm

Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said the filing of criminal cases against Senator Loren Legarda and Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste over an undelivered power supply by Leviste’s solar firm are forthcoming.
Remulla, however, won't commit to a timeline.
“Malapit-lapit na ‘yan. Mapit-lapit,” Remulla said in a press conference.
(It is coming quite soon. Quite soon.)
“I won’t give a timeframe. I'll go back down here when we have to file the case already,” he added.
Remulla stressed that the criminal cases against Legarda and son are merit-based when asked if this move is political persecution.
“Malayo yata ‘yun. You all saw the conflict of interest angle here. Hindi naman namin iniimbento ‘yun eh. Wala kaming iniimbento diyan,” Remulla said.
(This is far from political persecution. We are not inventing things here. We did not invent anything.)
“'Yung mga pagbebenta niyan, kumpanya, pag-flip ng franchise, pa-flip ng lahat. Hindi naman namin iniimbento ‘yun eh. We will present reports,” Remulla said.
(Leviste suddenly his company after getting the franchise...we did not invent those. We will present reports.)
Remulla said that Legarda and her son’s extended stay abroad is not helping their cause.

“Nung umpisa, we had an inkling na gusto niyo pa umuwi. But later on, from the accounts of a lot of people who we mutually know, parang ayaw niya na umuwi. So ang tingin ko, ayaw niya na umuwi. Tinatakasan nila,” Remulla said.
(Initially she has plans to go home but later on, I've learned from people who mutually know that she does not want to go home anymore. They are escaping accountability.)

“Ayaw nilang humarap sa charges. Kasi kung talagang wala kang kasalanan, humarap ka. Remember, in criminal law, flight is an indication of guilt. And if she wants a presumption to hold so be it. But it doesn't mean that they can hide forever,” Remulla said.
(They don't want to face the charges. If you are innocent, then face the charges.) —NB, GMA News

articles.title: More than half of 45,000 schools lack principals as most fail qualifying exam -- DepEd
articles.summary: An estimated 23,000 schools do not have principals as most applicants fail the qualifying examination, the Department of Education (DepEd) said Friday during its budget hearing before the Senate…

blocks.text: An estimated 23,000 schools do not have principals as most applicants fail the qualifying examination, the Department of Education (DepEd) said Friday during its budget hearing before the Senate Finance Committee.
DepEd Secretary Sonny Angara said they are considering relaxing the National Assessment for School Heads (NASH), in hopes that more principals could be hired and assigned to these schools.
“The finding from EDCOMM 2 led to certain moves as relaxing the NASH exam… so that more principals could be hired,” Angara said.

“... So what we did is we gave them the chance to—if they failed only certain parts or certain domains, they don’t have to take the exam again, they can just try to, in a way, remediate and pass the professional development area or intervention that’s needed,” he added.

In 2026, a total of 6,000 principal positions were secured, according to Angara. He noted that the agency is fast-tracking the filling of these positions, although only a few applicants have passed so far.
According to DepEd Undersecretary Wilfredo Cabral, out of the over 45,000 schools in the country, 22,000 have school principals.
Despite the shortage of school principals, Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian raised concerns over the zero budget for new principal positions in DepEd's proposed 2027 budget.

DepEd said they actually requested a budget for the creation of more than 14,000 school principal positions next year, but were not provided with funding. The agency eyes the promotion or reclassification of teachers as one of the ways to fill the vacancies.

“We actually requested for additional position… of more than 14,000 school principal positions for 2027, but it was not provided with budget. Nonetheless, by that time through reclassification, may mapo-promote for school principal under expanded career progression,” Cabral said.

(We actually requested for additional positions… of more than 14,000 school principal positions for 2027, but it was not provided with a budget. Nonetheless, by that time, through reclassification, some teachers will be promoted to school principal under expanded career progression.)
Cabral explained that for fiscal year 2027, DepEd targets to create more than 14,000 school principal items, which would require an estimated P10.5 billion.
New school counselor, teacher posts
Following concerns over school safety and incidents of bullying and gun violence, the government funded the creation of 10,000 school counselor associate (SCA) positions.
According to Angara, 5,447 or 54 percent of the vacancies have already been filled to date, while the remaining 45 percent of unfilled positions are undergoing the hiring process.
The agency targets to fill all positions by December 2026.
Under the 2027 budget, DepEd said it has already requested the creation of an additional 1,800 SCA positions, which is equivalent to P519 million.
Meanwhile, for teaching positions, more than 14,000 new items are targeted for creation next year.
During the budget hearing, the issue of teachers for Special Needs Education (SNED) was also raised, emphasizing the shortage given the large number of children under SNED.
According to DepEd, to date, there are over 6,000 SNED teachers across different plantillas, but noted that receiving teachers are currently undergoing training.

To meet the ideal 1:5 teacher-to-student ratio for around 400,000 SNED learners, the agency yielded to Senator Bam Aquino when asked to confirm if this means around 80,000 more teachers are needed. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Norwegian teenager hired as hitman by Iranian crime gang jailed for 20 years
articles.summary:
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, was arrested in Huddersfield with two guns and live ammunition

A teenage hitman who travelled from Norway to the UK with the intention of carrying out a…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent

blocks.text: A teenage hitman who travelled from Norway to the UK with the intention of carrying out a murder on behalf of an Iran-backed international crime gang has been jailed for 20 years.
Johannes Kongsnes Natland, 19, a talented footballer, had agreed to shoot an unknown target in return for €25,000 (£21,500).
He travelled to the UK in March last year from his home in Stavanger, and two days later – before he could carry out the hit – armed police arrested him at a hotel in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire.
Officers found him in possession of a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver, 12 rounds of live ammunition and gloves.

Natland admitted possessing the firearms and ammunition and said he had intended to shoot himself in the foot to get out of the “pickle” he was in. However, he was found guilty of conspiracy to murder and on Friday was sentenced to 20 years in detention.

The court heard that Natland had been recruited by another teenager, referred to as Generalen, who was working for the proscribed Swedish Foxtrot gang, which is backed by the Iranian regime and known for recruiting children as young as 13 to become involved in drug smuggling and violent crimes.
Natland had been controlled by an English-speaking boss called Agent 47, an apparent reference to the Hitman gaming and film franchise. The identity and whereabouts of Agent 47 remain unknown.
Natland flew into Manchester on a temporary passport and was stopped by Border Force officials, who bailed him to return to the airport to catch the next direct flight home.

Instead, he travelled by taxi to Huddersfield where he booked into the Briar Court hotel and picked up the guns and ammunition, as well as £2,000 in cash. He was directed to a stolen Nissan with false number plates, which was to be used in the murder.

While in the hotel, Natland took selfies with the guns and cash spread out on his bed, and bragged to his girlfriend that he had the “bangs in the bag”. Armed police arrived to arrest him at 5.15am the next day.

Paul Hynes KC, defending, pointed to Natland’s age at the time of the offending and said he had been a “young, popular, successful student and sportsman” before he went “off the rails” after he became addicted to drugs.
Giving evidence, Natland told jurors: “I wasn’t an international assassin. I thought people had this impression and expected me to be this guy. I knew I wasn’t.”

However, in a televised sentencing at Woolwich crown court in south-east London, Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb said messages he had sent showed “not only participation but at points excitement” about what he had been planning to do.

“You agreed to be the enforcer and pursued it, despite numerous opportunities to extricate yourself,” she said. “Although the fact that no one was shot dead or physically harmed is important, I am sure had the intervention of the police not prevented the plan from proceeding, you would have done what you had agreed to.”

articles.title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
articles.summary: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.

blocks.text: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of Durrës, Shkodër, Korçë and Vlora.
The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living.
Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers.
Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons.
Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony.
Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation.
A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too.

The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president.
They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night.
But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands.

The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership.
Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement.

Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard."

Another called Brunela said she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth."
An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward.
After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system.
Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos.

"All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday.
The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward".
Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama.
But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance.
So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it.
On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved.
Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU.
Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday.

"These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence."

articles.title: US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions
articles.summary: Ukraine says temporary speed limits to the Starlink internet network disrupted its battlefield missions.

blocks.text: A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an urgent investigation into reported disruptions to SpaceX's Starlink internet network in Ukraine.

Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and protect its own skies, but on Tuesday night Ukraine said it unexpectedly restricted how fast drones could fly while maintaining internet connection.
In the letter, sent on Thursday to the US Department of Defense inspector general, the senators say they have "grave concern" about reports of speed restrictions between 12 and 14 October.
The White House and Pentagon have not responded to the suggestion the US might have had a role in the alleged slowdown.

The letter, led by Jeanne Shaheen - a Democrat on the Senate's Foreign Relations Committee - calls for the inspector general to find out whether the restrictions were caused by the US defence department or its contractors.
It says "restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure".
Starlink, which is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, restricted speed limits on Tuesday night to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network.
The senators also say they are "deeply concerned" by reports of disruptions or "glitches" affecting intelligence-sharing and threat-warning capabilities relied upon by personnel operating in Ukraine.
"We are particularly alarmed by incidents in which U.S. diplomatic, military, and security personnel were unable to reach designated bunkers during Russian air raids," the statement says.
"Given the potentially deadly consequences, these incidents require immediate investigation," the senators add.

The letter's signatories include Republican Senators Thom Tillis, Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski and John Cornyn, alongside Senators Richard Durbin, Jack Reed, Richard Blumenthal and Christopher Coons from the Democrats.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind restrictions.
On Wednesday Musk wrote on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately [the US president]".

Starlink is a civilian service that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide internet access, particularly in remote areas. Starshield, which relies on the Starlink network, is designed for government and military use. Both are owned by Musk's SpaceX.
Ukraine's President Zelensky has accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks against Russian energy sites.

On Thursday, Zelensky said Ukraine's attacks would continue after Russia had continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure during an "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday.

Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days and would agree to the "energy ceasefire" if Moscow also abided by it. However, he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced.
The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal and Russia said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied.

Zelensky has also criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace, struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort.

That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing.

articles.title: Ombudsman files plunder complaint vs. Cagayan solon Lara over ties to contractor firms
articles.summary: Ombudsman investigators have filed a P1.9 billion plunder complaint vs. Cagayan Rep. Jojo Lara over his alleged ownership of construction companies which won government contracts, Ombudsman Jesus…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 8:11pm

Ombudsman investigators have filed a P1.9 billion plunder complaint vs. Cagayan Rep. Jojo Lara over his alleged ownership of construction companies which won government contracts, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Friday.
Remulla said the complaint for preliminary investigation has been filed before the Ombudsman for Lara's alleged stake in two construction firms that secured government projects.
“For PI, we filed against Jojo Lara for JLL Pulsar Construction and JDL5 Construction Corporation,” Remulla said in a press conference.

“There was supposed to be a divestment, which, we think, did not really happen, because the money paid to these construction companies still went to his private bank account. P1.9 billion pesos,” he added.
GMA News Online has reached out to Lara for comment and will publish his comment as soon as it is available.

Remulla's remarks on the day the Ombudsman filed three counts of graft against former Pampanga Rep. Aurelio “Dong” Gonzales before the Sandiganbayan over alleged engagement as a contractor while serving as a lawmaker.
This was confirmed by the Judicial and Records Division of the anti-graft court.
The Ombudsman is yet to provide further details and is expected to conduct a press briefing on the matter at 1 p.m.
Gonzales served as congressman representing the third district of Pampanga from 2007 to 2013, and again from 2016 to 2025.
Also facing graft charges before the Sandiganbayan is Uswag Ilonggo party-list Rep. James “Jojo” Ang.

Ang is facing 14 counts of graft for allegedly having a stake in a construction firm that won P214 million in DPWH contracts, and was paid nearly P199 million for them, even while he is in public office. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Gibo Teodoro hits Chinese envoy's statements: We are being threatened
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro slammed the apparent threat from the Chinese envoy to the Philippines, saying his department is currently studying the statement.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 7:47pm
Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro slammed the apparent threat from the Chinese envoy to the Philippines, saying his department is currently studying the statement.

Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan recently told reporters that if Beijing was to use force against Manila, the former would win. The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) has already called the statement a “thinly veiled threat”.

“Pinag-aaralan talaga namin ang statement na ito kasi hindi dulas yun eh. Mayroon talagang nilalaman ang mga statement na ‘yan at at least natalupan at, in the same statement, sinasabi niya ‘we want peace’ pagkatapos ‘we can use force and you will lose’. Banta ‘yon e. Yun ang tunay na laman ng statement na yan. Tinatakot tayo,” Teodoro said in a radio interview on Friday.

(We are really studying this statement because it is not a slip of tongue. Those statements have weight to it and when you unwrap it, in the same statement, he says ‘we want peace’ and then ‘we can use force and you will lose’. That is a threat. That is the true essence of the statement, We are being threatened.)
Teodoro said that while the threat was a cause for concern, it would not be patriotic to be afraid.

The defense secretary said that such statements could be fueled by Philippine authorities busting illegal activities associated with Chinese citizens, such as Philippine offshore gaming operators, fake steel, illegal mining, human trafficking among others.
The public statement revealed China’s true intentions, Teodoro said

After the Chinese Embassy of the Philippines recently stated that the Philippines shut down military-to-military communications with them, Teodoro explained that the said lines have already been closed for three years, as it was no longer beneficial for the Philippines.
Teodoro also said that the Philippines and China had no Status of Visiting Forces Agreement, or any alignment, so there was no reason to speak.
The Defense chief said that China may be setting the narrative that just in case something happened, it would be because of the Philippines’ side.
Relations between Beijing and Manila have grown tense over the territorial dispute in the West Philippine Sea.

Despite the Philippines winning its case for the West Philippine Sea in the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, China has disregarded the ruling and continuously claimed most of the waters for itself. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: Who is Edrieza Rimbang, the ex-solon allegedly linked to the P3.5-B shabu from Laos?
articles.summary: The Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) has revealed the Mindanao politician tagged in the attempted smuggling of shabu from Laos to the Philippines: former Bangsamoro Parliament…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 7:44pm

The Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG) has revealed the Mindanao politician tagged in the attempted smuggling of shabu from Laos to the Philippines: former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edrieza Rimbang.
But who is Rimbang?
According to his Certificate of Candidacy for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliamentary elections, the 44-year-old Rimbang is a native of Marawi City, Lanao del Sur.

During the 2026 BARMM parliamentary elections, he ran to represent the 3rd District of Lanao del Sur under the Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Laban, the political party of the Duterte clan. Rimbang lost to Abdul Rauf Adiong.
While running for a seat in parliament, Rimbang listed several of his previous positions on his office’s Facebook.
The former BARMM parliamentary member said that he was a member of the Philippine National Police Intelligence Group in 2002. He also said that he was in the military reserve.
Rimbang said that he is also the chairman of a group called the “Muslim-Christian Solidarity,” a position that he has held since 2014.
From 2014 to 2019, Rimbang was a “Deputy Mayor” of the Manila Muslim Affairs during the term of former president and Manila mayor Joseph “Erap” Estrada.
Former president Rodrigo Duterte appointed Rimbang as a member of parliament to the Bangsamoro Transition Authority in 2019.

Before the DILG named Rimbang and his alleged associates, the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA) had alluded to a Mindanao-based politician as being the financier of the plane in the attempted Laos-Philippines drug smuggling.
PDEA earlier stated that the Mindanao politician was against the administration of President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: India's 'cockroach' party founder detained ahead of protest
articles.summary: The youth-led movement planned a fresh Delhi protest after mass detentions last week and the jailing of two leaders.
articles.byline: Zoya Mateen, Azadeh Moshiri & Vikas Pandey

blocks.text: The founder of India's "cockroach" protest movement, Abhijeet Dipke, has been detained in Delhi ahead of a planned march in the heart of the capital.
His detention follows a police warning against holding Friday's march, with thousands of security personnel deployed across the city to prevent the gathering.
Dipke's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) is demanding the resignation of India's election chief over allegations of voter list manipulation. The Election Commission denies the charge.
The group had asked its supporters to come to a park in Connaught Place, one of Delhi's busiest commercial districts, to wave the Indian flag.

The turnout was smaller than at earlier CJP demonstrations though the crowd seemed to be swelling. The BBC saw some young protesters being detained and shoved into a bus which already held some female detainees - there were about 50 female police personnel in the bus, vastly outnumbering the protesters.

Dipke had just left home and was moments away from reaching his vehicle when the BBC saw police officers surround him and force him into a police car. Some CJP supporters tried to block the vehicle from leaving.
Anish Gawande, the opposition politician at whose house Dipke had been staying, questioned why police had detained him. Police have not yet publicly confirmed the grounds for the detention.
"Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," Gawande said.

It was the second time in less than a week that Dipke was detained. Last Saturday, police boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi and took him away before he could reach a planned demonstration.

Police barricades and mass detentions prevented thousands of other protesters from reaching the venue. Dipke was released the following day, but two other CJP leaders - Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka - were later jailed for five days after entering Jantar Mantar, a protest site recently declared off-limits by police.
Friday's march was partly intended to show solidarity with the two jailed leaders.
Dipke had acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again. In a video message on Thursday, he urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities.
"I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said.
Earlier on Friday, police had served Dipke with a notice warning him against holding the march without permission.
Authorities also closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons". Police offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location.
The CJP responded by changing its plans, urging supporters to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave.
"Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the group said in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour flag. It encouraged supporters to share their photographs online.
By the time the protest was due to begin, around 200-300 people had gathered near Central Park. Prevented by police from entering, they moved around the park, waving flags and shouting slogans.

Among those detained was Neha Bora, a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She was also detained during last Saturday's crackdown.

Security personnel, meanwhile, continued to arrive. More officers emerged from buses stationed around Connaught Place, joining the thousands of police and paramilitary personnel already deployed. Journalists also crowded the streets, with police and media in much larger numbers than the protesters.

Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry.

By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked examination papers. A march towards Parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

Police cited earlier demonstrations in their warning against Friday's march. In the notice served to Dipke, they accused the CJP of defying restrictions and said previous attempts to march towards Parliament had led to violence and damage to property.
They also warned that a large gathering in Connaught Place could disrupt traffic, affect businesses and obstruct emergency vehicles.

The CJP wants Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign, accusing the poll panel of favouring Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Both the commission and the government deny the allegations.

At issue is a sweeping revision of electoral rolls, known as Special Intensive Revision (SIR), that critics say has removed more than 130 million names, putting legitimate voters at risk of losing their right to vote.

Friday's march comes less than a week after police prevented the movement's last mass demonstration from taking place, detaining its leaders - Das, Dipke and Ranka - and putting the city under a sweeping security lockdown.

Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel had fanned out across Delhi, sealing roads, shutting metro stations and intercepting protesters long before they could reach Jantar Mantar, where the CJP had planned its mass demonstration.

The BBC witnessed dozens of people being detained, including journalists and students. In footage from across Delhi, protesters could be seen shouting as police seized them by the arms, dragged them across the pavement and pushed them into waiting buses.
Those who managed to gather elsewhere were swiftly dispersed. There were also reports of protesters being assaulted by police.
The BBC captured footage, external of a policeman slapping a detained protester inside a bus. The Delhi police did not respond to questions about the use of violence against protesters.
The scale of the crackdown drew widespread outrage, with the CJP likening the police action to India's Emergency, when civil liberties were suspended between 1975 and 1977.
Delhi police defended the measures as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings.
Dipke, Das and Ranka were released on Sunday after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour.

Police then took Jantar Mantar off Delhi's list of approved protest sites, designating three alternate venues. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory sits near parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused the authorities of pushing protesters away from the seat of power to make their demonstrations less visible and easier to ignore.
On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar.
Police said they had entered the restricted site without permission, some by climbing over a locked gate, and breached the conditions of their release.
The following day, the two were sent to jail for five days in judicial custody. Another organiser, Ajinkya Shinde, was released on a bond to maintain peace and good behaviour.
