articles.title: Shooter kills three children and one teacher at Oregon elementary school
articles.summary: Two people critical in hospital as officials in Bend say 16-year-old suspect shot dead by bystander

blocks.text: Schools in Bend, Oregon, will be closed on Friday after a 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an elementary school in the city on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot dead by a community member.
The children killed at Silver Rail elementary school were aged five, eight and 11, officials said.
A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old were also hospitalized with critical injuries, according to police.

The gunman, who was a Bend resident, has not been publicly identified and early on Friday the identities of those killed, those wounded and the armed bystander who followed the teen into the school and shot him were not publicly known. Officials said they are still investigating if the perpetrator had ties to the school. He shot his way through a locked gate into the school grounds and through locked doors to gain access to the premises, the authorities said.
Children and staff who heard gunfire rushed to lock classroom doors and hide.
The deadly shooting has rocked the city of 100,000 residents located on the Deschutes River, roughly 170 miles south-east of Portland, in central Oregon.

“Please hold your children, hold your loved ones tight tonight. Let them talk. Let them cry. Let them know we are going to rally and care for one another in this community,” said Steven Cook, the superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools.
“We will get through this – but not yet. We must grieve for the loss of our community members.”

blocks.caption: Police tape is placed outside Silver Rail elementary school, where a shooting took place. Photograph: Joe Kline/AP

blocks.text: At 1.02pm, police responded to Silver Rail elementary school after receiving several reports about an active shooter. One 911 caller reported an individual armed with a long gun firing at their car. Police did not specify the firearm’s make.
Dozens of callers stated the shooter had entered the school, continuing the attack inside.
By the time officers arrived on scene, the suspected assailant had been shot and killed by the bystander, who apprehended him inside.

The attacker used a pump-action shotgun, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.

In the aftermath of the tragedy, children were taken by bus to a nearby church serving as a reunification center for families. Parents hugged, kissed and held their kids’ hands as they walked to their cars, with some bringing along favorite stuffed animals or other comfort items from home.
The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade, roughly ages 5 to 11, and has about 450 students and 40 staff members, officials said.
Oregon governor Tina Kotek praised the intervention as heroic and extended her thoughts to the bystander. “Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden,” she said on Thursday evening.
Classes, sports and extracurriculars were canceled Friday for all 32 schools in the Bend-La Pine district.
The FBI is helping local authorities investigate the shooting, according to the agency’s director Kash Patel.
The shooting began about an hour before the school day was set to end.

“A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure,” said Bend mayor Melanie Kebler. “Like so many in our community, I’m struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable.”

blocks.caption: People gather for a candlelight vigil after the shooting at Silver Rail elementary school, in Bend, Oregon. Photograph: Rob Kerr/Reuters

blocks.text: Gun control advocate Gabrielle Giffords, ⁠a former congresswoman who survived a mass shooting in 2011, said in a statement she was “heartbroken” by the shooting.
“This cannot continue to be a reality ​in our country. Leaders at every level must step ​up and act,” Giffords said.

Thursday’s shooting is the latest event in a grim history of recurring gun violence at schools across the US. According to Everytown For Gun Safety, there have been at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds across the country in 2026, resulting in 33 deaths.

Oregon has passed several gun safety measures in recent years, including a law that requires gun owners to undergo a criminal background check and safety training before being approved for a firearm permit.

articles.title: EU debate Ukraine funding, as Zelenskyy's relations with the Trump administration ebb again
articles.summary: European Union leaders rallied around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit on Friday, as U.S. President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on ‌Russian…

image.caption: From left, European Council President Antonio Costa, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen speak with the media as they arrive for the EU summit in Brussels on Friday. (Geert Vanden Wijngaert/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

European Union leaders rallied around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit on Friday, as U.S. President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on ‌Russian refineries a "disgrace."
In the latest violence, at least 3 were killed in Russian strikes across Ukraine

European Union leaders rallied around Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit on Friday as U.S. President Donald Trump fired another salvo at Ukraine, calling its strikes on ‌Russian refineries a "disgrace."

The EU is ‌hosting Zelenskyy in Brussels at one of the most difficult moments for Ukraine, with missiles and drones raining down on Ukrainian cities as it faces a fifth full winter of attack since Russia's invasion, amid fears that the U.S. could pull back intelligence sharing and weapons support from Kyiv.

In the latest attacks early Friday, Russian drones killed at least three people across Ukraine, hit two ‌shopping centres and knocked out power to around 370,000 people in the northwest after strikes on the energy grid, officials said.

Two people died and ​12 more were wounded in attacks ​on three districts of the eastern city of Kharkiv, Gov. Oleh Syniehubov said. In the ⁠northwestern region of ⁠Volyn, which borders Poland, ‌a drone strike on a food-processing facility killed one person and wounded eight others, according to Gov. Roman Romaniuk.
Seven people were wounded by drones that hit a major shopping centre and other sites in Rivne, regional Gov. Oleksandr Koval said.
A deminer works at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike on Friday in the Rivne region. (State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Reuters)

"We want to end this war as quick ​as possible. We don't see now signals from the Russian side that they are ready for this, to end this war, that's why we have to prepare for the winter," Zelenskyy said as he arrived in Brussels.
"The winter package is not only energy, it's ​also air defence and funding," Zelenskyy said, adding that he would discuss Ukraine's needs for the rest of this year and for ⁠2027.

items: Starlink restrictions would hamper Ukraine's war effort. But the country can adapt, experts say

blocks.text: In an interview, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal ‌told Reuters that the EU would probably have to provide a new loan to Ukraine to help cover its budget gap for next year.
"Last winter was already hell, this one will be, once again, like hell," Michal said. "We have a lot of gaps to fill, and this is a European mission to fill the gaps that Ukraine needs."
Ukraine attacks 'a disgrace': Trump

Trump blindsided Zelenskyy last weekend by announcing a diesel transaction with Russia, and asserting that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other's energy facilities. Facing midterm elections in November, Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for pushing up energy prices that ​could cost him at the ballot box.

Ukraine ⁠struck a Russian oil refinery after Zelenskyy declared that Kyiv was abandoning the energy ‌ceasefire that Trump had announced, as he criticized the U.S. president's willingness to strike deals with Moscow.

"All he's doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that's a disgrace," Trump said in an interview with Newsmax, adding that Zelenskyy was more difficult to deal with than Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine says Starlink restrictions are disrupting military operations

Trump has had an often-contentious relationship with Ukraine's president, dating back to 2019 when he was impeached by the Democrat-led U.S. House of Representatives for pressuring Zelenskyy for a domestic political favour in exchange for military aid for Ukraine. Last year, Trump and Vice-President JD Vance publicly admonished Zelenskyy at the White House over what they viewed as a perceived lack of gratitude for U.S. support of Ukraine.

Ukraine's leadership has also been alarmed by disruptions earlier this week to the SpaceX Starshield satellite system, the military-grade version of Starlink used by Kyiv for battlefield communications and drone operations.

items: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president, blames Zelenskyy for U.S. diesel prices
'You're Russian now': Ukrainians raised in Crimea share how Russia trained them to become future soldiers

blocks.text: The U.S. government is a major Starshield customer. SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said this week that the U.S. government owns and controls the system, with decisions about its use resting with the U.S. military and, ultimately, the president. His remarks have fuelled questions about who was responsible for the latest restrictions affecting Ukraine.
By Thursday, some Ukrainian units said their connectivity had returned to normal, though uncertainty remained over what had caused the restrictions.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine. And unfortunately, in short term, Europe can't replace this capability," said the EU's foreign policy ​chief Kaja Kallas.

Front Burner29:04Is the world locked in an energy war?
Debate over Ukraine needs
EU leaders have also hit out at Trump's diesel deal and are also grappling with soaring energy prices since the Iran war started by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28.

Zelenskyy told ​Reuters earlier this month that Ukraine had agreed to a plan with European partners that would allow it to close a $27-billion deficit in its military spending for this year, allowing it to order ​the drones needed to continue fighting at the start of ⁠2027.

However, Ukrainian Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko said recently the country still faced an unfunded budget gap for next year of $32.6 billion — and that does not include an estimated $40 billion in direct military supplies from allies.
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker urged caution in the debate over making new, far-reaching financial commitments.
"There are so many figures being bandied about that we now need to put them into context, explain them and make it clear where this shortfall is coming ⁠from," he said.

articles.title: India's young workers have a new colleague: AI
articles.summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the way Indian workplaces operate, raising questions about productivity, skills and entry-level jobs.

image.caption: The use of AI is widespread among younger Indians, with a survey finding that 93% of Gen Z respondents and 95% of millennial respondents used AI in their day-to-day work Image: PUNIT PARANJPE/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Across India, young workers are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence (AI) to speed up routine tasks, whether researching news stories, translating copy, analyzing business data or sorting legal documents.
But the technology can get things wrong, and relying on it too heavily carries risks.
A faster way to work

Journalist Farah Kazmi, 28, who works for a news portal in New Delhi, used AI while reporting on rules governing stray animals and feeding them in gated communities. She asked an AI model to find the Supreme Court's latest guidelines, earlier court rulings and recent dog-bite cases.
"Since it can take quite a lot of time to search Google for specific articles about court rulings, previous judgments or recent dog-bite cases, I asked AI to find them for me," Kazmi told DW.
It gave her a starting point for relevant articles and cases, which she then read and cross-checked herself.
India's workers train AI that may replace them

She also uses AI to translate English copy into Hindi for the Hindi news team, and Hindi quotes into English. But translations need careful checking, Kazmi said, pointing out that in one case, AI interpreted the name "Suraj" as "sun," changing the sentence's meaning.

"Before using AI, I mostly relied on Google Translate. It was more literal and did not always understand the context. AI gives a much better and more context-based translation, although it still needs to be checked and corrected," she said.
AI has not fundamentally changed journalism, which still involves talking to people and reporting from the field, Kazmi underlined.
"Ultimately, I see AI as a tool that helps with research and saves time, but the actual verification and reporting still has to be done by the journalist," she said.

Yajatt Misra, 28, business strategy and international markets manager at Kanoria Chemicals and Industries, uses AI to analyze data, summarize large volumes of information, prepare first drafts and structure ideas.
It also helps him turn financial and business information from different sources into management updates and presentations.
"Things like summarizing information, preparing first drafts, analyzing data and putting together presentations take less time now," Misra told DW.
He said the challenge is knowing when to trust the output. AI can miss business context or get details wrong, so its numbers, logic and conclusions need checking.
"There is less need to spend time on repetitive tasks and more focus on analysis, problem-solving and providing useful insights to the business," he said.
India's AI power play
'A junior colleague' with limitations

Rakshanda Deka, a 30-year-old lawyer, uses AI to sort large bundles of client documents chronologically or by theme and produce a first list of important dates. Some systems link information to the original documents so lawyers can check the source.
AI can also help prepare standard applications and petitions using a lawyer's own format and style.
"If used sensibly, and without outsourcing the substantive legal thinking, AI is basically like having a sincere fresher or junior colleague," Deka told DW.
But AI can confidently produce false information, making human checking essential.
"AI often gives you false information dressed up very confidently as fact. So, it is imperative that you double-check everything," she said.
Deka is also concerned that some young lawyers may use AI as a substitute for their own thinking. "A lot of the youngest lawyers are beginning to use AI as a substitute for themselves," she said.
Widespread use of AI
The use of AI is widespread among younger Indians, with a survey by Deloitte this year finding that 93% of Gen Z respondents and 95% of millennial respondents used AI in their day-to-day work.
A separate Emeritus survey found that 82% of respondents aged 15 to 28 used AI tools at least weekly to learn or develop new skills.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated

Dimple Khubchandani, founder of recruitment firm Synoverge Consultants, told DW that employers increasingly want young professionals who can think critically, solve problems and check AI-generated work rather than simply handle basic research or drafting.
"AI is not necessarily eliminating entire job categories, but it is creating leaner teams and raising expectations," she said.
Khubchandani said a marketing agency that once might have hired four junior copywriters could now hire one to use AI for initial drafts, leaving more time to edit, refine the tone and shape strategy.
"AI is raising the baseline capability expected from employees on day one," she said.

Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), one of India's largest IT services companies, said in its 2025-26 annual report that it had scaled up its "Human+AI" operating model and was embedding AI across services and software development.
A changing job market
Shrijay Sheth, co-founder of LegalWiz.in, an online legal and compliance service, sees the shift across the economy.

"AI's impact on job profiles isn't an anticipation. It is a reality now," Sheth told DW. "From basic research to strategy, operations, marketing, design and development, AI is changing how work gets done."
In software development, Sheth said, developers are spending less time writing code from scratch and more time monitoring, testing and refining AI-generated output.
"Business, product and problem-solving ability, coupled with skills around working with AI platforms, is valued over mere technical ability to work with any particular coding language," he said.
How AI is changing the working world
What the numbers show
The question of what happens to entry-level work is becoming harder to ignore.

A 2025 report by NITI Aayog, the Indian government's public policy think tank, cites data from the Center of Advanced Study in India suggesting that more than 60% of formal-sector jobs could be susceptible to automation by 2030, particularly in IT and business-process services.
It also warns of slower hiring for entry-level software engineers and identifies junior quality-assurance and Level 1 support roles as vulnerable.
The World Bank's October 2026 India Development Update says AI's long-term impact on India's labor market remains uncertain.

The country could benefit from its technical workforce, IT sector and digital infrastructure, the report says, but stronger workforce skills and wider access to AI capabilities will be needed if the gains are to be broadly shared.
"The productivity enhancement and job loss are both real," Sheth said.

Deka believes lawyers will increasingly be distinguished by how rigorously they check AI's work. "I think the differentiation is increasingly coming from the thoroughness of post-AI verification and confirmation," she said.

articles.title: Senate OKs DepEd's 2027 budget; P147.93B more asked for ARAL
articles.summary: The Senate Finance Committee approved Friday the proposed budget of the Department of Education (DepEd) for fiscal year 2027, subject to the discussion and submission of requested documents.

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 7:18pm
The Senate Finance Committee approved Friday the proposed budget of the Department of Education (DepEd) for fiscal year 2027, subject to the discussion and submission of requested documents.
In the General Appropriations Bill (GAB), the agency and its attached agencies were allocated P969.79 billion. This is a P6.17 billion decrease from the 2027 National Expenditures Program (NEP).
Of the total allocated budget under GAB, P967.23 billion is earmarked for DepEd, with around P2.561 billion for its attached agencies.

These agencies are the National Council for Children’s Television, National Museum of the Philippines, National Academy of Sports, National Book Development Board, Philippine High School for the Arts, and the Teacher Education Council.

During the Senate budget hearing, DepEd requested an additional P147.93 billion allocation to fund its various initiatives, including the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program that received zero funding under the NEP.
The ARAL Program is a remediation initiative designed to support the agency's broader Learning Recovery efforts. DepEd requested P15.63 billion for the program.

“It’s delivering what it intends to deliver, which is to teach our children how to read, how to count. But this year na-zero yung budget ng ARAL, which is shocking. Kung ano pa yung gumagawa, ‘yun pa yung nawala,” Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said.

(It’s delivering what it intends to deliver, which is to teach our children how to read and count. But this year, the budget for ARAL was reduced to zero, which is shocking. The very program that works is the one that got cut.)
Senator Joel Villanueva likewise expressed concern, emphasizing that many students still urgently need learning remediation.

“When I found out that it was zero, the first word that came out in my mind was ‘stupid.’ Stupid talaga. I really can't comprehend bakit ginawa yon. Tapos ngayon dinagdagan P325 million [and] you're looking at P13 million needing remediation,” Villauneva said.

(When I found out that it was zero, the first word that came to mind was ‘stupid.’ It really is stupid. I honestly can't comprehend why that was done. Now they added P325 million, but you're looking at 13 million students needing remediation.)
For its part, the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) stated that it is aware of the ARAL Program.
The DBM explained that the program does have funding, but it was attributed to the budget for textbooks and instructional materials rather than given a standalone allocation.

“We are knowledgeable about the ARAL Program… so ‘yung sa funding po wala siyang line program, sariling line item po… pero may pondo po siya under textbook and other instructional materials, so attribution po siya,” DBM Director Vivien Labastilla explained.
(We are aware of the ARAL Program... regarding the funding, it doesn't have its own line item, but it has funds under textbooks and other instructional materials through attribution.)
The panel proposed creating a separate line item for the ARAL Program in the budget to ensure transparency and eliminate the need for the agency to carve out funds from other line items.
According to Gatchalian, the Year 1 report of the ARAL Program shows that 1.37 million learners from Grades 1 to 10 are no longer classified as struggling learners.
In addition, an estimated 730,000 more learners are now able to read at their respective grade levels. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: JAZA: Does the Philippines have what it takes to win big investments?
articles.summary: The Ayala chairman wants an 'honest conversation' on Philppine investments and talks teamwork to a roomful of rivals at Makati Business Club's sapphire anniversary

blocks.text: The Ayala chairman wants an 'honest conversation' on Philppine investments and talks teamwork to a roomful of rivals at Makati Business Club's sapphire anniversary

At a party packed with people who know a thing or two about winning, Ayala’s big boss had a rather inconvenient question for his fellow corporate titans. Everyone wants to bag the next big deal, but does the Philippines even have what it takes to attract those investments in the first place?

“We need, I think, an honest conversation among ourselves and with our partners in the public sector of whether we have the talent, whether we have the infrastructure, whether we have the energy, whether we have the regulatory environment and institutional stability needed to attract long-term investment,” Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala (JAZA) said on Thursday, October 15.
Quite the conversation starter for a night of cocktails, buttered scallops, honeyed sausage tarts, and plenty of schmoozing and boozing at the Makati Business Club’s (MBC) 45th anniversary bash.

But he did, after all, have quite the audience. Among those gathered at the Grand Hyatt Manila were MBC chairman and former Shell Philippines chief Edgar Chua, Aboitiz InfraCapital’s Cosette Canilao, PHINMA’s Ramon del Rosario Jr., shipping magnate Doris Magsaysay Ho, and former Microsoft Philippines CEO Peter Maquera.
And he sure had their ear.

“As global companies diversify their supply chains, we should think beyond which company, industrial park, or sector secures the next investment. A more important question to ask is whether the Philippines itself is winning,” the Ayala chairman said.

And if the country as a whole is to win, JAZA argued, his fellow “fierce competitors in the marketplace” had to work together on the things that make the country attractive to investors in the first place.

“We will not always agree. We will have different interests and conflicting views on policy, but we can agree on many of the first principles and, more importantly, identify practical areas where we could all make progress together,” he added.

And who better to ask a roomful of business rivals to play nice than JAZA? His uncle Enrique Zobel co-founded MBC and his father served as a longtime trustee. Even in BGC, a little beyond the Makati business district the family helped build, he was hardly away from home.

The Philippines has advantages, he said, including its young population, digital economy, and manufacturing base. But actually turning those into better jobs and better lives require businesses to cooperate on shared concerns, like education and affordable electricity. A promising country on paper would only get everyone so far.

blocks.caption: JAZA: Does the Philippines have what it takes to win big investments?

blocks.text: Infrastructure projects also needed to be built properly, with “every project and peso fully accountable for.” He didn’t mention corruption, but he didn’t have to, with the headlines still fresh in every businessman and investor’s mind. (READ: Flood control corruption cleanup spooks investors, drags PH growth – World Bank)

Even on the sidelines, the investment chatter wasn’t particularly upbeat. An MBC member familiar with the Jefferies-Regis Partners Philippines Conference, which brought together blue-chip companies and institutional investors earlier this week, told Rappler that turnout was thinner than expected this year, with fewer foreign investors making the trip to Manila. (READ: [READOUT] What a stickier inflation wave could mean for businesses)

A worrying sign, they reckoned. The broader numbers haven’t exactly been encouraging either. Net foreign direct investment inflows fell 23.9% to $4.071 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to data from the central bank.
Could AI and Pax Silica offer some hope? JAZA did mention the US-led technology supply chain initiative in passing as a “major initiative.”

But the AI pitch has its share of skeptics at the club. An MBC member told Rappler that earlier meetings had revealed disagreements, with some eager to back AI and hyperscale data centers, while others questioned their enormous water and electricity needs, and whether they would actually bring enough jobs for Filipinos.
One participant even reportedly brandished Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, which raises concerns about AI’s implications for workers, inequality, and the environment.
It’s not every day someone brings the Pope to a data center debate. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: The Senate Electoral Tribunal (SET) on Friday denied the motion for reconsideration for the dismissal of the quo warranto petition seeking the removal of Senator Erwin Tulfo from office due to his…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 6:59pm

The Senate Electoral Tribunal (SET) on Friday denied the motion for reconsideration for the dismissal of the quo warranto petition seeking the removal of Senator Erwin Tulfo from office due to his supposed citizenship issues.
In a statement signed by SET Secretary Luis Jose Geronimo, it was noted that the ruling was made with six members voting in favor, and three voting against.

The tribunal denied the motion for reconsideration with an amended petition for quo warranto filed by Berteni Cataluña Causing, as it “failed to comply” with the filing and service requirements of the 2020 SET Rules.
The motion was also reportedly “filed beyond the period prescribed” by the said rules, according to the SET.
The tribunal further said the amended petition of Causing “remained insufficient in form.”
The SET, however, emphasized that the motion was denied without prejudice to the filing of any other petition.
Causing earlier sought Tulfo’s removal as a sitting senator due to his supposed ineligibility on grounds of his alleged American citizenship.
The petitioner also accused the lawmaker of disloyalty to the Philippines and allegiance to the US, as well as belonging to a political dynasty and lacking academic qualifications.

Causing also filed a disqualification case against Tulfo when the latter was running for senator in the 2025 midterm elections. This was over multiple grounds, including disqualification due to a libel conviction in 2008.
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) later dismissed two petitions seeking to disqualify Tulfo over the petitioners’ failure to observe certain requirements.
GMA News Online reached out to Tulfo’s office for a comment and will update this story once it responds. —RF, GMA News

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Friday accepted the apology of House lead prosecutor Representative Gerville Luistro of Batangas for the wacky photos taken by the prosecution panel inside the session hall, but maintained that a warning will still be issued against them.
"May warning pa rin kasi nangyari na 'yun, just to put it on record. But of course, we accept the apology. And I'm sure naiintindihan naman nila 'yan," Gatchalian said in an ambush interview.
(A warning will be issued because the incident already happened, just to put it on record. But, of course, we accept the apology. And I'm sure they will understand that.)
The Senate President on Thursday said he asked the Office of the Sergeant-at-Arms (OSAA) to look into the circulating photos of certain individuals doing wacky poses while inside the session hall.
He did not drop any names, but such photos of the House prosecution panel recently circulated on social media.
He said the investigation would also apply to those who dance in the hallways of the Senate and those who sleep inside the session hall.
Luistro later issued an apology, explaining that the prosecution panel was simply happy when the photo was taken because they could take a break after months of impeachment hearings.
Gatchalian stood firm that the investigation on the matter would still proceed regardless of the apology.
"Well, we accept their apology. At alam naman nila dahil mga mambabatas rin sila. At doon sa session hall ng Congress, alam ko very strict rin 'yung mga rules nila pagdating sa decorum," he said.

(Well, we accept their apology. I know they are well aware of this, as they are lawmakers themselves. And I know that in the session hall of Congress, the rules regarding decorum are also very strict.)
"Nevertheless, tuloy-tuloy pa rin 'yung investigation kung totoo mang nangyari 'yun o hindi. Dahil may mga sumasayaw dito sa loob. So, bibigyan ako ng official report within the day," he added.

(Nevertheless, the investigation into whether or not this actually took place will continue, since there were people also dancing here in the Senate session hall. I will be provided with an official report within the day.)

Gatchalian also said it was fine to take photos in the session hall, but explained that at the time the prosecution team took the photos, the session hall was set up as a courtroom for the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. — VDV, GMA News

The Office of the Ombudsman will ask the House prosecution panel to submit its evidence on the confidential fund use of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd) under Vice President Sara Duterte for investigation and possible filing of charges, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla said Friday.
“We are collecting all the records now, and we're evaluating them so that we can actually evaluate them for proper filing if necessary,” Remulla said in a press conference.
“We will ask the prosecution to turn us to turn over to us their evidence for the other charges that have not been aired out yet. We are entitled to look at that,” he added.
Some of the revelations by the prosecution witnesses on the confidential fund use under the Vice President’s leadership include:

items: names of recipients of confidential fund not having birth, marriage or death records
names of recipients of confidential fund matching names of dead persons of very young children as young as three years old
names of recipients of the confidential fund, including Mary Grace Piattos, Mico Harina, Timon Pusa, Andy Lim, among others
absence of proof that the OVP’s confidential fund was used for successful information gathering or surveillance activities
absence of documentary evidence for payments to the recipients
Commission on Audit issuing a notice of disallowance for P448 million confidential fund disbursement of OVP
confidential fund allocation being released to military officers for disbursement instead of the Special Disbursement Officer mandated to do such job, among others

blocks.text: Remulla said such revelations on confidential fund use before the impeachment trial of the Vice President are all deeply concerning.

“Pare-pareho lahat yan eh. Basta't meron talagang series of wrongdoings, they're all the same to me. They're all disturbing, but we just have to live with the fact that our job is to prosecute these things. That's why we have been evaluating properly and filing the necessary cases when ready,” he said.
Asked if the comprehensive testimonies before the impeachment trial would speed up the Ombudsman's resolution on these confidential fund cases, Remulla said, "very possible."

"Very possible. Of course, ang deadline talaga ng trabaho ng Ombudsman is almost yesterday. That's why we always act with urgency. We just have to make sure that it will stand in court," Remulla said.
Under the 2015 joint circular on confidential fund use, the confidential fund can only be spent on the following:

items: purchase of information necessary for the formulation and implementation of programs, activities and projects relevant to national security and peace and order;
rental of transport vehicle related to confidential activities;
rentals and the incidental expenses related to the maintenance of safehouses;
purchase or rental of supplies, materials and equipment for confidential operations that cannot be done through regular procedures without compromising the information gathering activity concerned;
payment of rewards to informers supported with documents evidencing the success of the information gathering and/or surveillance activities on

account of the information given by the informer to uncover/prevent illegal activities that pose a clear and present danger to agency personnel/property, or other facilities and resources under the agency's protection, done in coordination with the appropriate law enforcement agencies

articles.title: How prepared is Kenya for an Ebola outbreak?
articles.summary: The first two confirmed Ebola cases in Kenya have raised urgent questions about the country's public health preparedness and border controls. But the health ministry says there is no need for panic.
articles.byline: Lucy Riley, Isaac Mugabi, Felix Maringa

image.caption: Kenya is on high alert after the country reported one death from Ebola and a second caseImage: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kenyais rushing to contain Ebola linked to the deadliest outbreak on record in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) . The East African nation has reported two cases and one death, while the DRC has reported over 9,000 cases and 4,400 deaths.
Kenya's first Ebola patient died at Nairobi hospital on October 5. The 40-year-old Kenyan had traveled by road from the DRC to Uganda before boarding a flight to Nairobi in Entebbe on October 3.

One of his relatives is now confirmed to have contracted the virus. The 39-year-old was under quarantine when he developed symptoms on October 13. "Both cases are linked, and ​there is no evidence of spread in the wider community," Kenya's health ministry said.

Contact tracing has been ongoing since officials first detected the case. Of the 128 people who came into contact with the first Ebola patient, 113 have been identified, according to the health ministry. All, except five—who are in unspecified countries abroad—have been quarantined.
Should Kenyans worry about Ebola spreading?
Public anxiety is rising, with fears of lockdowns and economic disruption and skepticism about government readiness.

"It's a very dangerous disease, so it's very shocking," a Nairobi resident told DW. Another citizen said he was disappointed: "The government has been caught unaware. It appears to me that the government was not prepared, especially at the entry point of this particular person who was found to be suffering from Ebola."
One woman said she felt there was a lack of public information on the disease. "The government should do more in educating and sensitizing about it, and raising awareness," she said.

Kenya's Health Ministry, through its Cabinet Secretary, Aden Duale, has been seeking to allay fears, urging Kenyans to remain vigilant and encouraging anyone who develops symptoms to report to the nearest medical facility. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), symptoms can develop between 2 and 21 days after infection.
Early symptoms include: fever, fatigue, malaise, muscle pain, headache and sore throat. Later, a patient may suffer from vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and kidney and liver infection.
However, these symptoms might be similar to other illnesses such as malaria or typhoid, and only an Ebola test can confirm if one has been exposed to the virus.

blocks.caption: Kenya's Minster of Health Aden Duale (left) has sought to calm the nation as health officials rush to contain the virus from spreadingImage: Monicah Mwangi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Criticism and calls to improve screening

Several prominent figures, medical unions and opposition politicians have criticized Kenya's response to its first Ebola cases. Former Chief Justice David Maraga, who has declared interest in running for the presidency in the 2027 election, questioned how a man carrying the Ebola virus could pass through screening at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, Nairobi.
"We don't know how many have been infected. We must demand appropriate action be taken so that we don't have deaths arising from that disease," Maraga told The Standard.
Kalonzo Musyoka, Kenya's vice president from 2008 to 2013, meanwhile noted that doctors at Nairobi Hospital, not border systems, detected the danger.

blocks.caption: A hand santitation station at the Kenya-Uganda borderImage: James Keyi/REUTERS

blocks.text: Dr. Dennis Miskellah of the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union believes that the Ebola cases show that Kenya's health system is not pandemic-ready. "This system is not yet resilient. This system did not learn from the COVID pandemic that we had a few years ago," he said.
"Since May, we've had this outbreak in the region. Uganda, our immediate neighbor, had almost 20 cases. So, we had ample time to prepare adequately. But it seems like somebody dropped the ball."
Kenya went on high alert after the DRC declared the Ebola outbreak in May. The government designated several hospitals as isolation centers.
It also enhanced screening at airports and border points, deploying mobile labs. Flights from several African countries were ordered to land in designated airport wings for screening.
Where are the gaps in Kenya's health system?

"Top of it all is that there's has been a serious lapse of leadership in governance of healthcare this country," said Miskellah. "All those broken pillars, there's no clear responsibility or chain of command, whether its the Ministry of Health or the 47 county governments who are semi-automous."

Capacity at some isolation centers is limited. Rural facilities lack resources such as the protective gear available at major hospitals, according to Miskellah. And there's also a shortage of health workers due to a freeze on public service workers.

Meanwhile, healthcare workers, many of whom have no healthcare cover, are reportedly wary of putting their lives at risk. Dozens of Kenyan nurses and doctors lost their lives during the COVID-19 pandemic.
What makes this Ebola outbreak different
Kenya's agreements on Ebola with its neighbors are being called into question since the first case was recorded in Kenya, which has one of the strongest healthcare systems in the region.

Experts are questioning the state of regional cooperation on Ebola, where borders have largely remained open despite the surge in cases and deaths. "Before we trust these agreements and cooperation, then we have have to audit them and question them so that we don't just blindly believe that Kenya is doing the right thing, or that the DRC is doing the right thing," said Miskellah.

Then, there's the question of individual responsibility. Kenya requires travelers arriving from Congo, Uganda, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, Zambia, Rwanda, Burundi, Central African Republic and South Sudan to complete a health declaration form — truthfully.
Adapted from the Africalink Podcast by Benita van Eyssen.

Major aiports in cities like Rome and Milan warned of likely disruptions and advised passengers to check with their airlines.
What did authorities say about the problem?

"We would like to inform you that this morning we guaranteed the greatest possible number of departures, including intercontinental flights," ENAV said.
Shorter-distance services were more likely to be interrupted.

"Despite the anomalies encountered on the data transmission network, we are deploying all avaialable resources to minimize disruption and restore full operations as soon as possible," ENAV said. "We confirm an operational capacity of 50% of total air traffic, ensuring maximum safety at all times, which remains the Company's top priority."
ENAV said it had ruled out the possibility of the disturbance being caused by "malicious acts."

Rome airports operator ADR warned passengers that "flight delays and cancellations may occur" and advised passengers to contact their airline if uncertain. Milan airports company SEA issued a similar notice.

articles.title: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back
articles.summary: From challenging Big Tech to protecting independent journalism, Maria Ressa offers a roadmap for fighting authoritarianism in the digital age

items: Maria Ressa warns of the threats to democracy posed by authoritarian governments, technology companies, and artificial intelligence, emphasizing the need for citizens to resist authoritarianism.

Ressa identifies a dangerous alliance between political leaders and tech companies, which she describes as an 'authoritarian stack,' and highlights the lack of accountability for technology executives compared to political leaders.
She urges individuals to be proactive in defending democracy through independent journalism, conscious technology use, and community organization, stating that hope comes from collective action.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – In a wide-ranging discussion with WNYC’s Brian Lehrer for the second edition of Democracy Dialogues on October 16, Nobel Peace Prize laureate and Rappler CEO Maria Ressa warned again of the growing, still unaddressed threats to democracy posed by authoritarian governments, powerful technology companies, and now, artificial intelligence.

blocks.caption: From Duterte to Big Tech: Maria Ressa’s blueprint on fighting back

blocks.text: The conversation, held at The Greene Space in New York, centered on Ressa’s new book, The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators, which lays out practical strategies for citizens to resist authoritarianism, and reclaim control over the technologies shaping their lives.

Drawing from Rappler’s experience under former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, Ressa argued that the Philippines offers important lessons for the United States and other democracies now confronting similar threats, emphasizing how the fight can start at the individual level, and that it will take a global effort to reverse the current course of the world.

Ressa identifies two forms of authoritarian power threatening democracy: traditional political dictators and technology companies that have long wielded enormous influence over information, public opinion, and society.

She argued that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg represents an even greater concentration of power than Duterte because, unlike political leaders who can face prosecution, technology executives operate with limited mechanisms for accountability.
“The bigger dictator, and you’ll see this in both How to Stand Up to a Dictator and The Fight Back, is actually Mark Zuckerberg,” Ressa said.
“While Duterte is now detained at The Hague… We have systems of accountability for that, but for the technology that rules our lives, we have none.”
She added: “My dictators: One is on trial and the other one has gained more power.”

Ressa also warned of an emerging alliance between political leaders and technology billionaires, which she describes as an “authoritarian stack.” Through political funding, government contracts, and control over critical technology infrastructure, powerful companies can gain influence over government functions and democratic institutions.
“This is power and money. Look at the power and money,” she said, arguing that the concentration of political and technological power amounts to a “tech coup” unfolding in plain sight.
Ressa also described the Philippines as an early example of how social media could be weaponized to undermine democracy.

She recalled how during the Duterte administration, Rappler faced coordinated online attacks followed by legal cases and government investigations, and how the hashtag #ArrestMariaRessa began circulating in 2017, two years before her actual arrest.
She realized later that that had been “fertilizer” for a narrative that allowed the government to shape public opinion in order to make the arrest.
“When you repeat a lie a million times, it becomes a fact,” Ressa reiterated.
Beyond social media, Ressa warned that artificial intelligence presents a new and potentially more dangerous challenge to democratic accountability.

She described three stages in the evolution of technology’s influence over individuals: social media capturing attention, chatbots creating a sense of intimacy, and autonomous AI agents acquiring the capacity to perform actions independently.

Speaking about her work as co-chair of the United Nations’ Independent International Scientific Panel on Artificial Intelligence, Ressa argued that increasingly powerful AI systems are being deployed without sufficient safeguards or accountability.
“As early as July, we had actually already said, and these are from the scientists, that the frontier models cannot be controlled by the people who are making it,” she said.
“And if you really feel that, then you should not be releasing these. You should not be treating the public around the world as Pavlov’s dogs.”

Ressa criticized the argument that rapid AI deployment is necessary to compete with China, saying geopolitical competition should not become an excuse for exposing the public to potentially harmful technologies.
“The question here is, if we go back to impunity, right? Who is accountable for this?” she asked, saying the problem is the lack of legislation.

She emphasized that AI governance cannot be left to the United States and China alone. Developing countries and other governments must have a meaningful role in shaping global rules, particularly because they may bear significant consequences of decisions made by the world’s largest technology companies.
“The world needs to have a place at the table,” Ressa said.

She also discussed how AI has undermined journalism, noting that Google Search’s use of AI summaries has caused a drop that is “catastrophic for news organizations. This is part of the tech-fueled crisis that journalism faces now, along with how 85% of digital advertising in the Philippines now goes to these tech companies owning the platforms.

blocks.caption: Maria Ressa: Journalists must build, own technology to protect information integrity

blocks.text: That fuels the “market failure” for journalism right now she said.
Without journalism, authoritarian power wins.
“Why do you need journalists? Because the journalists are the ones that do the investigative report that hold power to account,” she said.

Ressa urged audiences to support independent news organizations through subscriptions and donations. She also argued that societies must consider building alternative, public-interest technology infrastructure rather than remaining dependent on platforms controlled by a handful of corporations.

Aside from supporting independent journalism, she also outlined other strategies for fighting authoritarianism, which includes identifying authoritarian forces in one’s country, protecting elections from manipulation, and organizing communities to resist abuses of power.

blocks.caption: Limit AI now or humanity will lose its agency, says Nobel laureate Maria Ressa

blocks.text: She also urged people to become more conscious of how technology influences their behavior.
“Track your screen time. Track how much time you spend on screens,” she advised. “And then the second step in chapter one is delete the social media app that makes you angriest.”
Ressa cautioned against becoming overly dependent on AI chatbots, warning that outsourcing thinking and writing to these systems could weaken people’s ability to reason independently.

“Don’t stop thinking, especially if you’re young. Like, write. Don’t stop writing because using a chatbot is like trying to run a marathon and outsourcing going to the gym,” she said. Avoid “cognitive surrender,” she said.
Again drawing from Rappler’s experience under Duterte, Ressa emphasized that organizations and individuals must prepare for authoritarian threats before they become crises.
“What we learned in Rappler, and this is like practical advice, whatever it is you’re most afraid of, imagine it. Take it, own it, embrace it, and then workflow a response to it,” she said.

She recalled how Rappler developed contingency plans for a possible government shutdown, dividing responsibilities among teams and regularly conducting drills to ensure the newsroom could continue operating.

Ressa also urged journalists to avoid amplifying authoritarian propaganda merely to criticize it. Rather than becoming distracted by inflammatory statements, she said journalists should identify lies, provide context, investigate underlying systems of power, and help audiences understand why events matter.
“If it’s a distraction, don’t amplify. If it’s a lie, just call it a lie and then find the deeper meaning,” she said.
Ressa closed the discussion by emphasizing that defending democracy is ultimately a matter of individual and collective action.

Her central message was that hope is not something citizens should passively wait for. It must emerge from their willingness to defend democratic institutions, support one another, and confront abuses of power.
“Hope comes from action,” Ressa said. “Act! That’s what I’m saying. Act, right? That’s what the moment demands. If we act, we can do something about it.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Museum releases historical photos of island where Amelia Earhart may have crashed
articles.summary:
Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance

A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the…

blocks.text: A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.

The black-and-white images were published by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand after renewed interest in one of the biggest mysteries of the 20th century, spurred by a US expedition to the Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro in search of new clues.

While some low-resolution copies have been uploaded on blogs, the Air Force Museum of New Zealand said it had received several requests for the photos and had released the full set of 47 images in digital high-resolution format on its website.
The negatives were found more than a decade ago by the archivist Matthew O’Sullivan, the keeper of photographs at the museum in Christchurch.

blocks.caption: One of 47 images released by the Air Force Museum of New Zealand of Gardner Island, now Nikumaroro. Photograph: RNZAF/RNZAF Official

blocks.text: Earhart’s most prominent investigator, Ric Gillespie, described the images as a “goldmine” in his blog, saying they were a complete set of aerial photos taken on 1 December 1938 by an amphibious biplane during a New Zealand survey of Pacific islands that was looking for suitable airbase locations.

What happened to Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan when they disappeared on 2 July 1937 during an attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator has been a stop-and-start search over eight decades, and filled with false leads.

A leading theory is that the aviator who broke several records, including becoming the first woman to fly a nonstop solo trip across the Atlantic, ran out of fuel and was marooned on Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

The hypothesis is that she survived for a while, drinking rainwater and eating fish and turtles, based on signs of a castaway’s campsite and artefacts, including glass from a jar that is thought to have contained cosmetic cream.

blocks.caption: Amelia Earhart standing in front of the Lockheed Electra in which she disappeared in July 1937.  Photograph: Alamy

blocks.text: This week, archaeologists and scientists from Earhart’s former benefactor, Purdue University in Indianapolis, are searching a part of the island for the “Taraia Object”, an elongated shape in a lagoon named after the part of the island where it was first noticed in a 2020 satellite image. Other longtime Earhart explorers, including Gillespie, are not convinced, saying it is probably a fallen tree and not the wreckage of her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. The small atoll had been visited dozens of times.

In their latest update on Nikumaroro, which is part of the archipelago country of Kiribati, the expedition said “severe weather” had hampered their metal-detecting but that they would release an update within 48 hours.

“Despite Thursday’s weather delay, the expedition remains on schedule, with two more days of field operations planned – and an update on the identification of the Taraia Object expected,” Purdue University said.

“We understand the tremendous interest in what we’re doing at Nikumaroro, and we appreciate everyone’s patience,” said Rick Pettigrew, the expedition lead and executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute. “This is a complex scientific process. You don’t simply arrive at a site and immediately identify what’s there. We have to carefully collect the data, analyse it and reach sound conclusions.”
The New Zealand military images are some of the earliest photographic evidence of the island. There is no immediate sign of an object in the Taraia area.

articles.title: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus
articles.summary:
Joshua Foster pleaded guilty over death of toddler who fell from fourth-floor window of hotel during family holiday

A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his…

blocks.text: A British man has been handed a €3,000 (£2,500) fine after his two-year-old son fell nearly 12 metres (40ft) to his death from the fourth floor window of a hotel in Cyprus.
Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed the boy on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard.
The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
Foster, an auditor, held back tears as his sentence was read out by the district judge Froso Christodoulidou.
After the 25-minute hearing, Foster hugged his lawyer before embracing his parents.
The boy fell from the fourth floor of the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday.
The court previously heard that Foster, his wife, two children and in-laws had arrived in Cyprus in the early hours of the morning on the date of the incident.

blocks.caption: The family were on holiday at the  King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas, Cyprus, when the incident happened. Photograph: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA

blocks.text: After various activities, including visiting the pool, the family returned to their rooms to get ready to go out for dinner.
At about 6pm, Foster, his father-in-law and son walked towards the lift, and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou told the court that the defendant was in a “good mood” and was playing with his son.
The court was told that as they approached the lift, the boy noticed a waterpark outside.
It was said that Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill, the boy looked out, and the “inconceivable” unfolded before Foster had a chance to react.
Alexandrou told the hearing, which took place on 6 October, that Foster’s life “changed for ever” from that moment.
It was heard that Foster had not realised that the section of the window was open, and that he thought there was protective glass.
Prosecutor Chryso Pergandi said that at around 6.40pm, police received reports that a child had fallen from the fourth floor of the beachfront hotel under unknown circumstances.
The boy was taken to Paphos general hospital where, despite efforts to resuscitate him, he was pronounced dead.
In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said that when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy “fell before he had a chance to grab him”.
After the incident, Foster was taken to Paphos general hospital and a blood sample to detect drugs and alcohol was taken.
Tests showed that the alcohol concentration in his blood was an estimated 124mg.
Alcohol consumption did not form a significant part of the case against Foster, and his lawyer said there was no testimony that he was drunk.
The lawyer told the court that Foster had no previous convictions and his remorse “is clear”.
He said he was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident, adding that while grieving for his child he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened.
The court heard the window was 2.85 metres wide and 1.2 metres high.

articles.title: ‘Opening the lid of a horrible secret’: Jamaicans confront enslavement with taboo-busting stories on screen
articles.summary:
As violent spirits are unleashed in Sky’s Possession, observers see confident creatives reclaiming the island’s narratives in a form of ‘cultural reparation’

A woman opens a 300‑year‑old…

blocks.text: A woman opens a 300‑year‑old box, unleashing a violent spirit – it is the spirit of colonialism and oppression roaring back to life. It is a pivotal scene in Sky’s supernatural series Possession and symbolises a wider shift in Jamaica’s film industry, where directors are increasingly using the landscape to tell Jamaican stories – including those that confront enslavement, trauma and historical memory.

The series is about a biracial British lawyer who travels to Jamaica to investigate a multimillion-pound inheritance dispute, only to uncover a dark, vengeful spirit tied to the plantation’s brutal colonial past.

For the Jamaican director, Storm Saulter, ensuring that the trauma and enduring legacy of enslavement and colonisation were powerfully represented was critical. Caribbean countries are increasingly arguing that centuries of enslavement have left the region at a lasting disadvantage – fuelling renewed calls for reparations.

Dr Lisa Tomlinson, a lecturer in film studies at the University of the West Indies, says the themes in Jamaican films are changing. “They’re now very much connected and reflective of Jamaican stories – stories that were previously taboo or avoided.”

blocks.caption: Mbatha-Raw plays a lawyer who travels from Bristol to Jamaica to handle an inheritance claim over a former slave plantation. Photograph: Des Willie

blocks.text: While Jamaican films are not always explicitly about reparations, she argues that many are engaging with the legacies of enslavement through cultural memory. “Reparation is not just a political act,” she says. “It’s also culture. These African‑derived spiritualities, the historical knowledge – when they come through creative expression, what they do is give us authority to tell our own stories.”

This, she says, is a form of “cultural reparation”, a reclaiming of narratives devalued or suppressed under colonialism, and a way of educating audiences about the past in ways that academics or politicians struggle to do. “The arts play a critical role in how we are educated in public awareness around reparation,” she says.

Jacqueline Jackson, Jamaica’s film commissioner, sees the shift too. She says productions such as Possession and Delroy Lindo’s Jabari’s People – shot entirely in Jamaica – reflect growing confidence and ambition among Jamaican creatives. “We are well established as a destination for international productions,” she says. “But what we want to see more of is local production and international collaboration that enables us to tell our own stories.”

blocks.caption: Delroy Lindo’s directorial debut Jabari’s People (he is pictured here in Spike Lee’s Da 5 Bloods) is shot entirely in Jamaica.  Photograph: Netflix

blocks.text: Both productions, she notes, worked closely with Jamaican talent to ensure authenticity and demonstrate what is possible when international financing and distribution unite with Jamaican creativity. “They show the growing interest in Jamaican stories and their potential for global audiences,” she says.

Tomlinson believes diaspora film-makers are playing a particularly important role in this shift. Unlike foreign productions that often use Jamaica as an exotic backdrop, diaspora directors are “moving away from the tourist‑gaze depictions” and are “capturing Jamaican everyday life”.

Saulter sees his series as part of a broader political awakening. “The mask has slipped … We’ve been told it’s one thing, and that thing is proven to be false. So there’s a seeking of what is true,” he says.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: Storm Saulter, Possession’s director, aims to ‘open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret’.  Photograph: Bertie Watson

blocks.text: He says the box‑opening scene is not simply a plot device, but a metaphor for something larger: the resurfacing of long‑suppressed histories and the growing willingness among Caribbean creatives to confront the legacies of enslavement, inherited trauma and colonial violence through film.
“Literally, we’re going to open up the lid of a 300‑year‑old horrible secret,” Saulter said. “It’s the spirit of colonial enslavement and oppression coming roaring back.”

That “spirit”, he explains, is embodied in a character who has lived through centuries of brutality – “a witness to history” – whose presence forces the protagonists to reckon with the past they have inherited.
Saulter’s interest in the subject is rooted in his upbringing. “I grew up in the countryside,” he says. “The Obia man, the church … nine nights … I’ve lived through all of those things.”

His experiences inspired him to tell stories that educate and have “real societal political impact”, while remaining thrilling, intriguing and entertaining. That approach, he argues, allows film-makers to tackle difficult histories. “As opposed to doing something that was like talking heads … we’re bringing you on a journey,” he says.
For Dr L’Antoinette Stines, a Yoruba priestess and cultural expert who advised on Possession, the series’ engagement with Afro‑spiritualist traditions is part of a longer history of resistance.

blocks.caption: Sheldon East plays Cudjoe East, the son of a British man who grew up at the Hope Hill plantation in Jamaica. Photograph: Des Willie/©Sky UK Ltd

blocks.text: “Black people have been fighting and using the arts for a very long time. It’s just that there is greater attention on it today,” she says. For decades she has choreographed similar work, she says, and stresses the importance of honouring the academics, poets and creatives who paved the way for today’s boom in authentic Jamaican storytelling.

She praises Saulter’s insistence on authenticity and creating a series that feels both contemporary and deeply rooted, exploring inherited trauma, ancestral memory and the unfinished business of colonialism.

articles.title: Burnham to deliver speech in Scotland on devolution – UK politics live
articles.summary:
The prime minister is expected to announce plans on devolving decision-making powers away from both Westminster and Holyrood towards regions and towns

Good morning and welcome to our UK…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoBurnham in Scotland as SNP minister accuses PM of 'hypocrisy' over indyref stance

blocks.text: Burnham in Scotland as SNP minister accuses PM of 'hypocrisy' over indyref stance

Good morning and welcome to our UK politics live blog. Prime minister Andy Burnham is in Scotland today where he is expected to invite Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, to collaborate on devolving decision-making powers away from both Westminster and Holyrood and pushing control further down to Scottish regions and towns.
The newswires have reported an extract of his speech, which he is expected to deliver in Lanarkshire around midday:

double quotation markDuring my first week in office, I told the first minister that I wanted to work with him to spread opportunities to communities across Scotland’s regions and cities. Through No10 North, we are rewiring the state and I want to make sure regions in Scotland are fully part of this. This is me making an offer to the Scottish government. With us working together, there is no limit to what we can achieve for the Scottish people.”
Burnham’s visit coincides with the SNP’s annual party conference in Aberdeen, which the party has said will launch the biggest pro-independence campaign since the 2014 referendum.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham’s visit to Scotland coincides with the SNP’s annual party conference in Aberdeen.  Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The Guardian

blocks.text: The prime minister has repeatedly ruled out another independence referendum, but he has been accused of hypocrisy by the SNP for proposing to reopen the debate on Brexit and re-examining the UK’s relationship with the EU.
“That hypocrisy is there for all to see and I think the Scottish electorate will take a pretty dim view of it,” SNP minister Stephen Flynn told the Press Association.
He added: “Mr Burnham wants power pushed out of Westminster – so do we.
“But let’s make sure that power and that decision making is taken by the Scottish people and they have the opportunity to do so in an independence referendum.”
In other news:

items: Young people who rely on benefits will be given less money in exchange for more intensive health and employment support under plans for a separate youth welfare system, the Financial Times reported. Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will recommend benefits for young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) be delivered through a different process, sources told the newspaper.

Reform’s Robert Jenrick has responded to claims made by his colleague Sarah Pochin that the party is “chauvinistic”, after she was caught by an undercover ITV news reporter complaining about the party’s culture. “That’s not my experience of Reform,” Jenrick told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme.

articles.title: Marcos seeks stronger, more ready PCG amid maritime challenges
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday renewed his administration"s commitment to strengthening the capabilities and readiness of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in order to better…

blocks.text: Published October 16, 2026 5:44pm

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday renewed his administration’s commitment to strengthening the capabilities and readiness of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) in order to better respond to evolving maritime issues.

In his speech during the PCG’s 125th founding anniversary celebration, the President lauded the efforts of the coast guard in watching over the Philippine waters for many years now, protecting lives and answering the call of Filipinos in times of uncertainty.

“As we mark 125 years of the Philippine Coast Guard, let us look to the horizon with confidence and a renewed commitment to strengthening its capabilities and readiness to respond to increasingly complex maritime challenges,” Marcos said.
“With capable personnel, sound leadership, and unwavering dedication to the Filipino people, I am confident that we can fulfill this mission,” he added.
The President also acknowledged the contributions of the PCG in safeguarding the marine environment and biodiversity through coastal clean-up and tree-planting activities.
He noted that the PCG also continues to engage with international partners to protect the waters that connect Philippine islands.
“We can work with the world while remaining firmly guided by our national interest and without losing sight of our duty to the Filipino people,” Marcos said.
“The waters that connect our islands must be a source of opportunity for our people, not a source of fear or uncertainty,” he added.
The President also reported that the agency conducted more than 1 million pre-departure inspections of vessels at ports nationwide to ensure the safety of maritime passengers.
He said the PCG also rescued or pre-evacuated almost 95,000 individuals through its search-and-rescue operations and assisted close to 138,800 people during disasters and emergencies. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Clashes erupt at Argentine student protests against President Milei's austerity policies
articles.summary: Demonstrators clashed with police as President Javier Milei's decision not to release funding for universities brought students and employees to the streets. Protesters say the country's future is at…

image.caption: Police used tear gas and water cannons against the protesters in Buenos AiresImage: Emiliano Lasalvia/AFP

blocks.text: Protesters took to the streets in Argentina's capital, Buenos Aires, to demonstrate against libertarian President Javier Milei's cost-cutting measures for education.
Thousands of students, university staff, trade unionists and opposition supporters crowded outside the parliament, demanding the implementation of a law to finance universities.

While the rally was largely peaceful, clashes also erupted, with reports of masked individuals throwing stones at police, injuring at least eight officers. Some 25 people were arrested, according to the country's National Security Ministry.
Reports said other protesters had tried to push those throwing stones back. Police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Security Minister Alejandra Monteoliva said the protesters wanted to "sow chaos," posting on her X account that the right to protest is not "a right to exercise violence."
Milei vetoes law, refuses to release funding

This was the fifth protest over the Milei government's education spending to take place since Milei entered office in 2023.Such a demonstration also took place in May, in which organizers say some 1.5 million people took part.

blocks.caption: Argentinian President Javier Milei was elected in 2023 after promising to dramatically cut the state's costsImage: Juan Carlos Rojas/picture alliance

blocks.text: Milei vetoed a law, passed by Congress in 2025, requiring the government to invest more money in public universities.

The University Funding Law says the state should increase employees' salaries in line with inflation dated to December 2023. It also calls for the restoration of student scholarships and more funding for universities' operations.
Congress subsequently overrode Milei's veto, and several court rulings have instructed the government to release the funds, but it has so far refused to do so.
According to Milei, who was elected after promising wide-ranging cost-cutting measures, justified his veto by saying "there is no money" for inflation-linked spending increases.

blocks.caption: Public universities in Argentina offer studies free of chargeImage: Pedro Lazaro Fernandez/REUTERS

blocks.text: A government spokesperson said the law had been "suspended" due to the government's legal action against it.
The first half of 2026 saw public spending on universities fall by 41% in real terms, according to the Center for National Economic Research of the University of Buenos Aires.
Argentina's education system is considered to be among the best in South America. Study at public universities is free, drawing students from across the region.
