articles.title: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case not ‘prioritised’ due to high workload, inquest hears
articles.summary:
Eight-year-old Queensland girl died in 2022 after being denied insulin by her religious parents

Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because…

blocks.text: Elizabeth Struhs’ child protection case was not “prioritised” or worked intensively because the staff member assigned to her case was “very busy”, a coroner has heard.

The Queensland coroners court also heard the case worker may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of Struhs’ “upper class home”, putting cases that believed to involve a more immediate risk ahead of Elizabeth’s.

The eight-year-old died on 7 January 2022 of diabetic ketoacidosis, after her father, Jason Struhs, stopped providing insulin to treat her type 1 diabetes at their home in Toowoomba, Queensland. A long-term sceptic of his wife’s beliefs, he had converted to them and joined her religious sect – which subscribed to an extreme form of Christianity and denied the use of medicine – in 2021.

Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard is holding an inquest into Elizabeth’s death. She has previously heard the eight-year-old came to the attention of child safety after a 2019 incident where she presented to hospital in a coma.
Child safety ended its involvement with the family after just 17 weeks of what was supposed to be an intensive intervention, assessing her as “safe”.

But the single child safety officer assigned to Elizabeth’s case told the court on Friday her approach wasn’t intensive and she didn’t make weekly check-ins during that period, despite departmental guidelines.

The department chose to release her back into Jason’s sole care over the objections of specialist doctors who treated Elizabeth in Brisbane, subject to a voluntary intervention with parental agreement (IPA).
The coroner heard just a single child safety officer was assigned to the case, and would often conduct home visits alone.
The officer gave evidence on Friday.

“Ideally I wanted to visit with the family at least once a week, in accordance with our IPAT (intervention with parental agreement team) guidelines,” according to her statement, presented to the court.

“During my management of the IPA for the Struhs family, I recall that I was not always available to conduct home visits with the family. I recall this being a very busy time for the CSSC (child safety service centre) and I also recall being regularly out of the office travelling to visit other families.
“I note that one of the home visits to the Struhs family was conducted by a student who was working in the team at the time.”
She said Elizabeth’s case wasn’t treated as a complex case, which it should have been due to the intervention.

But at the time, she had a “big caseload” – approximately 25-28 children in 15 families on the same intervention– she said. The coroner has previously heard that the Toowoomba region was among the busiest in the state for child safety.

Counsel assisting Simon Hamlyn-Harris said most of them were experiencing significant domestic violence, drug use, sexual abuse and it was not often that she was required to work with “upper class families” like the Struhs.
The case worker agreed that she may and may have been “overly influenced” by the presentation of the Struhs home.
“I believe that we may have prioritised other cases at the time for children who were presenting at more immediate risk,” she told the court.
She also told the court that she may have had a bias because her own child had nearly died of type 1 diabetes at age 6. She had asked not to be assigned to the case, she said.

Several witnesses have previously told the coroner they expected the intervention to last months or a year, but the case worker said they were supposed to not last longer than three months, because they were an intensive approach.
On Friday, Kirkegaard asked another child safety witness whether they felt “organisational pressure to get a matter like this finalised quickly”.
“Absolutely,” the witness said, adding an IPA could be intrusive and potentially harmful to a child if dragged out.
“I don’t believe it impacted our decision making,” she said.
On 13 November 2019, a more senior child safety officer assessed Elizabeth as “safe” and the intervention was ended.
The case worker told the coroner on Friday that she hadn’t appreciated the danger of Elizabeth’s mother’s church group, which was considered a source of support for the family.
All 14 adult members of the sect – known as the Saints – were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including Elizabeth’s parents, Kerrie and Jason, and the group leader, Brendan Stevens.
In her statement she said Jason had agreed to continue to treat his daughter against his wife’s beliefs and that she had “faith” that should Kerrie stand in the way he’d leave her.
None of the witnesses can be identified for legal reasons.
The inquest continues.

articles.title: One Nation proposes $2,000 baby subsidy in Victoria but says it won’t touch state abortion laws
articles.summary:
Announcement comes a day after Liberal and Labor parties say they will cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care

  • Get our

blocks.text: One Nation has proposed a $2,000 baby bonus for new parents in Victoria – a day after the Labor and Liberal parties both agreed to cover out-of-pocket costs for abortion care.

The deputy leader of One Nation in Victoria, Colleen Harkin, announced the plan on Friday to remove out-of-pocket costs for pregnant women in the public healthcare system and a $2,000 subsidy for those accessing private maternity care.
She said it would cost $136m over four years but admitted it was a “ballpark” figure that would depend on how many babies were born each year.
“We don’t go hard on figures, because we actually don’t have access to the detail of this stuff,” Harkin told reporters.
She said One Nation “will not touch the abortion laws” in Victoria despite the federal party’s national platform pledging to “seek every opportunity to roll back brutal and extreme abortion law”.
“We have no state abortion policy because it is not our focus whatsoever,” Harkin said, accusing the Labor party of “lying” and “engaging with really cheap American-style scaremongering”.

On Thursday, Labor announced that, if re-elected in November, it would eliminate out-of-pocket costs for abortion care, costing $30m over four years, and claimed One Nation could use abortion as a negotiating chip with the Coalition in the event of a hung parliament.

Under Labor’s plan, private providers would be paid to deliver medical and surgical abortions up to 16 weeks’ gestation. Women would no longer have to pay for GP and specialist consultations, scans, tests or medication, which can cost up to $1,000. Those in regional Victoria who must travel long distances for care would also be eligible for a subsidy.
The government would extend access to medical abortion from nine to 10 weeks’ gestation, while commissioning a clinical review into whether it could safely be offered at up to 12 weeks’ gestation.

Within hours the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, said the Coalition would match the plan to cover out-of-pocket costs and the travel subsidy. In a statement she said “the Liberals and Nationals will not allow Labor to play politics on this issue”.
On Friday, Fiona Carroll, the wife of the premier, Ben Carroll, defended her husband for raising abortion in the leadup to the election.
“It does build on the Labor legacy, and I don’t think I’m politicising this because it is fundamental to the women in this state,” she said.
Fiona said it was “even better” the Coalition had matched the commitment, as it would “take some of that fear” out of the election for women.
Neither the Liberal party nor Labor responded to a request for comment on One Nation’s policy.

Anti-abortion activist Joanna Howe criticised Wilson, describing the Liberals as being in “lock step with Labor on every vile and evil policy” and directing her followers in Victoria to back One Nation. The Australian Christian Lobby’s Victorian director, Jasmine Yeun, said it was “getting more difficult to vote for a major party”.

But the chief executive of Women’s Health Victoria, Sally Hasler, welcomed the bipartisanship on the issue. It means no matter who is elected, Victoria will become the first state to provide abortion free.
“We are very reassured to know that it won’t be an election issue because we have support from both the ALP and the Coalition to not just protect rights but to expand rights,” Hasler said.
She described One Nation’s announcement as a deliberate attempt to frame reproductive healthcare as a choice between abortion and maternity care.
“Responding to an abortion care announcement with a maternity care announcement is a false trade-off, and it’s a deliberate one,” she said.
“It is a well-played move from the international anti-rights agenda to wind back women’s rights – one which narrowly defines women’s reproductive health.”

articles.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
articles.summary:
Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia

Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla…
articles.byline: Stefano Valentino in Sulawesi and Ajit Niranjan

blocks.text: Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.

Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.

Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland.
Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people.

“We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.”

blocks.caption: Wadimula: ‘Destroying [the forest] means destroying our own life.’ Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined.

Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes.

In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam.

blocks.caption: Morowali industrial park on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary. Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL.

The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform.

The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found.

Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year.

The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared.

Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm TreeMap suggests.

blocks.caption: A track cut through forest in the Hengjaya concession. Photograph: Stefano Valentino

blocks.text: Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral (SCM), the company that operates the Cahaya mine, contributed to clearing an additional 330 hectares of forest in 2024, according to an analysis by Auriga, an Indonesian nonprofit. The same year, it delivered 11m tonnes of limonite ore – almost all of its production – to Huayou’s smelter. Deliveries increased to nearly 12.5m tonnes throughout 2025. The plant also continued to receive ore from the Hengjaya mine by road, local lorry drivers said.

SCM received two administrative sanctions last year for illegally clearing more than 450 hectares of forest beyond the boundaries of its permitted clearing area. The company is a subsidiary of Merdeka Battery Materials, part of a group whose shareholders include Huayou and CATL.

The carmakers identified as end-users of Huayou cathodes or recipients of shipments from CATL include Volkswagen, Volvo, Ford, General Motors, Tesla, BMW, Stellantis and Hyundai. Mercedes-Benz was separately linked to Huayou.

Many of the companies said they did not source nickel directly, they assessed and mitigated adverse impacts, and they required suppliers to comply with responsible sourcing standards. They declined to share the results of on-site audits.
Volkswagen, Europe’s leading manufacturer, which powered one-quarter of its vehicles with CATL systems in 2024, said it could not rule out that the companies may fall within its supply chain.

Volkswagen said: “We take potential risks in our supply chain very seriously. However, due to contractual obligations with our business partners, we cannot disclose specific details on our supplier relationships or their supply chain.”
Ford said: “We are committed to protecting human rights and the environment. We are reviewing the allegations and will determine any appropriate next steps based on that review.”

Mercedes-Benz said: “We take reports of environmental and social harm in raw material supply chains – including nickel from Indonesia – seriously and assess them as part of our risk-based due diligence.”

Renault Group said: “We have identified a nickel mining site in Sulawesi, Indonesia, as being a tier-n supplier (eg. indirect) in our battery supply chain. We have engaged with the relevant business partners to verify some ESG information concerning Sulawesi Cahaya Mineral.”

Volvo Cars said: “During 2025, we conducted […] onsite audits […] on suppliers [who are] part of our battery supply chains, two of them located in Indonesia […] with further battery supply chain partners during 2026 and onward.”
General Motors said: “We are aware that nickel mining in Indonesia presents significant environmental, human-rights and community-related risks.”

Stellantis said: “We are aware of the environmental and social challenges associated with nickel production in Indonesia, including risks related to deforestation, biodiversity loss and ecosystem degradation.”

Hyundai said: “We recognise the importance of protecting forests, biodiversity and local communities. We regularly monitor and assess our suppliers, including mineral suppliers, to ensure compliance.”
CATL, Huayou, SCM and Tesla did not respond to requests for comment. Tsingshan, the main shareholder of Nickel Industries, which operates Hengjaya mine, did not respond to a request for comment.
This investigation was supported by Journalismfund Europe and The Pulitzer Center. Lorenzo Di Stasi and James Jackson contributed reporting.

articles.title: Exclusive Brethren head denies knowing church members were volunteering for Liberal party during 2025 election
articles.summary:
Bruce Hales also denies church was a cult while son tells parliamentary committee it was ‘a bit rough’ being labelled as such

  • Get our

blocks.text: The most senior member of the Exclusive Brethren has denied any knowledge of or involvement in thousands of members from his church volunteering for the Liberal party at the 2025 election.

The Plymouth Brethren christian church has rejected claims it coordinated volunteers and a campaign for the Coalition, and that it secretly paid far-right figures to stage stunts against the prime minister and other Labor MPs.

The fiery parliamentary committee hearing on Friday was marred by clashes, with members of the committee accusing one another of “religious persecution” and “running a protection racket” for the church.
Bruce Hales, the Brethren’s most senior member, said he had no involvement or knowledge of church members volunteering for the Coalition.
“I want to be clear and unequivocal. I had no involvement whatsoever in relation to any members who volunteered or took part in any aspect of the 2025 federal election,” he told the inquiry.
“I did not plan such activities. I did not coordinate such activities. I did not direct such activities. I did not fund such activities.”
Hales denied that his church was a cult, a term used by the prime minister, while his son, Gareth Hales, who also appeared before the committee, said it was “a bit rough” being labelled as such.

Gareth Hales gave evidence on Friday he had met Morgan C Jonas and Chris de Bruyne separately in a business capacity, and briefly discussed the “general direction the government was headed”. The independent MP Andrew Gee referred to the two as far-right activists, although Gareth Hales denied knowing their political affiliations at the time.

Nine newspapers have reported Jonas and de Bruyne were involved in a campaign that targeted Labor and other left-leaning politicians during the election. Gareth Hales denied reports his company Sante Global paid the two men to disrupt other campaigns.
There was turmoil in the committee as Coalition members likened questioning by Labor and crossbench MPs to a “Spanish Inquisition”.

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie and Liberal MP Ben Small repeatedly interrupted questions, calling them “disgraceful” and “disrespectful”. McKenzie said the line of questioning looked “a lot like religious persecution”, while Small was accused of trying to answer questions for the church.
Gee, who was previously a Nationals MP, said the two were running an “old Liberal party protection racket”, a comment he was forced to withdraw.

On 20 April 2025, just under two weeks before the federal election, Bruce Hales gave a sermon where he told members to be “fervent in prayer for good government”, and that the country needed to be happy again and smiling again.
after newsletter promotion

The latter two phrases were seen on posters endorsing the Liberal party during the campaign. Bruce Hales denied his sermon was a call to action and said he had no knowledge of his words being used in billboards and advertising at the election.

Nine newspapers reported the sermon had been broadcast and then turned into a text message by Gareth Hale and his brothers, which said, “We need to make sure our booths are manned and our volunteers are fired up.”

Gareth Hales, who has no official role in the church, said he could not confirm or deny whether he had written this message but denied instructing members to join the campaign. He said he had encouraged members who had already been volunteering to “keep doing what they were doing”.
Gee, who claimed he was tailed by several Brethren members in his regional New South Wales electorate, said it “defies belief” that the church had no role in coordinating volunteers.
Gareth Hales said they were not acting as members of the church.

“I can understand it’s difficult to believe but they weren’t members of the church, they were members of concerned business groups and members of private citizens – they weren’t there on behalf of the church,” Gareth Hales said.
Gee replied: “I, for one, am not buying what you are selling but I do appreciate you giving evidence today.”

articles.title: Trump calls Ukraine’s resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries a ‘disgrace’
articles.summary:
US president says Zelenskyy ‘more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin’ after so-called energy ceasefire collapses

Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has called Ukraine’s renewed strikes on Russian oil refineries a “disgrace”, while renewing his criticism of Volodymyr ⁠Zelenskyy after an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine collapsed.

Ukraine resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries ⁠after Zelenskyy said that Kyiv was abandoning a ceasefire abruptly declared by Trump last week, one that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
“All he’s doing is making the world oil price higher. Well, I think that’s a disgrace,” the US president told the Newsmax news outlet in an interview aired on Thursday.

“There are a lot ‌of targets you can ‌hit, but when you shoot at diesel refineries where you make, you know, ‌diesel oil, and we need that, and the world needs that, then he’s not doing a good service for the world.”
Relations between Kyiv and Washington have soured since last week, when Trump eased sanctions on Russia in exchange for Moscow releasing large amounts of diesel on to global markets.

Zelenskyy slammed the agreement, which was widely interpreted as an attempt to curb high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm election, saying it would allow Russia to press on with its full-scale invasion of Ukraine that began more than four and a half years ago. US efforts under Trump to end the war have made no progress.

Trump repeated to Newsmax his views of the two leaders involved in the conflict. “I’m not a big fan of Zelenskyy,” Trump said. “I think they actually both would like to see it ⁠end, but I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult ​to deal with ​than Putin.”

Kyiv’s relationship with Washington was strained further this week when Ukraine said Starlink services had been restricted, in effect hobbling Ukrainian drone strike missions and crucial air defences with a flick of the switch.
During a visit to London this week, the Ukrainian president said the sudden restriction of Starlink had left him feeling personally betrayed by Trump and lamented losing a partner.

British defence secretary Wes Streeting said on Thursday his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, had assured him in a face-to-face meeting that the vital satellite communications system had been restored. In an interview with the BBC, he said it was unclear what had caused the disruption, but added: “This is not the first time we’ve seen a falling out between Washington and Kyiv.”

Amid growing doubts about long-term US commitment to Ukraine, European leaders have shown their support for Zelenskyy, who met Nato chief Mark Rutte in Brussels and held a string of bilateral meetings before he was set to join an EU summit on Friday.
After meeting Zelenskyy, French president Emmanuel Macron said it was “crucial” that Ukraine receive “all the means necessary to protect itself”.
“I can reassure you, dear Ukrainian friends and President Zelenskyy: YOU ARE NOT ALONE,” Polish prime minister Donald Tusk posted online.
As he met with Macron in Brussels, Zelensky said that the Kremlin had “launched yet another vile drone strike on Ukrainian energy infrastructure” in the city of Lutsk, which caused blackouts.
The Kremlin meanwhile accused Ukraine of derailing US peace efforts by resuming its strikes on refineries.

articles.title: Sara Duterte was told prosecutors might drop 3 impeachment charges
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte and her defense team had an inkling that House prosecutors would reduce the impeachment case against her to a single charge, as rumors of the move had already been abound,…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 1:32pm

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte and her defense team had an inkling that House prosecutors would reduce the impeachment case against her to a single charge, as rumors of the move had already been abound, two of her defense lawyers said.

In separate interviews, defense spokesperson Michael Poa and deputy spokesperson Justin Nicol Gular said Duterte was told of the possible withdrawal before prosecutors formally made a motion for it on Tuesday, October 13. At the time the vice president was briefed, she had wanted to think things over before acting.

"Actually, when I heard the rumors, I already updated her," Poa said on ANC's "Headstart" on Thursday, October 15. "When I spoke to her right after, all she said to me was, 'You know what, let's sleep on this. Let's think about things first.'"
"She wasn't surprised because, as we said, she had been informed beforehand of the possibility," Gular said in Filipino in an interview with One PH on Thursday.
The prosecution on Tuesday withdrew Article I on the alleged misuse of confidential funds, Article III on alleged bribery at the Department of Education and Article IV on alleged grave threats.
Only Article II, on unexplained wealth, remains.
The Senate impeachment court accepted the withdrawal and lifted the sub judice rule on the three dropped charges, allowing both sides to discuss them in public.
Poa said he would meet Duterte in the coming days because the defense must file a manifestation stating her position on the ruling.
Days before the hearing, the defense had been picking up "chismis" or gossip, that prosecutors might drop three articles, Gular said.
But as the defense team prepared for October 13, formally, only one withdrawal was certain, Gular said, as prosecutors had already filed a manifestation to drop the bribery charge.
"We receive a lot of information during the course of this trial. But you never know if it will happen or turn out to be true," Gular said.
Why the defense objects
Poa said the defense's first reaction to the lifting of the sub judice rule was that it creates "complications."
The grave threats charge is one article that Duterte's lawyers cannot yet speak about in public, as a regional trial court hearing Duterte's separate criminal case has issued a gag order, Poa said.
The defense spokesperson also lamented the limitations that would come with defending allegations at a press conference and not in court.
Some witnesses the defense wanted to subpoena "are not necessarily aligned with us," Poa said, and could not be summoned to a press conference.

He would not speculate on whether the court will still let the defense call witnesses on the dropped charges. The burden is on the defense to show they are relevant, he said, and prosecutors have the right to object.
"We also don't want to be seen as wasting the time of the court. But again, fairness is something we've always asked for," Poa said.
'Court still trying to balance' issues, Poa acknowledges
Asked whether the court has remained fair, Poa said, "I would like to say yes."
"I don't want to say the court is unfair because the court is still trying to balance the situation, as I've seen the presiding officer do," he said.
"Without casting aspersions on the prosecution, perhaps they had a strategy that they had to tweak along the way," Poa said.
The defense will begin presenting its evidence on November 9. The trial is on hold while the Senate takes up the proposed 2027 national budget.
Asked if the defense would likely finish before Christmas, Poa said: "I don't want to box us in to a schedule. It's not about delaying or prolonging the proceedings or shortening the proceedings."
The withdrawal forced the defense to "restrategize," he said, and it may drop witnesses or call others it had held in reserve.
"I think all of us would want to finish, personally, before Christmas, but we can't box the defense in," Poa said.

But will the vice president take the stand? Poa said: "If there's a trigger point, meaning aspects of the case that we feel may only be explained by the vice president herself or attorney Mans Carpio himself, we will have to advise them," he said.
"But at the end of the day, it will be their decision if they want to take the stand or not," he added.
Article II accuses Duterte of having unlawful business interests and amassing wealth she did not declare in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
articles.summary:
Rights group says Youssef al-Manasif was tortured and first met his lawyer five years after arrest for non-violent crimes

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending…

blocks.text: A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.
The charity Reprieve says Manasif was tortured and coerced into signing a false confession and only met his state-appointed lawyer for the first time in 2022 – five years after his arrest.
Manasif’s death sentence has now reportedly been upheld by the Saudi supreme court, which was likely to be his last hope of avoiding execution.

His family have not spoken in public about the case and could face harassment or arrest if they do so. “There is nothing they can do now but wait,” said Duaa Dhainy, a consultant for Reprieve and the European Saudi Organisation for Human Rights.

Saudi Arabia has seen what activists describe as a “horrifying” surge in executions under the rule of the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Last year saw a record 356 people put to death in the country. Most of those executed are foreigners convicted of minor and non-violent drug crimes.
At least 17 people, who were children at the time of their alleged offences, have been executed in Saudi Arabia since 2015, according to Reprieve.
Saudi Arabia issued a royal decree abolishing the death penalty for children in 2020, stating that individuals would not be sentenced to death for crimes committed when they were minors.

However, it has since upheld the death penalty in a number of cases involving child defendants. In April, it executed Ali al-Subaiti, along with his uncle, Mustafa al-Subaiti, for non-lethal “terrorist” offences committed when he was 12 years old.
after newsletter promotion

The UN’s independent human rights experts have previously expressed concerns about Manasif’s case. It said Saudi Arabia should immediately halt planned executions of people convicted of offences allegedly committed when they were under 18.

“They are using execution as a tool to show how powerful they are and how they can threaten anyone who does not follow their rules,” Dhainy said of the Saudi regime. “We think he should be treated as a minor and not sentenced to death as his charges relate to when he was under 18.”
Human Rights Watch said executing Manasif for a non-violent crime committed as a minor would be “an unconscionable new low”.

articles.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
articles.summary: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
articles.byline: Joshua Cheetham, Thomas Copeland, Alison Benjamin

blocks.text: ByJoshua CheethamThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC Verify
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

blocks.caption: Map of the Gulf and Strait of Hormuz showing 12 reported attacks on ships between 5 and 11 October. Red dots indicate the approximate locations of incidents, with the majority clustered around the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman, near the Musandam Peninsula. Additional attacks are marked f…

blocks.text: Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks

blocks.caption: Two images showing a tanker on fire - taken from a smaller boat

blocks.text: The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

blocks.caption: Two images showing (left) a container ship listing to the stern and (right) smaller boats gathered near a shipping container

blocks.text: Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.

About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.

blocks.caption: Area chart showing the 7-day rolling average of oil shipments exiting the Strait of Hormuz since the first of August. In early August daily shipments were about six million barrels on average, which trended upward to 15 million barrels per day in late September. This has dipped slightly down to 1…

blocks.text: The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

blocks.caption: An annotated satellite image showing a number of tankers carrying out ship-to-ship transfers off the coast of Oman

blocks.text: So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.

Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.

blocks.caption: Three images from a ship at sea showing smoke rising on the horizon. In the left image, thick dark smoke billows into the night sky beside a vessel's deck. In the centre image, crew members wearing safety gear stand on a ship's deck as smoke rises in the distance. In the right image, a large plum…

blocks.text: Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

articles.title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
articles.summary: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.

blocks.text: Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum.
"It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia.
Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier.

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face.
US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement.

In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account.
The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours.
"At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere."
Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home.
"I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?"
Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees.

Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia.

One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison.
"We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee.
And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere.

Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025.
"Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC.

Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data.

Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns.

Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds.

Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries.

Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face.

"I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me."
He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt.
"I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'".
Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad.
"Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life."
The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them."

The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase.
The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment.

Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home.
Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information".

Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence.
The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned.
"We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!"
"We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly."
Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned.
The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages.
For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving.

There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia.

Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge — or send them back.

articles.title: ‘It’s about the underdog’: Ben Roberts-Smith launches brand to support family amid legal battle
articles.summary:
Accused war criminal announces venture with video on Instagram of him walking along beach and working out

  • Get our

blocks.text: Accused war criminal Ben Roberts-Smith has launched a brand, saying he needs the income to support his family and fund his legal expenses after being charged with murdering or ordering the murders of five unarmed detainees while deployed in Afghanistan between 2009 and 2012.

Roberts-Smith launched the label with a video on Instagram of him walking along a beach on the Gold Coast and working out, soundtracked by media reports about him being awarded the Victoria Cross and his subsequent arrest. The video included the caption: “Get ready….the time has come. #neveroutofthefight #underdog”.
Roberts-Smith, 47, was arrested in April and charged with murdering or ordering the murders of five unarmed detainees while deployed in Afghanistan between 2009 and 2012.
In a statement released that month, he said he categorically denied all allegations against him and that he had “always acted within my values, within my training and within the rules of engagement”.
Roberts-Smith said the brand EPIC 1 TWO was named after his radio call sign on the mission for which he was awarded the Victoria Cross.
“The whole premise of doing a brand, from my perspective, is to, one, I mean, I’ve gotta try and find some way to make money for my family,” he told news.com.au.

blocks.caption: Ben Roberts Smith has launched a brand. Photograph: Epic 1 TWO

blocks.text: “At the end of the day there is too much pressure from media outlets on organisations that want to support me. The classic example of that is anyone that had a profile and wants to support me gets trashed in the media just simply for saying that they think I should be entitled to a fair process.

“EPIC 1 TWO for me is 100 per cent about that. It’s about the underdog, it’s about people just knowing that no matter how hard it is for them, no matter what struggle that they face, they are going to get through it. They’ve just got to keep going.”
In a statement, Roberts-Smith said the brand represented “something very personal to me”.
“It is about accepting your personal situations but never losing hope.”
News24 commentator Peta Credlin and boxer Danny Green were among those who commented on the Instagram post congratulating Roberts-Smith.
Roberts-Smith was released on bail after his father, Len Roberts-Smith, a former Western Australian supreme court judge, paid a $250,000 surety.
Roberts-Smith facing charges
The charges against Roberts-Smith, Australia’s most decorated living soldier, relate to three separate incidents, according to court documents.
after newsletter promotion
Charges one and two against Roberts-Smith relate to two alleged murders committed at the village of Kakarak in southern Afghanistan on 12 April 2009.
Two men, a father and son named Mohammad Essa and Ahmadullah, were found hiding in a tunnel in a compound given the designation “Whiskey 108”.

It is alleged Ahmadullah, who wore a prosthetic leg, was then carried outside the compound walls, “thrown to the ground and shot multiple times by Roberts-Smith with a belt-fed machine gun”, in an act witnessed by several Australian soldiers.
Roberts-Smith then allegedly walked back into the area inside the compound where Mohammad Essa remained, and ordered another soldier to kill him.
The third charge relates to an incident on 11 September 2012, during a search for a rogue Afghan national army soldier, Hekmatullah, who had killed three and wounded two Australian soldiers.
Roberts-Smith allegedly ordered that another soldier kill a farmer named Ali Jan during that mission.

The fourth and fifth charges against Roberts-Smith allege he was complicit in the murder of two prisoners who were marched to the edge of a cornfield under the control of Australian soldiers during a mission in the village of Syahchow in October 2012.
The prisoners were allegedly shot dead, either by Roberts-Smith or at his direction.
In June, he successfully applied to vary his bail so he could attend the opening of the Anzac Hall at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra. He attended the opening on Sunday.

articles.title: Future of western security is at stake in Yemen civil war, says country’s former PM
articles.summary:
Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills…

blocks.text: The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
Appealing for more western help, Saeed said he had no doubt that the Houthis intended to seize control of all of Yemen, and claimed their goal was “to help Iran to expand the chaos”.

blocks.caption: Houthis ride in a funeral procession for their fellow fighters in Sana’a, Yemen, in September. Photograph: Yahya Arhab/EPA

blocks.text: Saeed admitted the lack of coordination among government-backed troops, competition between Gulf states and a slowness to appreciate the implications of Yemen acquiring long-range drone technology had contributed to the pressure facing his government, and its chief backer Saudi Arabia.
“We only have light weapons and Saudi Arabia did not plan at an early stage for this escalation, but it is never too late to regain our position,” he said.
Saeed called on the west to think through the implications of allowing the Houthis to take control of Yemen, arguing the country would never be secure with Houthis on the land.
Saeed is not only an adviser to the Yemeni president, Rashad al-Alimi, he was prime minister between 2018 and 2024 and a former negotiator with the Houthis.

He said: “The battle around Taiz is not just a battle for Taiz, but a broader battle that involves the whole of the western world, and one of the most important maritime straits. The Houthis know controlling Taiz is controlling the straits and it’s the highlands before the straits and the coastal city of Mocha and the Gulf of Aden. If Taiz is lost, access to the strait will be lost. The rest of the country will come later. The Houthi plan is to control the whole of Yemen.”

Taiz has become the new frontline in the war between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces after the Houthis launched a military campaign last month to take Yemen’s Red Sea coast, ending four years of relative calm in Yemen after a UN-brokered ceasefire froze the frontlines in 2022.

He said existing intelligence showed the Houthis were already seeking to control parts of the south, including the former Soviet camp at al-Sabiha, in the Lahij governorate, and eventually Aden. “The Houthis bleed a lot,” he said, “they suffer a lot, but they always want quickly to use their gains or any collapse to gain more land.”

With some Houthi leaders offering safe passage to armed groups to leave the city, he said for now the Houthis were allowing some fuel and commodities into the urban area of Taiz which houses more than 500,000 people, but in the meantime they were expanding their control of rural areas and smaller major cities.

Saeed said: “In a matter of days there will be a full siege and they will try to enter the city. I know the Houthis. They will show some flexibility until they are ready to control. It will be much worse than the siege of 2015. It will be catastrophic.”

He described Taiz as a modern democratic city untied to tribal culture, and predicted the Houthis would try to impose their Zaydi education, financial and tax systems very quickly, but the citizens would continue to resist. “The loss of Taiz would have a very significant symbolic impact on the idea of the modern state in Yemen and of resisting the Houthi project which relies on tribal networks and extremist religious education.”

blocks.caption: Displaced Yemeni families from al-Kadha, west of Taiz, at al-Akdaf refugee camp toward the end of last month. Photograph: Abdulnasser Alseddik/AP

blocks.text: Saeed admitted Taiz only had light weapons and the government had not been prepared for the loss of the west coast, allowing the Houthis to attack Taiz from four different axes.

“We have good troops,” he said, “but the problem is the coordination. We needed more communication between the National Shield Forces, National Resistance Forces and the Giants Brigades. It’s been a wake-up call inside the government and the army because not enough happened between the truce of 2022 and the restart of the fighting this year to reorganise the troops. The Houthi ideology solely is to fight.”

He added: “I hope now that the knife has come to our neck, and the Houthis represent a critical threat, the priority would be to come together to defeat the Houthis, and then to discuss other demands and guarantees.”

The exiled leader of the southern secessionist force, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, on Tuesday called for a mobilisation of southern troops against the Houthis, but coupled this with a demand for a referendum on secession within two years. He brought tens of thousands on to the streets in support on Wednesday, but his return would be a bitter pill for Riyadh to swallow.
Saeed said it was not a coincidence that the Houthi attack along the Red Sea coast in September had come when Iran was under heavy pressure.

“Its airplanes and airports cannot operate, 90% of the oil was coming out of Hormuz. That is why they attacked the Saudi east-to-west pipelines. The Houthis, by talking about a Saudi blockade, have found a reason to hit the Saudi oil installations, airports and they want to do it now because the only thing Iran can do is to keep expanding the consequences of the war for America.”

He said Houthi military capability and negotiating power had been transformed over the last decade leading to its ability to target key sites in Saudi Arabia now. “In 2017, the Houthis had nothing but blind missiles to fire at us that missed their targets.” By 2020, he said intelligence existed that Iranian experts operating from the Houthi capital Sana’a were training Houthis and in December of that year, in a devastatingly effective attack, they fired ballistic missiles at Aden airport. The attack left 28 dead and 107 injured, including Saeed himself, newly installed as prime minister. The missile travelled 186 miles (299km).

He explained: “We thought even then they did not have that many missiles, but since then the Iranians have expanded their manufacturing lines.” In January 2022, using missiles, the Houthis attacked Abu Dhabi oil tanker trucks more than 900 miles away.

In October 2022, inside Yemen, they struck the Nushayma oil terminal and al-Dhabba port, severely damaging government finances. By the time the US attacked Yemen in March 2025, he said “it was clear the Houthis had dozens of targeted missiles, land sea missiles and drones. They had become a unified front with Iran, and developed their missile base.”

He warned: “This is a new era of radical terrorism. It is not the old chaotic one of Isis and al-Qaida. It is semi-state actors and militias threatening powerful states with cheap technologies, and smuggled third-party components. The way Iran has invested in the Houthis could become a model for threatening navigation elsewhere. It is a new model of war, without traditional armies, needing different air defences. Gulf countries have to reshape and rethink their defences”.

articles.title: Marcos: Chinese ambassador's force remark ‘sounds very much like a threat’
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Friday, October 16, that Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan’s remark about China’s ability to use force “sounds very much like a threat and not a…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 10:33am

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said on Friday, October 16, that Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan’s remark about China’s ability to use force “sounds very much like a threat and not a diplomatic statement to be made.”

Marcos told reporters the government would like to understand “what it is exactly he means.” Asked if he would summon the envoy, the president said: “It deserves a discussion between the ambassador and myself.”

The president weighed in after the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), late Thursday, October 15, rebuked Jing for a “poor choice of words” that it said seemed to convey “a thinly veiled threat of the use of force.” The department asked diplomats in Manila to watch their language.

“The business of diplomacy requires tact and restraint in order to create space necessary for discourse, dialogue and engagement, regardless of the disparity in positions or perspectives,” the DFA said in a statement released late Thursday, October 15. It called the remark “hardly helpful” given the “complicated bilateral ties” between the two countries.
Such language risks further eroding “mutual trust and confidence," the DFA added.
Jing uttered the remarks in question to reporters on Thursday on the sidelines of the second Diliman Dialogues, organized by the Philippines-China Studies Center of Diliman College in Quezon City.
Rejecting the "troublemaker" tag for China, Jing said: "If we want to use force, we may easily win. But no, we will not use force. You know, we love peace."

“Who is the troublemaker?” the Chinese diplomat asked. He cited efforts to “go after” Chinese teachers, the use of the army to arrest “innocent” Chinese workers, and daily “smear” attacks that he said were meant to incite hatred between the two countries. He said the Philippines “should feel fortunate” to have a neighbor like China in the region.
The exchange is the latest public clash between the Philippines and the Chinese Embassy since Jing arrived in Manila in December 2025.

In January, the department made firm representations to Jing over the embassy’s increasingly combative social media posts targeting senators. Since then, there has not been a let-up in the tone and frequency of the embassy's public criticisms of Philippine officials expressing disagreement with Beijing's stance on the 2016 arbitral ruling and Manila's sea rights, among others.
'Selective quotation'
The embassy on Friday morning publicly responded to the DFA and argued its ambassador was the subject of "selective quotation." It said the DFA's admonishment was "regrettable."

“This kind of selective quotation and overinterpretation demonstrates that there is still a long way to go in fostering effective communication and dialogue between China and the Philippines,” the embassy said in a statement.

The embassy said relations were at “an extremely sensitive stage” and that “certain individuals,” whom it did not name, were trying to undermine exchanges between the two countries. It urged the DFA to “play a more responsible role” in preventing such actions.
Jing’s remarks on teachers appeared to refer to the recent withdrawal of about 150 Chinese volunteer teachers from Chinese-language schools.

The Federation of Filipino Chinese Chambers of Commerce and Industry Inc. said the teachers were recalled at their parents’ request, with the approval of the federation and the embassy, after reports by Ray Powell of the monitoring group SeaLight raised suspicions about Chinese-language schools in the country.

The Chinese ambassador did not specify which worker arrests he meant, but Philippine authorities have detained hundreds of Chinese workers this year in raids targeting suspected human trafficking and illegal online gambling. The embassy has singled out a May raid on a steel plant in Misamis Oriental, insisting the Chinese workers held there had valid permits and blaming Teodoro for sending in the military to join the arrest.

Jing himself has warned that Manila faces a greater risk of confrontation unless direct military-to-military communication with Beijing, suspended by Teodoro, is restored. On October 12, the embassy accused Teodoro of shutting down those channels for “political self interests.”

The Armed Forces of the Philippines has backed Teodoro's action, saying this "direct communications has been used as a smokescreen by the Chinese Communist Party to perpetuate their illegal presence, coercive and aggressive actions and deceptive messaging not only on our maritime domain but even on land."

articles.title: 3 children, 1 teacher dead after shooting at Oregon elementary school, police say

articles.title: 'Vote like Canada depends on it,' Carney says at Calgary rally ahead of Alberta referendum

image.caption: Supporters cheer as Carney makes his speech. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

items: October 16Carney calls Alberta the 'heart' of nation-building energy projectsSupporters cheer as Carney makes his speech. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)We're wrapping up our live coverage of the rally. All five speakers at the podium tonight spoke about the importance of Canadian newcomers and their contributions to the country.Throughout his speech, Prime Minister Mark Carney emphasized the necessity of a united Canada, and the contributions Alberta has made to the nation throughout its history.He also highlighted Alberta's place as "the heart" of nation-building energy projects, and its key role in helping the country reduce its dependence on the U.S. as a trading partner. Carney will make a campaign stop with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on Friday morning at a brewery in Red Deer, before heading to Edmonton for another Forever Canadian rally.Other rallies on both sides of the separation debate are planned throughout the weekend, as Albertans prepare to head to the polls on Monday.Catch up on all of our referendum coverage here, and find out how to follow our live reporting on referendum night here.

'We came here to be Canadian'Alex BoydNick and Trish Tannahill became emotional listening to the pro-immigration comments at the Forever Canadian rally. (Alex Boyd/CBC)As the crowd filed out after Carney's speech, Nick and Trish Tannahill remained seated in front of Lukaszuk's RV, which had been parked beside the stage. The couple moved to Canada in the 1970s to escape apartheid South Africa.As an immigrant, Trish said she'd been brought almost to tears a few times when the speakers mentioned welcoming newcomers. "We came here to be Canadian," she said. The couple had come tonight because they wanted to do their part to show support for the country. "We wanted to make sure that there was a big crowd that the rest of the country would see," Nick said.

No 'No to the Nine'Jason MarkusoffCarney's speech didn't touch on the other nine referendum questions, after making a splash with his "No to the Nine" message in media interviews and a public event earlier Thursday. If he said it, it may have landed well with this partisan crowd, but created tension with Premier Danielle Smith, who’s been pushing for those ballot measures to prevail and strengthen her hand in federal wrangles.The prime minister will appear with the premier Friday morning at an event in Red Deer.

Moderate cheers for Pacific Link — big cheers for less U.S. dependenceJason MarkusoffCarney says Calgary at the heart of building CanadaPrime Minister Mark Carney spoke to all the funding coming through the Major Projects Office in Calgary, and how it will allow Canada to become less reliant on the Unites States.The crowd cheered moderately when Carney said he was building the Pacific Link pipeline. And a bit more when he said it would create 140,000 jobs.But they absolutely roared when the prime minister said the pipeline would reduce dependence on the United States. "Careful: they might think that’s election interference," Carney quipped, a nod to a recent warning from U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra about Canadian rhetoric verging on politicking during the U.S. midterms.

Kelsea ArnettSharing his own experiences growing up in Alberta, Carney said he identifies with many of the frustrations some have voiced over the province's energy relationship with Ottawa."Growing up, I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren't our own," he said.The Pacific Link pipeline — designated earlier this month as a project of national interest — is a "nation-building" project, he said, with Alberta "at the heart of it."

Bradley van ParidonCarney speaks about the First Nations that are part of Alberta and the signing of Treaty 7. CBC News has heard from Indigenous people in Alberta, with many saying the looming threat of separation has them feeling under attack.Carney acknowledged this, saying the promises between Canada and Indigenous people have "been broken many times.""Because when something is not right, when it isn't fair, we don't hide from it, we don't walk away from it, we fix it. We fix it together and [we are] stronger for it. That is Alberta. That is Canada."

Medical emergency interrupts speechAlex BoydThere appears to be a medical emergency in the crowd, and Carney pauses his remarks as police officers wade in.The crowd starts chanting Carney's name, which he pretends to hear as "Canada" and redirects them. Someone yells a question about Nico. Carney says he's home alone and has put on weight. Then clarifies that Nico is his cat. He then says that the person has received assistance and gets back to speech-ing.

'Our country and your futures are too precious to play games'Alex BoydCarney takes the stage at the Forever Canadian rally. (Todd Korol/Reuters)Big smiles, waving flags and cellphones held high for photos as Carney takes the stage. The crowd is on their feet, many draped in flags. This has been a jovial crowd so far, but there are loud boos when he mentions those outside our borders who would "break" us.He directly addresses those who would vote to go ahead with a referendum to send a message to Ottawa, something we've all come to know as soft separatism. "This is not poker," he says. "Our country and your futures are too precious to play games."

'A dangerous bluff': CarneyKelsea ArnettCarney is now delivering his speech, making a strong personal appeal for a united Canada, saying the referendum isn't a game of poker."A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and for Canadians," the prime minister says to cheers from the crowd.

Pro-immigration message a focus of evening's speakersJason MarkusoffThe crowd watches as Carney takes the stage. (Rukhsar Ali/CBC)All four people at the podium so far have spoken about the importance of Canadian newcomers and their contributions. They also spoke of their own family's immigration stories, or in Lukaszuk's case, his own. Part of that is playing to Canada's self-image as a mosaic that's welcoming to immigrants. The other part is a subtle message on the referendum's five immigration questions. It's worth noting, though, that only Mayor Jeromy Farkas gave a shoutout to voting "No to the Nine" other questions on Alberta's ballots

articles.title: Tip-off foiled US teen suspect's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
articles.summary: The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police.

blocks.text: A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say.
Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon.
Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said.
Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people.
Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis.
"These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief.
According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis.
Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime.
The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother.
According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast".
Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago.
He is thought to have acted alone.
The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour.
Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack.
In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS.
Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative.
The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures.
India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US".
US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident.
In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday.
The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US.
