articles.title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
articles.summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.

blocks.text: The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe.

Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs.
For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets.
This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France.
Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement.
France's prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election.
The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history.
Jérôme Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations.
The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video.
"Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added.
So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy?

Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt.
Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of?
"You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me.
She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt.

"The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary."

"Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates.
"The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself."
"Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes.
Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected.
But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further.
France's national motto is liberté, égalité, fraternité (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts.
I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest.

They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs.
"France likes to speak of égalité," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit."
None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway.
The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities.
They are part of a defiant French tradition.

Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les Misérables, also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: "Si vous n'êtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas."
("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.")
Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity."
Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response.
Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in.

This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand.
France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations.

Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said.
At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity.
"My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now."

Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the ­biggest general strike in French ­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left.

Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon, is weaponising student frustration.

"Members of [Mélenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence.
"This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu.
But "Mélenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets.

Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me.
For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's €11bn contribution to the EU's budget.
There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances.

France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Persian Gulf.

Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services.
In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide.

Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck.
But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine.
"We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me.
"Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws."
For France to progress, she says, that has to change.

The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours."
In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me.

"Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity."
Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier.
She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology.
Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard".

"Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately."

I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country."

"My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris."
"That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics."
It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year.
But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply.

articles.title: Lawyer urges Supreme Court to clarify ruling on senior discounts, promos
articles.summary: In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 7:00am
The logo of the Supreme Court at the Supreme Court Building in Manila.
Philstar.com / Ian Laqui

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court should issue a clear elaboration on its ruling barring the application of a senior citizen discount after other promotional discounts have been applied, a senior citizen advocate said.

In a statement on Thursday, October 15, senior citizen advocate and lawyer Romulo Macalintal warned that the decision could be exploited by business establishments to evade granting senior citizen discounts.

According to the Supreme Court’s ruling released in a press briefer on October 14, senior citizens cannot stack their statutory 20% discount on top of existing promotional prices, reinforcing that elderly consumers must choose between the promotional price and the statutory 20% discount, whichever yields greater savings.

While the ruling acquitted a hotel executive in Bacolod City after finding that the guests had already received a 20% discount through a pre-negotiated group rate, Macalintal emphasized that the public briefer lacks critical legal distinctions.
Macalintal pointed out that the denial of the discount in the Bacolod hotel case stemmed specifically from a pre-negotiated group association rate rather than a standard commercial sales promotion.

Without explicit clarification from the justices, he warned that commercial establishments might improperly label regular transactions or self-run "house promos" as promotional offers to deny elderly customers their rightful 20% discount.

“This clarification is very crucial and imperative because establishments may have the impression that they can just conduct promos on their own or run house promos to deny a senior citizen their 20% discount,” Macalintal’s statement read.

“This distinction is vital. Without it, establishments might falsely label regular transactions as ‘promos’ to evade granting senior discounts, entirely defeating the protective intent of the law,” he added.

Addressing the legal mechanism behind promotional pricing, Macalintal stressed that under Article 116 of Republic Act No. 7394, or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, any company intending to conduct a promotional campaign must first secure a permit from the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) before launching the offer.

According to Macalintal, an establishment cannot legally invoke the non-concurrence or "double-discount" rule unless the promotion has prior approval from the DTI and is set for a specified timeframe.
“Clearly, an establishment conducting a promo without a DTI permit is still obligated to extend to a senior citizen the 20% discount over and above the unauthorized promo price,” Macalintal said.
Macalintal also pointed out that the prohibition against double-discounting does not strip senior citizens of their statutory value-added tax exemption.

He also urged the high court to clarify in its full written decision that senior citizens utilizing hotel services remain entitled to their 12% VAT exemption alongside their applicable price reduction.

articles.title: How the $90M Lotto Max jackpot stacks up against other big Canadian lottery prizes
articles.summary: Friday's $90-million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada. We break down your odds of winning and how this jackpot compares to past prizes.

image.caption: A clerk at a gas station near Newcastle, Ont., hands a customer their Lotto Max ticket in October 2022. Thinking of getting in on the $90-million jackpot currently up for grabs in the Lotto Max? We break down your odds of winning Canada's largest lottery prize to date and compare it to past wins. (D

blocks.text: Canada·New
Friday's $90-million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada. We break down your odds of winning and how this jackpot compares to past prizes.
Friday's jackpot will be the largest prize in Canadian lottery history
Friday's $90 million Lotto Max draw will be the largest lottery jackpot prize ever available to win in Canada — may the odds be ever in your favour.
(Even though, statistically, they're very much not.)
Draws take place every Tuesday and Friday at 10:30 p.m. ET. Tuesday's previously record-setting $85-million jackpot rolled over after no one claimed it, which allowed the prize pool to keep growing.
Lotto Max, a national lottery, announced in April that it was increasing its jackpot cap from $80 million to $90 million, but this is the first time it's actually happened.
So, what are the odds of winning? And how does this compare to past jackpots?
Let's break it down.
Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by two friends in London, Ont., last December. At the time, the men said they were still overcome with shock that they'd won. (OLG)
What are the odds of winning?
Don't quit your job in anticipation just yet.

The odds of winning the main jackpot are one in 33 million per $6 play, according to the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Corporation (OLG), the Crown agency that manages and conducts gaming and lottery operations across the province.
Let's put that into perspective.

You're almost exactly as likely to flip a coin 25 times in a row and have it land on "heads" each time — an extremely rare probability of one in 33.5 million, according to the scientifically developed coin flip probability calculator.
Meanwhile, the odds of being struck by lightning in Canada are less than one in a million, according to the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety.
And we're sorry to say that you're actually far more likely to be killed by an asteroid's impact on Earth on your way to buy the ticket than you are of winning the $90-million jackpot.
How does the $90M compare?
However, despite these odds, people do win the lottery. And the prizes keep growing.

Previously, Canada's biggest lottery prize was $80.4 million, won by a pair of long-time friends in London, Ont., last December. They won the $80-million Lotto Max jackpot and the $403,285.40 second prize in the combination play option.
At the time, the men, identified only as Greg S. and Krys P., said they weren't sure how they would spend the money.

Before that, the top prize was claimed by a B.C. man who won the $80 million Lotto Max jackpot in May 2025. Justin Simporios of Surrey quit his job hours before the news conference where he claimed his cheque.

items: Pair of longtime friends in London, Ont., win over $80.4M in largest-ever lottery payout in Canada
Who won the lottery? Why you may never know the full name of some jackpot winners going forward

blocks.text: Lotto Max's first $80-million draw in September 2024, was split between two winning tickets sold in Ontario and Quebec. The first $70-million prize was in 2020, and the first $65-million draw was in 2019. (It was actually the second time the $65-million winner, a family in Montreal, had won the lottery).

The first Lotto Max draw for $60 million was in 2015, after the lottery changed the rules previously capping the jackpot at $50 million. Two years before that, however, a record-breaking $63.4 million Lotto 649 prize was split between four tickets.

Some may also recall 2005, when 17 oil and gas workers from Alberta split Canada's biggest jackpot to date, a whopping $54 million. Before that, the previous lottery record was $37.8 million, split between four tickets in a Super 7 draw in 2002.
Canada's first national lottery dates back to 1974, when nine women from Quebec City split the $1-million prize in a lottery held to raise money for the Montreal Olympics.

blocks.text: Calgary·Breaking
Police responded to a fire involving a City of Calgary bus early Thursday afternoon in the Saddle Ridge neighbourhood.
Fire involving city transit bus occurred Thursday afternoon in Saddle Ridge neighbourhood
Police are responding to a fatal fire involving a bus in Calgary’s northeast Saddle Ridge neighbourhood.

Police are reporting at least 10 people were injured as a result of the incident involving a City of Calgary bus. Three people have been declared dead. One person has sustained life-altering injuries and one person suffered serious injuries, according to police.
The fire occurred just after 1 p.m. on Thursday on the 800 block of Saddletowne Circle, near the neighbourhood’s fire station.
At an unrelated news conference Thursday afternoon, Calgary Transit director Sharon Fleming confirmed the collision involved two buses.
Access to Saddletowne Circle is closed for “a significant amount of time,” police said, advising people to avoid the area.
A Calgary Police Service member also sustained minor injuries.
More to come.

articles.title: Hilary Swank, 52, reacts to criticism after announcing pregnancy with third child
articles.summary: After actress Hilary Swank, 52, announced she's pregnant with her third child, she posted a clip defending later-in-life mothers by pointing out that men don't receive the same scrutiny. People…

image.caption: Hilary Swank, 52, is pregnant with her third child. In an appearance on an upcoming episode of The Drew Barrymore Show, she defended later-in-life mothers, pointing out men don't receive the same scrutiny. (Charles Sykes/Invision/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Entertainment·Updated

After actress Hilary Swank, 52, announced she's pregnant with her third child, she posted a clip defending later-in-life mothers by pointing out that men don't receive the same scrutiny. People choosing to have children later in life is part of a growing trend in Canada and the U.S., but there are some risks, one expert says.
Star's later-in-life pregnancy reflects a wider trend in Canada and the U.S.
Hilary Swank may be 52, but it's not slowing down her family — the Yellowjackets star has announced she's pregnant with her third child.

And she's hitting back against detractors, pointing out in a clip from The Drew Barrymore Show shared on her Instagram stories Thursday night that men often become fathers in later stages of life without a microscope being put on them.
"There's a lot of backlash women get for having children older," Swank said in the clip, a preview for an upcoming Oct. 20 episode of the talk show. "But not men, which is interesting."
The two-time Oscar winner is already mom to two children with her husband, Philip Schneider. After freezing her eggs at age 37, she welcomed twins Aya and Ohm in 2023 when she was 48.

Swank dropped the news on Wednesday with a light-hearted Instagram video showing her family dancing in a dark room with glow sticks on their bodies to make them look like stick figures. In the video, Swank turns around to reveal a tiny glow-stick-figure in a circle on her belly.

"A lot of people have been asking what project I'm doing next," she wrote in the caption. "This one releases in December," she added, with an emoji of a baby angel, suggesting this is when the baby is due.

Swank told Barrymore in the clip shared Thursday that one criticism she'd heard of older parents is that they may die when their children are still relatively young, recounting the story of a woman who said she lost her father, her favourite person, when she was in her 20s.
But Swank, who said she was also close with her father, pointed out that this only highlights how special having that parent-child relationship is.
"I would rather be born and have that person, that was my favourite person, and experience that, than not at all," she said.

items: After years of calls for data, study confirms Black Canadians face higher risk of maternal complications
How to support someone through pregnancy or infant loss

blocks.text: Swank has previously spoken about how happy she is to have waited to have children, telling Women's Health in 2025 that she feels she's a different parent than she would've been even in her early 40s.

"I'm much more patient. I'm much more understanding," she said. "And I have my career that's already established, so I'm not divided. I'm able to really sink in and be present with them and be a hands-on parent."

The American actress won her first Oscar at 25 years old with her starring role in the 2000 film Boys Don't Cry, following it up with a second best actress Oscar for the 2004 film Million Dollar Baby. Most recently, she appeared in the Netflix series Away and Showtime's Yellowjackets.
Hilary Swank has announced she's expecting her third child, with the 52-year-old hinting on Instagram that the due date is in December. (Charles Sykes/Invision/The Associated Press)
She's also spent the past few years lobbying the California government to pass bills requiring manufacturers to disclose ingredients in diapers and in prenatal vitamins.

Swank isn't the first celebrity to welcome kids in her 50s. Pop icon Janet Jackson and supermodel Naomi Campbell both had children at age 50, in 2017 and 2021 respectively, with Campbell welcoming a second child at age 53. Brigitte Nielsen, of Beverly Hills Cop II fame, gave birth to her fifth child and only daughter in 2018 at the age of 54.
Late pregnancies a growing trend
Advanced maternal age pregnancies — defined as occurring past the age of 35 — are becoming more common in North America.

In 2021, a quarter of mothers were 35 or older when they gave birth, compared with just 16 per cent 20 years earlier, according to Statistics Canada. In the U.S., federal data shows 21 per cent of births in 2023 were to those aged 35 or older, up from nine per cent in 1990.

Those who can get pregnant are born with a set number of eggs, which drop in number and quality as we age. This drop gets "more dramatic after your mid-to-late 30s," said Dr. Prati Sharma, a reproductive endocrinologist in Toronto, and the past president of the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society.

items: 6 moments from the untold history of childbirth
Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?

blocks.text: Natural pregnancy is possible at any time before menopause, but as eggs reduce, the odds get steeper.
Anne Hathaway, 43, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child, telling Access Hollywood in July she was "overjoyed" that it had happened.
"When you get to a certain age, that hope looks like it's about one per cent to two per cent," she said. "It's a blessing that we do not take for granted."
Anne Hathaway, 43, seen on the red carpet last month in New York City, announced in June that she was pregnant with her third child. (Evan Agostini/Invision/The Associated Press)

The vast majority of pregnancies as late-in-life as Swank's are possible through modern technology such as egg-freezing, implanting donor eggs and in vitro fertilization (IVF), which can cost tens of thousands of dollars.
"If you freeze your eggs or embryos at a younger age … you can use those later on in life because the uterus does not age at the same rate that ovaries do," Sharma said.
"The uterus can carry a pregnancy even upwards of 60-plus years old."

items: $100K and epic drives: The harsh reality of IVF access in Canada

blocks.text: Egg-freezing allows families to press pause by extracting and preserving eggs from the ovaries at a younger age. The eggs can be stored at fertility clinics for decades, if desired, before being reimplanted when a person decides they're ready to try to conceive a child.
Swank and husband Philip Schneider attend the 80th Annual Golden Globe Awards in Beverly Hills, Calif., in 2023, prior to the birth of their twins. (Mario Anzuoni/Reuters)

But while developments in medical care have made pregnancy and birth safer over the years, medical experts caution that the risk of complications with pregnancy still increases at an advanced maternal age.

"Yes, science can make it possible for a woman to have a child at 52. That being said, it's not without risk," Sharma said. "The fertility clinic and the doctor has to assess each patient, make sure that they're safe enough to get pregnant."

And although egg-freezing is growing in popularity in Canada, providing more options for when to start a family, the procedures averaged $12,000 to $15,000 in 2024 — not quite accessible for every Canadian.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Houthi missiles strike Saudi-led coalition forces HQ at presidential palace in Aden
articles.summary:
Witnesses report at least six explosions near palace used by Yemen's internationally recognized government

At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by

blocks.text: At least six explosions struck on Thursday near the palace used by Yemen’s internationally recognized government in the port city of Aden, witnesses said.

An official told the Associated Press that at least two people were killed, and Iran-backed Houthi rebels based in northern Yemen quickly claimed responsibility. Government military sources in Yemen told Agence-France Press (AFP) that at least four people were killed and 10 wounded.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that the Yemeni prime minister, Shaya al-Zindani, had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way”.

It was a rare attack on the palace area, as fighting has escalated between the rebels and a Saudi-led coalition on the latest front in the Iran war. The explosions caused panic among residents, who fled the area.

At least two people were killed and six wounded, said the official, who spoke to the Associated Press on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the press. The government said the Houthis attacked with missiles and drones, the Aden-based Saba news agency reported.
A security official told the AP that at least two explosions were on top of the hill near Al-Maashiq palace, and two others were near the security gate.

AFP also reported that a Yemeni government minister said on condition of anonymity on Thursday that a Houthi missile attack on the presidential palace in Aden had hit a command center for the Saudi-led coalition. The official added that the command center was hit by three missiles, and the headquarters of the coalition forces at the presidential complex with two missiles, adding that there were Yemeni and Saudi casualties, without providing a specific toll.

There was no immediate confirmation of the report that the prime minister was in the presidential palace at the time of Houthi attack. Many of Yemen’s government leaders are living in exile, and those in Aden were safe, a government official told the AP.

The Houthis said they attacked a military operations headquarters with the “Saudi enemy”, part of their strategy of attacking Saudi targets that has included a series of attacks on airports and oil infrastructure inside the kingdom.

The escalation has complicated efforts to end the wider Iran war and further rattled global markets as Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s top oil exporters, faces repeated attacks. Regional aviation is affected, too, as the rebels have warned airlines about their use of Saudi airspace for attacks. Thousands of flights across the kingdom have been disrupted.

Earlier on Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it intercepted a cruise missile over the province of Medina. Flightradar24, a tracking platform, said dozens of flights were canceled or delayed at Jeddah’s airport.

The coalition statement did not assign blame for the attack. The Houthis’ military spokesperson, Brig Gen Yahya Saree, denied the rebels carried it out. The group previously pledged not to attack airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia also said it destroyed a drone over the country’s eastern province, a major oil-producing region, and intercepted a drone in Khamis Mushait, near a major military airbase.
Earlier this week, Saudi Arabia said the headquarters of the oil giant Saudi Aramco were hit by Houthi attacks, and reported damage to the building.

Inside Yemen, the fighting has revived a devastating civil war after four years of relative calm. One focus of alarm is the Houthi-besieged city of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where residents were running short of basic necessities.

articles.title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US election offices
articles.summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.

blocks.text: Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US.
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received.
Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters.
Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail.
"This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday.
The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder.
The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances.
Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it.
Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, was also sent a letter containing a suspicious substance, but it was intercepted before reaching the office, his spokesman said.
The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC.
The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress.
Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages.
A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states.

articles.title: Danielle Smith has said no to a second referendum. But that decision might not be hers to make

image.caption: Mitch Sylvestre, separatist leader and a UCP constituency association president, delivers the StayFree Alberta petitions to Election Alberta in May 2026 alongside lawyer Jeff Rath, standing to his right. A First Nations court challenge tossed the petitions into legal limbo. (Alice Burgat/Radio-Canad

blocks.text: Calgary
The premier's pledge raises questions about the fate of the original citizen’s initiative petition — still mired in litigation — that called for the vote in the first place.
Should an appeal of the original separation petition win, it could still move ahead
Premier Danielle Smith has drawn a line in the sand, saying that she will not hold another referendum on Alberta separation should the majority of her province vote to remain in Canada.

But her statement raises questions about the fate of the original citizen’s initiative petition that called for a vote on separation — one of the first falling dominos to put Alberta on the referendum path — that remains stalled before the courts.

Should an appeal by the Alberta government and a separatist group be granted, that petition could again move forward, potentially reviving the referendum conversation, legal experts say, whether Smith wishes it to be or not.

"When it comes to the prospect of a government referendum (on holding another referendum) and a citizen’s initiative coexisting in the world, “nothing like this has happened before,” says Kathleen Mahoney, professor emerita of the faculty of law at the University of Calgary.

items: Carney says Albertans should vote ‘No to the Nine’ in referendum

blocks.text: “We're in uncharted waters,” added Gerard Kennedy, a constitutional law professor at the University of Alberta.

The potential quagmire dates back to January, when separatist group Stay Free Alberta began gathering signatures for its petition, which wanted an unabashedly-separatist question put to the province in a constitutional referendum. The petition asked: “Do you agree that the province of Alberta should cease to be a part of Canada to become an independent state?”

But that effort was quashed by a judge who found the group had failed to consult with First Nations, a decision sharply criticized by Smith. She would ultimately announce the government would pose a referendum question of its own on the province’s relationship with Canada, on which Albertans will vote next week.

items: Cross Country Checkup is asking: What’s at stake for you in the Alberta referendum? What conversations are you having with friends and family? What questions do you have? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

blocks.text: Both Stay Free Alberta and the provincial government appealed the court decision that put the first petition on hold. In June, Court of Appeal Justice Alice Woolley granted a partial stay, which allowed the signatures to be counted while the appeal continued.

In July, Elections Alberta confirmed that the first petition met the bar for a successful petition, having amassed roughly 220,000 verified signatures. But it’s not clear when a final decision is expected on the appeal.

items: Who else besides Danielle Smith is saying 'yes to the nine' in Alberta's referendum?

blocks.text: If it is ultimately allowed to proceed, “the government could find itself legally required to deal with it,” Mahoney said.
“Whether that obligation would actually force a second referendum, and how quickly, remains an open legal question.”

In an email, a spokesperson for Elections Alberta said that the government has the ability to make the final decision on most citizen’s initiatives. But the exception is proposals for constitutional referendums, such as the petition from Stay Free Alberta.
The legislation says that, should the proposal be successful, the minister “shall refer [it] to the Lieutenant Governor in Council for the purpose of a constitutional referendum.”

But even if that happened, many wild cards remain. There are still unresolved questions about when Alberta would be required to consult with Indigenous people on a proposed referendum that could affect treaty rights, Mahoney said.

The government has made recent changes to the legislation, including removing rules against having two referendums on the same topic and requiring a referendum to be held within a certain time period after a successful petition.
That means the government would have a lot of control over the timing and form of such a referendum, Kennedy says. There are also restrictions on proximity to an election, he added.
A government spokesperson declined comment, referring CBC News to the premier’s previous comments.

When asked whether his group would continue to pursue another vote even if most Albertans vote to remain next week, Jeffrey Rath, counsel for Stay Free Alberta, responded “yes” in a text, before adding four cry-laughing emojis.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alex Boyd is a senior reporter based in Calgary, interested in politics, provincial affairs and misinformation. She is a former national and investigative reporter for the Toronto Star. Reach her at alex.boyd@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: Ukraine says there has been a restriction to the speed of SpaceX's Starlink internet network in the country.
Starlink - owned by Elon Musk - plays a vital part in the war between Ukraine and Russia, allowing Kyiv to guide drones to Russian targets and also protect itself.
Elon Musk has suggested the US government may be behind the restriction on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connect to the network.

articles.title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills two, minister says
articles.summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.

blocks.text: Two security personnel have been killed in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, but that many others were injured.
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden".
A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemeni Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour".

He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines.

Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines.

The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa.
On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.
Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom.
"Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency.
"We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added.
There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically.
Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases.

articles.title: Watch: Moment drone hits supermarket in Odesa

blocks.text: CCTV video verified by the BBC shows the moment of a drone strike on a supermarket in the town of Mayaky in Ukraine's Odesa region.
The drone can be seen flying into the roof of the Tavria supermarket and exploding on impact.

articles.title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
articles.summary: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.

blocks.text: Venezuela's former leader Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture.
The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week.
Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail.
The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027.

In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured.
Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me."
"I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator.
Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro.
"I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator.
Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn.
The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states.
The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system.
Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups.
Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.
He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal.

Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.

articles.title: Police raid the major pro-opposition Halk TV channel in Turkey
articles.summary: Turkish police raided the Istanbul headquarters of an important pro-opposition television station on Wednesdazy, the day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu was set to start his defense against…

image.caption: The police raided Halk TV in the middle of a live broadcast Image: Emrah Gurel/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Wednesday morning, the live broadcast was halted, Halk TV's headquarters in the city of Istanbul were searched, and a new administrator was appointed by the government to run the media outlet. An arrest warrant was issued for the station's CEO, Cafer Mahiroglu, who currently lives in London. According to prosecutors, 11 people were arrested.

Turkey has faced criticism for years over restrictions on press freedom. Halk TV is one of the country's best-known opposition television stations and regularly broadcasts critical reports about Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Justice and Development Party (AKP). After the raid, journalists were initially prevented from entering the building. Pre-recorded programs were broadcast instead of live reports.

The timing is particularly sensitive: Halk TV was raided on the very day that jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoglu was scheduled to begin his defense against corruption charges in court. The channel has been an important source of information for those following the trial.

Imamoglu, who won the mayoral election in Istanbul in 2019 and remained in office until his arrest on March 19, 2025, is one of Erdogan's most significant rivals, considered a beacon of hope for the opposition. He is still expected to run for president in 2028.

He is accused of establishing and running a criminal organization, as well as of various related financial crimes. Prosecutors are seeking a prison term of 2,352 years related to 142 charges. Imamoglu denies the allegations, arguing that the case is politically motivated.

blocks.caption: 11 people were arrested in conjunction with the raid on Halk TV headquarters Image: ANKA

blocks.text: Raid linked to investigation into Cafer Mahiroglu
Istanbul prosecutors said that the raid on Halk TV was linked to an investigation into its CEO Mahiroglu, who is accused of bribery, bid rigging and money laundering.

They said that arrest warrants had been issued for 17 people, on top of the 11 arrests. Assets belonging to companies allegedly linked to Mahiroglu were also seized and a trustee appointed to run the firms.
The opposition responded with sharp criticism of the police raid. Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the social democratic New Party (Yeni Parti) said it was a dark day for Turkey.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," Mahiroglu said.
"Showing solidarity with Halk TV means supporting the struggle for democracy in Turkey," Ozel said.

He added that "only dictators" would launch "a dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee […]" and criticized the fact that this had occurred on the day that Imamoglu was due to begin his defense.

blocks.caption: Many people in Turkey protested in support of Ekrem Imamoglu when he was jailed in 2025, like here in Izmir on May 19, 2025Image: Berkcan Zengin/Middle East Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Journalists' union slams raid
The Journalists' Union of Turkey (TGS) also condemned the raid on the platform X, describing it as arbitrary and arguing that the press was free and should not be censored.

Editor-in-chief Suat Toktas tried in vain to persuade the new state-appointed administrator to continue live broadcasts. In a video released by the TV channel, he said that what was happening was "illegal."
Halk TV began broadcasting on January 10, 2005 and its live broadcasts gained widespread attention particularly during the 2013 Gezi Park protests. Cafer Mahiroglu took over the station in 2020.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’
articles.summary:
Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture

Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that…

blocks.text: Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.

Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
Judge Alvin K Hellerstein entered a not-guilty plea on behalf of Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores. They were seized from their Caracas home by the US military in a night-time raid in January.

Hellerstein announced that he was entering the plea on behalf of Maduro after Maduro twice responded to the judge’s request to enter a plea by criticizing the indictment, saying it contained “false accusations and false testimony”. Maduro spoke through an interpreter.
Attorney Barry Pollack said when the charges were announced last week that Maduro, 63, denied them and “looks forward to his day in court”.

According to the rewritten indictment, Maduro oversaw a violent torture system that beat, asphyxiated and delivered electric shocks to its victims. He is accused of personally recommending torture methods, receiving updates on specific victims’ treatment and threatening to kill one prisoner’s child as a form of psychological torture.
Flores, 70, a former attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment alleges.
When she was asked to enter a plea, she said through an interpreter: “I am completely innocent. I am not guilty.”

Maduro, who served as Venezuela’s president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the international criminal court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied wrongdoing.
Prosecutors told the judge during the hearing that lawyers on both sides want the trial date moved from 1 June to 14 June.

Torture is a crime under international law and can be prosecuted outside the country where the abuse occurred and regardless of the victims’ nationality. But the prosecution of foreign officials in the US is exceedingly rare, having been tried only a few times, including against the son of the former Liberian president Charles Taylor, Russians responsible for war crimes in Ukraine and a former prison warden in Bashar Assad’s Syria.

Earlier this year, Maduro and his wife pleaded not guilty in the US drug case, which said they conspired to flood the US with cocaine. Their attorneys say the case should be dismissed on immunity grounds because they were the leader and first lady of a foreign country.
The revised indictment covers allegations of torture stretching back to Maduro’s ascent to power in 2013, when he took over as president from his mentor Hugo Chávez, who died of cancer that year.

articles.title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
articles.summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.

blocks.text: "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school.
The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?"

Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad.
Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people.
Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that.
President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail.
Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally.
But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni.
The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order".

Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class.
According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since.
The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed.
Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN).
Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran.
The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself.
On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites.
A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility.
Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said.
The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh.
The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states".
President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation".
His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake".
"A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X.
Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in.

Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by Köklü Değişim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group Özgür-Der.

President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.
Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life".

Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil.
Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries.

That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall.

articles.title: Poll: Inflation, corruption top concerns of Pinoys
articles.summary: More than four years into the Marcos administration, reducing the basic cost of goods remains the most urgent concern of most Filipinos, based on a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia.

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 12:00am
Results of the Sept. 17 to 24 survey released yesterday found that 71 percent of the respondents considered inflation as among the three most urgent national concerns of the respondents.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — More than four years into the Marcos administration, reducing the basic cost of goods remains the most urgent concern of most Filipinos, based on a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia.
It went up by 14 percentage points from 57 percent in a similar survey conducted in July.
Reacting to the survey results, Malacañang assured the nation efforts are being made to fight hunger.
“These interventions are continuously being undertaken by the government,” Palace press officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said at a media briefing.

“If some of our countrymen are not yet covered by the assistance of the government, we would want to know where they are located so we can assess the situation, determine what is lacking and identity the assistance we can provide,” she added.
Based on the survey, controlling inflation was ranked first by 36 percent of the respondents, the largest proportion among issues included in the poll.
It was also the issue selected by most respondents across geographic areas and socio-economic classes.
Meanwhile, 39 percent of the respondents identified graft and corruption as among their top three concern. It went down from 43 percent in July.

Other top issues included in the survey were increasing the pay of workers (36 percent), fighting criminality (24 percent), reducing poverty (21 percent), creating more jobs (18 percent), fighting the widespread sale and use of illegal drugs (18 percent) and lowering the price of gasoline (14 percent).

Selected by less than 10 percent of the respondents were issues such as providing assistance to farmers, promoting peace, addressing hunger, equal enforcement of the law, reducing taxes, responding to needs of areas affected by calamities, stopping the destruction of the environment, providing support to small businesses, defending the integrity of Philippine territory, protecting overseas workers and preparing to face any kind of terrorism.
The survey had 2,400 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus two percent.

articles.title: PCC slaps P1.76 billion fine on 2022 onion cartel
articles.summary: The Philippine Competition Commission has imposed a record fine of P1.76 billion on six firms whose activities as an onion cartel sent retail prices soaring to as high as P800 a kilo in 2022.

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 12:00am

At a press conference yesterday, PCC executive director Kenneth Tanate said the fine was imposed on the six firms and their officers for their involvement in an illegal market allocation scheme in the importation, cold storage and wholesale distribution of onions.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine Competition Commission (PCC) has imposed a record fine of P1.76 billion on six firms whose activities as an onion cartel sent retail prices soaring to as high as P800 a kilo in 2022.
The scheme allowed the firms to control nearly 50 percent of all import clearances for onions.
The PCC issued its decision on Oct.1. The firms have until today to pay the fine.
“The members of the cartel were fined a total of P1.76 billion, representing the biggest amount imposed so far by the Philippine Competition Act (PCA) on violators of the law,” he said.
As onion is classified as a prime commodity, he said the PCA mandates automatic trebling or tripling the penalty.

Fined were freight forwarder Golden Shine International Freight Forwarders Corp., cold storage operator Tian Long Corp., and onion importers La Reina Fresh Vegetables & Young Indoor Plants Inc. and Yom Trading Corp.

Also penalized were Mark Castro Ocampo as sole proprietor of Vegefru Producing Store, Nancy Callanta Rosal as sole proprietor of Rosal Fruit and Vegetable Trading, Golden Shine president Lilia Cruz, Golden Shine corporate executive officer and Tian Long corporate secretary Eric Pabilona, La Reina and Yom Trading chairman and president Renato Francisco Jr., and Golden Shine incorporator Letty Baculando.
The PCC’s decision stemmed from an investigation on surge in onion prices to as high as P800 a kilo in late 2022.

Evidence retrieved during a court-ordered dawn raid conducted in September 2023 revealed how the cartel operated. Base on investigation, Golden Shine applied for import clearances using the other importers’ credentials and assigned the same importers as consignees. Imports were routed to Tian Long’s cold storage facilities and then distributed nationwide.
Tanate said the firms may file a motion for reconsideration.
The fines were calculated using actual import clearance volumes and wholesale prices reported by the Philippine Statistics Authority as the firms understated financial performance.

“By imposing the maximum fines, the PCC underscores its commitment to holding cartels accountable across all sectors of the economy and protecting consumers from the harmful effects of anti-competitive conduct,” Tanate said.
Aside from imposing administrative penalties, the PCC may recommend a criminal case before the Department of Justice.

articles.title: China envoy urges dialogue on West Philippine Sea tensions
articles.summary: Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan has urged the Philippines to exercise caution in discussing its maritime dispute with his country, calling for face-to-face dialogues to manage tensions as officials and…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan has urged the Philippines to exercise caution in discussing its maritime dispute with his country, calling for face-to-face dialogues to manage tensions as officials and analysts pushed for stronger regional cooperation during a forum in Quezon City.

“Through communication and dialogues, we find ways to manage disputes,” Jing said at the second Diliman Dialogues hosted by Diliman College, titled “Southeast Asian Voices on China-ASEAN Relations: Pathways to Peace in the South China Sea.”

Jing acknowledged the complexity of Manila-Beijing relations, saying they could not simply be described as good or bad. He urged both sides to separate areas of disagreement from other aspects of their relationship and encouraged more exchanges.

“We should encourage the two sides to visit each other more and sit face to face,” he said, adding that the Philippines should maintain balanced relations with China, the United States and other countries.

National security experts and lawmakers at the forum also stressed the need for dialogue, but emphasized that cooperation should protect Philippine interests and support a rules-based approach to the maritime dispute.

Former national security adviser Clarita Carlos said the Philippines should pursue multilateralism without becoming beholden to any country while House special committee on the West Philippine Sea chairman Antolin Oreta III said the dispute was not only about territory but also about upholding the law.

Philippines-China Studies Center director Rommel Banlaoi said Manila should maintain diplomatic balance and pursue cooperation in areas of mutual benefit, which could help create conditions for resolving maritime disputes.

Meanwhile, Association for Philippines-China Understanding chairman Raul Lambino called for greater cooperation in technology, energy and food security, maintaining that partnerships with neighboring countries could support national development.

Diliman College president and CEO Anna Dominique Coseteng, however, cautioned against rhetoric that could deepen distrust, saying national security concerns should not fuel prejudice against Filipino-Chinese communities.
But while Beijing’s ambassador was calling for caution, the Philippine Coast Guard was driving away Chinese fishing boats from Lawak Island.
According to the PCG, four small boats were reportedly deployed by the Chinese fishing vessel Yuetaiyu 63168 when it anchored within the territorial sea of the island.
Lawak Island is a Philippine-occupied feature in the West Philippine Sea. It is part of the Kalayaan municipality in Palawan.
PCG spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela said the Chinese vessels ignored repeated radio challenges but eventually left.
Meanwhile, Tarriela slammed the Chinese ambassador’s statement that Beijing “may easily win” if it chooses to use force against the Philippines in the West Philippine Sea.
In a chance interview, Quan said the Philippines is “fortunate to have a neighbor like China” which does not use force to address the tensions in the area.
“A guest who reminds his host that he could easily beat him up, but has graciously decided not to, is not describing friendship,” Tarriela said.

At the recent South China Sea International Conference in Hanoi, Vietnam, the Philippines underscored the importance of upholding the rule of law and strengthening maritime cooperation in addressing emerging challenges to the regional maritime order.
The conference brought together over 300 participants composed of government officials, policymakers, maritime experts, academics among other stakeholders.

Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) Undersecretary Leo Herrera-Lim said unilateral actions beyond what is permitted under international law, as well as coercive conduct, have heightened risks for coastal states.
Herrera-Lim emphasized that, for the Philippines, lasting peace and prosperity at sea can rest on nothing other than the rule of law.

The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) and the final and binding 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, he said, serve as the twin anchors of Philippine maritime policy. – Pia Lee-Brago, Andrew Ronquillo

articles.title: Pulse: VP Sara ratings still higher than Marcos Jr’s
articles.summary: Even with the ongoing impeachment trial against her, Vice President Sara Duterte continues to enjoy much higher trust and approval ratings than President Marcos, a survey for the third quarter…

blocks.text: October 16, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte and President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Even with the ongoing impeachment trial against her, Vice President Sara Duterte continues to enjoy much higher trust and approval ratings than President Marcos, a survey for the third quarter conducted by Pulse Asia showed.
The survey conducted from Sept. 17 to 24 found that 29 percent of the respondents trust the President, almost similar to the 28 percent he obtained in a similar survey in July.
Those who distrusted him fell from 51 percent to 48 percent, while undecided respondents hardly changed, from 21 percent to 22 percent.
Marcos had an approval rating of 30 percent, from 29 percent, and a disapproval rating of 49 percent, from 50 percent. Undecided respondents were unchanged at 21 percent.
Unlike Marcos, Duterte retained a majority trust and approval ratings.
Those who said they trust her dropped from 58 percent to 55 percent, while those who distrust her remained at 27 percent. Undecided respondents increased from 16 percent to 19 percent.

In terms of approval, Duterte obtained a rating 54 percent, down from 56 percent. Her disapproval rating also dropped from 29 percent to 27 percent, while undecided respondents increased from 15 percent to 18 percent.
The Pulse Asia survey was conducted amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Duterte at the Senate. It had 2,400 respondents and a margin of error of plus/minus two percent.

The Office of the Vice President (OVP) gave away P5.16 million worth of medical and burial assistance in 2025 from its own budget, which is more than 99 percent lower than the P820.77 million it distributed in 2024, according to a report by the Commission on Audit (COA).

Based on the OVP’s financial statements attached to COA’s audit report, the agency was able to distribute medical and burial assistance worth P59.936 million in 2025, but this was sourced from donation in cash from the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corp. (Pagcor).
In the previous years, the OVP distributed P29.93 million cash assistance for medical and burial purposes from the same Pagcor donations.

Funding for the medical and burial assistance program of the OVP was removed in the 2025 national budget after COA flagged unexplained confidential fund expenditures involving millions in a matter of days.
Lawmakers had proposed cutting the funding for the OVP’s social welfare projects as it overlapped with programs of the Department of Health and the Department of Social Welfare and Development.
The OVP received appropriations totaling P2.448 billion in 2023, P1.898 billion in 2024, and P766.146 million in 2025. - Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows
articles.summary:
Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president

The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei,…
articles.byline: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands

blocks.text: The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.

In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region.
Milei shared Caputo’s on the social media platform X.

The intervention from Buenos Aires comes at a moment of heightened tension between Argentina and the UK over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory, which is 300 miles off the South American coastline.
Labour’s Abdi-Wali was elected as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras in London this month, seeing off a challenge from the Green party leader, Zack Polanski. She took her seat in parliament on Monday.
Milei has sought to criminalise executives involved in the Falkland Islands’ nascent oil industry and has threatened to target the fishing sector on which the islands’ economy depends.

Argentina has long sought sovereignty over the islands. The intensity of Argentinian pressure relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by the then Argentinian dictator, Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.

blocks.caption: Javier Milei shared his adviser’s post on X. Photograph: Francisco Loureiro/Reuters

blocks.text: The 74-day conflict in 1982 ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of their military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.

This week, Andy Burnham restated the UK’s position that it would respect the wish of the 3,600 islanders to remain British, and the government announced its intention to protect the interests of businesses working in the Falklands.

The Guardian revealed that the Foreign Office had written to Interpol seeking assurance that the law enforcement agency would not respond favourably to requests for the detention of individuals working in the Falklands.

In his statement on X, Caputo – who has worked for Milei since 2021 – wrote that the “United Kingdom was, in many ways, the cradle of modern western civilisation” but that it now posed a threat to the west.

He wrote: “Seeing the United Kingdom being colonised by Islam is not only an imminent risk to the cause of the west as a whole, but also a historical tragedy for those of us who defend the ideas of liberty.

“This is yet another reason why Argentina must firmly project itself toward the south Atlantic and reclaim the Las Malvinas [Argentina’s name for the Falklands]. Given the strategic geopolitical importance the south Atlantic will assume in the coming decades, the west cannot afford the encroachment of an Islamic state within that sphere of influence. Reclaiming the Malvinas is not merely a national cause, it is a cause for the west.”
Caputo accompanied his post with an image of Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia, being sworn into parliament.

Under the image, Javier Negre, a rightwing Spanish journalist, commented: “Here is a Somali Muslim woman taking her oath of office on the Qur’an in the English parliament. She has taken the seat formerly held by Prime Minister Keir Starmer. Islam is steadily gaining more power in the country.”
In a 2013 referendum, 99.8% of the Falkland Islands’ residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

articles.title: Was Neanderthal life violent? This wound suggests lethal fighting was more common
articles.summary: A 75,000-year-old Neanderthal spear wound may be evidence violence shaped human life far earlier than thought.

blocks.text: A Neanderthal who died 75,000 years ago may have been struck through the chest by a sharpened wooden spear, archaeologists say.
They say a 15mm hole found in a shoulder blade in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan could be the earliest evidence of lethal violence involving such a weapon.

From the angle of the wound and other evidence, the researchers believe the spear entered the individual's chest and passed through the body - probably damaging a lung and major blood vessels - and exited through the left shoulder blade to leave a near-perfect hole.
The research is the latest in emerging evidence that suggests Neanderthal societies experienced more violence than previously thought.

Neanderthals were a separate species of humans that went extinct around 40,000 years ago. They lived across a large expanse of Europe and western and central Asia, and sometimes overlapped with our species, Homo sapiens.
The wounded Neanderthal's remains were found in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan. As well as the left shoulder blade, the individual's right hand, three ribs and some teeth were also found.

A hole in the shoulder blade may be the earliest evidence of "lethal interpersonal violence" from a wooden spear, according to Dr Emma Pomeroy, study lead author from Cambridge's Department of Archaeology.
"The fatal strike may have been an intended heart shot," she told BBC News.
Archaeologists call the remains Shanidar A, named after the cave in which they were found. Remains of at least 10 Neanderthals were discovered in excavations in the cave in the 1950s.
The wound is thought to be the first evidence for use of sharpened wooden spears in the prehistoric Middle East, according to Pomeroy.
"It is not the kind of break that you would get naturally, because it is so circular," she said. "Experiments with reconstructed wooden spears produce very similar round holes in bone."
But the interpersonal violence is by no means certain, she says. It may be a case of friendly fire, a wound caused as a result of a hunting accident.
But Prof Chris Stringer of the Natural History Museum in London, who was not involved in the research, told BBC News that an attack by a rival was the more plausible explanation.

"The researchers leave it open whether this resulted from a hunting accident or interpersonal violence, but in my view the latter seems more likely, given the positioning and extent of the wound," he said.

This discovery has echoes of an earlier find in the same cave, in 1957. Those remains involved another Neanderthal who lived more recently, around 50, 000 years ago. Their ribs had evidence of a partly healed wound, which archaeologists believe was probably caused by a stone-tipped spear.

We can't tell for sure whether these Neanderthals were hurt by a companion during a hunt or murdered by a rival.
